en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the *Parivāra* of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Sixteenth Major Section: Explanation of the Section on Formal Rules (Paññattivāra-vaṇṇanā).
In the Dispensation, "the section" (parivāra) refers to that which surrounds the Pure [Section] (Visuddha).
Having now set aside the method already established for that which has been included in the compendium following the Khandhakas of the body of the Dhamma-aggregates,
I shall now provide an exposition of the meanings not yet explained.
1. Herein, as for the question introduced by the words "What was laid down by that Blessed One...

and so forth, this is the summary of the meaning: That Blessed One, having been requested by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) who—with great speed arising from reverence and esteem for the True Dhamma—placed his joined palms upon his head for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation, laid down the formulation of the Vinaya based on ten reasons.
By that Blessed One, knowing the time for the proclamation of each respective training rule and seeing the ten purposes for the proclamation of each training rule—
furthermore, knowing through the recollection of past lives and so forth, seeing with the divine eye,
knowing by means of the three true knowledges or the six direct knowledges, and seeing everywhere with the unimpeded universal eye—
One who knows through wisdom capable of knowing all phenomena;
one who sees with the extremely pure physical eye forms that are beyond the range of the visual faculty of all beings, even those situated behind walls and such;

one who knows through the wisdom of penetration which has concentration as its proximate cause for accomplishing one's own welfare; and one who sees through the wisdom of teaching which has compassion as its proximate cause for accomplishing the welfare of others.
“Where was that first *pārājika* offense laid down by the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One?
With reference to whom was it laid down? On account of what matter was it laid down? Is there a formal rule (*paññatti*) therein... [and so on] ...by whom was it brought forth?
2. In the answering of these questions: “That which was laid down by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One...”
The phrase "the first *pārājika*" is merely the extraction of the opening word that arrived through the inquiry.
However, by means of the method beginning with, "Where was it laid down? It was laid down at Vesālī; concerning whom?
Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka," each individual word here is again questioned and then answered. "A single laying down" (*ekā paññatti*)— [End of excerpt]
“Whatever bhikkhu should engage in sexual intercourse, he is defeated and no longer in communion”—this is one formal rule (*paññatti*).

There are two subsequent rules (*anupaññatti*): namely, “even down to an animal” and “without having renounced the training,” which were stated on account of the cases of the female monkey and the son of Vajjī respectively—these are the two subsequent rules. Up to this point, there is...

In this regard, regarding the question, "Therein, there is a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti)," two sections have been answered.
To answer the third, however, it is stated: "The rule for what has not yet arisen does not exist therein.
For this so-called *anuppannapaññatti* is a rule laid down when a fault has not yet arisen; it pertains exclusively to the bhikkhunīs by way of the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭha garudhammā*).
[They] have come; it does not exist elsewhere. Therefore it is said: "The unarisen prescription (anuppanna-paññatti) does not exist therein.
Regarding "prescriptions for all places" (sabbattha-paññatti): they are prescriptions for all places, both in the Middle Country and in the bordering provinces.

Indeed, these four—ordination, sandals with double soles, the removal of hair by blowing, and the use of leather mats—are [established] by a group consisting of five members, including one who holds the Vinaya.
The training rules (sikkhāpada) are prescribed only for the Middle Country (majjhima-deso). It is only here that an offense occurs through them, not in the bordering regions (paccantima-janapada).
All the remaining rules are called "prescribed everywhere" (sabbattha-paññatti).
"Commonly prescribed" (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) refers to those rules prescribed in common for both monks and nuns; [others] are for monks alone.
For indeed, a training rule prescribed for pure bhikkhunīs alone is called a non-common prescription (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*).
However, regarding this [rule], when the matter arose concerning a bhikkhu, it was also prescribed for bhikkhunīs:
"Whichever bhikkhunī should intentionally engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, she is defeated (*pārājika*) and no longer in communion (*asaṃvāsā*). Thus it is said.
There is no talk of their being "laid down" (*vinīta*) as such; rather, there is a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). Therefore it is said, "a common laying down" (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).
The same principle applies to a "laying down for both. For here the difference is merely in the phrasing (*byañjana*);
it is a "common laying down" because it is common to both monks and nuns, and it is so called because it was laid down for both.
"Proclaimed on both sides": there is no difference in meaning. "Submerged in the origin" (*nidānogadha*):
because all offenses are included therein in the passage, "He who has an offense should reveal it," it is "submerged in the origin";
the meaning is that they are included within the origin. By the second recitation, even that which is submerged in the origin—that is, included within the origin—is [recited].
It comes under the same summary as the second summary, beginning with: "In this regard, there are these four *pārājika* offenses.
Regarding the "four failures": these are the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and so forth.

For the first two classes of offenses are called the failure of virtue, while the remaining five are called the failure of conduct (*ācāravipatti*). Wrong view and extreme views constitute the failure of view (*diṭṭhivipatti*).
Furthermore, the six training rules prescribed for the sake of livelihood are called "failure in livelihood.
Thus, among these four types of failure, this *pārājika* offense is called "failure in virtue" (*sīlavipatti*).
"By a single origin" means by a single origin consisting of two factors; for here, the mind is the factor, [accompanied] by the body.
However, one incurs an offense. Therefore it is said: "It originates from both body and mind. It is settled by two means of settlement:

when being questioned face-to-face with the words, "Have you committed [an offense]?", and one confesses, saying, "Yes, I have committed it," at that very moment the quarrels, disputes, and strife are stilled, and it is possible to conduct the Uposatha after having removed that person.

or to perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*). Thus, it is settled by two means of settlement: by resolution in the presence of the accused (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*);
and because of this, no further trouble arises.

As for what is stated later in the *Paññattivagga*—"it is not settled by any means of settlement"—that was said with reference to the fact that one cannot effect a non-offense by applying that particular means of settlement.
*Paññatti-vinaya* means that the *mātikā* (matrices) stated in the manner beginning with "Whatever monk... is the *paññatti-vinaya*; such is the meaning.
*Vibhatti* refers to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*); for "vibhatti" is indeed another name for the *vibhaṅga*.
*Asaṃvara* is transgression (*vītikkama*). *Saṃvara* is non-transgression (*avītikkama*). "For whom it applies" refers to those for whom both the Vinaya Piṭaka and the commentary [apply].

"And all [the rules] are mastered"—this is the meaning. "They bear them in mind" means they bear this first *pārājika* in mind both according to the text (*pāḷi*) and according to the meaning (*attha*);
for it is not possible for one who does not know the entire *Vinayapiṭaka* to know the meaning of this.
"By whom was it brought?"—this first *pārājika*, by way of its text and by way of its meaning, [has been transmitted] down to the present day.
"By whom was it brought? [The answer is: "Brought down in succession. This means it was brought down by way of a lineage.
Now, in order to show the lineage by which it was brought, verses were composed by the ancient Great Elders in the manner beginning with "Upāli and Dāsaka.
Regarding what should be said therein, that has already been explained in the commentary on the Nidāna.
It has been stated. By this same method, the analysis should also be understood regarding the questions and answers concerning the second *pārājika* offense and those that follow.
The commentary on the section on the formulation of the rules (*paññattivāra*) in the *Mahāvibhaṅga* is concluded.
Now begins the commentary on the section on the commission of offenses (*katāpattivāra*).
157. Following this is the section on committed offenses (*katāpattivāra*), beginning with: "While engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?

and so forth; the section on failures (*vipattivāra*), beginning with: "Of the four failures, how many failures do the offenses incurred by one engaging in sexual intercourse fall under? and so forth; and [the section on] the offenses incurred by one engaging in sexual intercourse...
The section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*) begins with: "By how many classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) among the seven classes of offenses are [these] included?

The section on origination (*samuṭṭhānavāra*) begins with: "For one who engages in sexual intercourse, by how many of the six origins of offenses (*āpattisamuṭṭhāna*) do the offenses originate? The offenses for one engaging in sexual intercourse...

The section on legal issues (*adhikaraṇavāra*) begins with the classification: "Of the four legal issues, which one is it? The section on settling methods (*samathavāra*) begins with the classification:
"For one who commits an offense by engaging in sexual intercourse, by how many of the seven settling methods is that offense settled?
Immediately following these is the section on compendium (*samuccayavāra*). These seven sections have their meanings already explained.

188. Following that, there is one section on the formulation of the rule (*paññattivāra*) by way of the condition, beginning with: "Where was the *pārājika* offense prescribed for the condition of engaging in sexual intercourse? and so forth.

Based on that, there are seven further sections—the section on the commission of the offense (*katāpattivāra*) and the rest—identical to the preceding ones. Thus, these eight [sections] have been stated; as for the previous ones...
In the Mahāvibhaṅga, eight sections are shown; beyond that, by the same method, sixteen sections also appear in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.
Thus, these thirty-two sections in both Vibhaṅgas are to be understood according to the very method of the Pāḷi.
For there is nothing here whatsoever that has not already been determined.
The commentary on the sixteen great sections in the Mahāvibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section concerning origins (samuṭṭhāna).
257. Furthermore, regarding the discussion on their origination immediately following that: "the determination that 'it is non-self'" means it is determined as "non-self.
"Of similar phenomena" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) that are similar by way of their impermanent aspect and so forth.
"'Mere name' does not appear" means that even a mere name is not discerned. "The destruction of suffering" means the eradication of suffering. And the summary of the chapters (*khandhaka-mātikā*).

The meaning is: "the Khandhakas and the Mātikā. Or rather, this is the reading itself. "The origin has been made fixed" means that the origin (samuṭṭhāna) has been rendered fixed (niyatokata), i.e., determined (niyatakata); the meaning is "of fixed origin.
By this, the inclusion of the triad of training rules concerning the reporting of what has occurred, the theft of a robe, and the ordaining of one who has not been permitted should be understood.
For these three training rules alone have a fixed origin, whereas [others] together with others...
They have unmixed origins.
"Another origin and another mixture" means there is yet another origin and another mixture.
In that context, by the term "mixture," one should understand the inclusion of a mixture of origins; for, setting aside those three training rules, the remaining ones...
[The training rules] have mixed origins. By the term "source" (nidāna), the source consisting of the location where the training rules were prescribed should be understood.
"Seen in the Sutta above" means that these three—namely, the determination of the origin of the training rules, the mixing, and the source—are seen in the Sutta itself;
the meaning is that they are made known therein. Among those, [the phrase] "by a single origin..."
In such passages as "It originates from both body and mind," the determination of origination and its classification are seen according to the previous method.
However, the other [method] is called the "Source" (nidāna):
"Vesālī, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, and Āḷavī;"
“And at Kosambī among the Sakyans, and indeed among the Bhaggas, it was laid down.
Thus it appears above; it should be understood that it is seen in the subsequent sutta as well.
Regarding the line in the verse, “In two Vibhaṅgas,” this is the meaning: whichever training rule was laid down in two Vibhaṅgas...
"On the Uposatha day, both monks and nuns recite [the Pātimokkha]; I shall explain its origin according to how it was understood.
Listen to that from me.
"And the instruction regarding matchmaking" means both matchmaking and formal admonition. "And an extra robe" means an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).

"Kathina" is the meaning. "Wool and reciting the Pāṭimokkha" means both sheep's wool and the recitation of the Pāṭimokkha. "A true person and by appointment" means both reporting what has actually occurred and traveling on a journey after making an appointment.

"Teaching the Dhamma to a thief and a woman" means both teaching the Dhamma to one carrying a stolen caravan and teaching the Dhamma to one who is not ill while holding a sunshade, as well as causing a thief to be released. To one who is not authorized...
"Thirteen" refers to these thirteen origins (samuṭṭhāna) which pertain to one who has not been permitted by her mother, father,
or husband. "Similar ones are seen here" means that within each of these thirteen headings of origins in both the Ubhatovibhaṅgas,
other similar origins are also seen.
Commentary on the Origin of the First Pārājika: 258.
Now, in order to show those [factors], it is said: "Sexual intercourse, emission of semen," and so forth.
Therein, "sexual intercourse" (methuna) is first of all one head of origin known as the First Pārājika; the remaining [Pārājikas] are similar to it. Therein—
"Contact with semen" refers both to the emission of semen and to physical contact. "The first undetermined offense" refers to the first undetermined training rule (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*).

"One who has previously approached and prepared" refers to the training rule concerning "knowingly [approaching] a monk who has already arrived" and the training rule concerning alms-food prepared by a nun.
"In secret, together with a nun" means together with a nun.
And the training rule on sitting in private (*raho-nisajja-sikkhāpada*).

"Two [rules] regarding sitting in private with one who is eating" (*sabhojane raho dve*) refers to the training rule on intruding and sitting in private with a family that is eating, and the two training rules on sitting in private.
"Fingers in water, laughing" refers to the training rule on poking with fingers and the training rule on laughing in water. "Blows" (*pahāre*).
"And 'both throwing up'" refers to the training rule on giving blows and the training rule on throwing up with the palm of the hand.
"And the fifty-three trainings" refers to the fifty-three training rules beginning with "the lower robe must be worn even all around," which are stated at the end of the *Khuddakavaṇṇanā*.
"A lustful woman going from village to village" refers to the training rule for bhikkhunīs concerning [a nun] below the collarbone and the offense of a lustful woman traveling between villages.

The training rule regarding the taking of hard and soft food from the hand of one who is lustful; and "with the palm-smeared" and "pure" refers to striking with the palm smeared with lac and cleansing with water, etc.

"Those who have completed the rains residence" and "exhortation" refers to the training rule concerning those who have completed the rains residence traveling five or six yojanas [to receive] exhortation, and the training rule regarding not going for exhortation. "One should not follow after a woman."
Furthermore, there is the training rule stated: "Whatever nun does not follow her preceptor for two years after she has been ordained.

"These trainings" means these rules of training; the change in gender (from feminine to neuter) has been made. "Performed by body and mind" means performed by the origination of body and consciousness.
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the second *pārājika* offense.
259. *Adinnaṃ* (what is not given): this, first of all, along with *adinnādānaṃ* (taking what is not given) or the second *pārājika*, constitutes one origin-source (*samuṭṭhānasīsa*);
the remaining [offenses] are similar to it. In that regard, *viggahuttarī* refers to the training rules concerning human beings and superhuman states (*manussaviggaha-uttarimanussadhamma*).
*Duṭṭhullā attakāminī* refers to the training rules concerning lewd speech and sexual service for one's own pleasure (*duṭṭhullavācā-attakāmapāricariya*). *Amūlā aññabhāgiyā*... [and so forth].
There are two training rules concerning corrupt offenses (*duṭṭhadosa*). The second undetermined rule (*aniyata*) is the second undetermined training rule.
"Taking back" and "diverting": giving a robe oneself and then taking it back, as well as diverting to oneself a gain belonging to the Saṅgha.
"Falsehood," "insulting speech," and "slander": false speech, insulting speech, and slandering monks. "Corrupt offense" and "digging the earth."

The announcement of a grave offense (*duṭṭhullāpatti*) and the digging of the earth; the training rules concerning one who, knowing it to be real, complains, and one who speaks falsely regarding a living plant (*bhūtagāma*).
"Expelling" and "sprinkling" refer to expelling [someone] from the monastery and sprinkling grass and so forth with water.

"For the sake of material gain, having eaten" refers to the training rule concerning "admonishing nuns for the sake of material gain," and [the rule concerning] one who has eaten and [gives] what is not left over.

The training rule on invitations (*pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*) regarding hard food and so forth; the training rule beginning with “Come, friend, [go] to the village,” which concerns disrespect and causing fear among the monks;
the training rule on the concealment of bowls and other items, and the intentional depriving of a living being of life.
"Knowing it is an action involving living beings" refers to the training rule regarding water containing living beings and the reopening of a legal act that has already been concluded.

"Dwelling with one who is less than [the required age]" refers to the training rule regarding those under twenty years of age, the training rule regarding dwelling together with one who has been suspended, and the training rule regarding social interaction with a novice who has been expelled.
"A legitimate ground for complaint" refers to the training rule concerning being spoken to in accordance with the Dhamma.

"Leading to vexation" refers to the training rule concerning [false] accusations. "Delusion by means of what is groundless" refers to the *pācittiya* training rule on causing delusion, and the training rule on formal accusation (*anuddhaṃsana*) by means of what is groundless involving a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"Giving a legitimate robe while causing remorse" refers to the instigation of remorse, and the giving of consent for legitimate legal acts (*kamma*).

“Having given [a robe], it is a transgression; having given a robe, it is a transgression. “One should divert [it] to an individual” refers to the training rule regarding the diversion of communal gains to an individual.
“Why do you withhold it at the wrong time? refers to the training rule concerning [the monk who says], “What will this man do for you, Noble Lady?
and the training rule regarding the use of a vessel after having determined that an out-of-season robe is a seasonable robe.
The training rule concerning the taking back of a robe after having exchanged it with a bhikkhunī;

and the two training rules: that concerning reviling another because of what was wrongly grasped or wrongly maintained (the *duggahita*-rule), and that concerning the cursing of another by means of "hell" or "the holy life" (the *niraya*-rule).
The rules concerning the distribution of the community’s robe-cloth (*gaṇavibhaṅga*) and the weak expectation of robe-cloth (*dubbalacīvarapaccāsā*) are those stated as:

“One should create an obstacle to the community’s acquisition of robe-cloth,” “One should obstruct the lawful distribution of robe-cloth,” and “One should cause the robe-season (*cīvarakālasamaya*) to be exceeded due to a weak expectation of robe-cloth.
The *kaṭhina* robes provide comfort and shelter; [the rule is]: “One should obstruct the lawful suspension of the *kaṭhina*.”

The training rules stated as: "If she should intentionally cause discomfort to a bhikkhunī," and "Having given a dwelling place to a bhikkhunī, if she, being angry and displeased, should drive her out.

The training rules stated as: "A reviler and one who is fierce," meaning: "She should revile or abuse a bhikkhu," "being fierce, she should abuse the Saṅgha," and "she should be stingy toward families."
"Regarding a pregnant woman and one nursing": these refer to the training rules stated as "one should ordain a pregnant woman" and "one should ordain a woman nursing.

"Two years of training by the Saṅgha": these refer to the training rules stated as "one should ordain a trainee who has not trained in the six rules for two years," and "one should ordain a trainee who has trained but has not been approved by the Saṅgha."

“Three for those who have gone forth from the household life” refers to the training rules stated thus: “one who has gone forth from the household life and is less than twelve years old; one who has gone forth from the household life and is full twelve years old, but who has not trained in the six rules for two years;
and one who has trained in the six rules for two years but has not been authorized by the Saṅgha.
“Three for those who have been maidenhoods” refers to [the rule] beginning with “one who has been a maidenhood and is less than twenty years old,” and so forth.

Three [rules] are stated by way of method. "Approved as less than twelve years" refers to the two training rules stated thus: "If she should give the full admission to one who is less than twelve years [of seniority]," and "If she should give the full admission to one who is twelve years [of seniority] but has not been approved by the Saṅgha.
"Enough, for now, of this dwelling in grief" refers to both: "Enough, noble lady, of giving the full admission to her," and [the case of] a trainee (sikkhamānā) who is fierce and dwells in grief.

And the two training rules stated as “she should ordain [her]”; and the three training rules stated as “by giving consent for one undergoing probation she should ordain a trainee,” “she should ordain every year,” and “she should ordain two in one year”—these are the three training rules.
“The origins were made into triads” means they were made into triads of origins.
Commentary on the Origin of the Offense of Acting as a Matchmaker (Sañcaritta-samuṭṭhāna): 260.
"Acting as a matchmaker" (sañcaritta) refers to building a small hut by means of begging for materials and building a large monastery.
"Washing and receiving" refers to having an unrelated bhikkhunī wash an old robe and the receiving of a robe [from her].
"Bringing what exceeds a formal request" refers to the training rule on requesting robe-cloth from an unrelated householder and the training rule on accepting what exceeds that.

"By messenger for both" refers to the two training rules introduced with the words "a means of purchasing robe-cloth has been set aside," as well as the training rule on sending a messenger with a means of purchasing robe-cloth.
The five training rules beginning with "a blanket made of silk" (kosiyamissakaṃ santhataṃ) refer to: "silk," "pure [wool]," "two parts," and "the sitting mat for six years.
"They neglect the money" refers to the washing of wool and the training rule on receiving money, as stated in the Vibhaṅga: "they neglect the recitation.
"Both in various ways" refers to the two training rules concerning the bartering of money and buying and selling.
"Deficient-binding and the rainy-season robe" refers to the training rule on the bowl with fewer than five patches and the training rule on the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*).
"By means of a thread and by way of assignment" refers to both requesting thread for having a robe woven and approaching a weaver to have the robe assigned.
"The giving of the opening and the sewing" refers to the fixing of the bolt as far as the frame of the door.
The triad of training rules stated as: “One should give a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī,” and “One should sew a robe [for an unrelated bhikkhunī].

“And the invitation regarding cakes and gruel” refers to the training rule concerning invitations to receive cakes or gruel brought by others, as well as the training rules concerning the four-month invitation for requisites and the kindling of fires.
“A gem, a needle, a bed, cotton, a sitting mat, a scratcher, and the *vassikā* flower—[these] with the Sugata” refers to the training rule concerning gems, and so forth.

And there are seven training rules beginning with the needle-case rule (*sūcighara-sikkhāpada*). There are nine training rules beginning with "Whatever nun, having requested one thing, should request another," which concern requesting (*viññatti*), exchanging (*aññaṃ cetāpanā*), and two rules regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha or a group, as well as two rules regarding what belongs to an individual—light and heavy.
And there are two rules concerning refuse (*vighāsa*), such as: "Excrement, urine, rubbish, or refuse... and "The *sāṭikā* [garment]..."

"Or over a wall, or over a rampart, he should throw it away or cause it to be thrown away, or on green crops, he should throw it away or cause it to be thrown away"—thus were the two training rules concerning refuse-food (*vighāsa*) and the training rule concerning the water-cloak (*udakasāṭikā*) spoken.
"With a robe of a recluse" means this was said with reference to the statement: "He should give a robe of a recluse."
Commentary on the Origin of the *Samanubhāsanā* (Formal Rebuke): 261.

"Schism, following [a schismatic], abusive speech, corrupting families, grave offenses, and views"—these refer to the training rules concerning: causing a schism in the Saṅgha, following one who causes a schism, abusive speech, corrupting families, concealing a grave offense, and not relinquishing wrong views.
"Consent, loud laughter, and two"—this refers to the training rule regarding departing without giving consent, and [the rule regarding] loud laughter within an inhabited area.

And the two training rules concerning walking and sitting. And the two words "with little noise" refer to the two training rules: "I will walk with little noise in an inhabited area" and "I will sit with little noise.
"One should not speak" refers to the training rule: "I will not speak with a mouthful of food in my mouth.
"On the ground" means standing on low ground or behind by a side path; that is, having sat on the ground or having sat on a low seat.

The training rules for teaching the Dhamma [to those who are] standing while one is sitting, walking behind while one is walking in front, or walking on a by-path while one is walking on the main path.

"Following the faulty" (*vajjānuvatti*) refers to concealing a fault, following one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and the three *pārājika* offenses consisting of taking the hand and so forth. "Renouncing after being reinstated" (*osāre paccācikkhanā*).

The two training rules stated as: “If one should restore [a nun] without having obtained the permission of the performing Saṅgha and without knowing the will of the group,” and “I renounce the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase “in what association are there two murderers? it refers to: “In some legal matter they have been accused,” and “the nuns...”

The training rules stated as: “...living in close association,” and “Whichever nun should say, ‘Venerable ladies, you should indeed live in close association,’ ” and “She should weep, striking herself again and again.
And regarding “having unfastened [the robe] from one who is suffering”: “Having unfastened a nun’s robe, or having had it unfastened...”
And the two training rules stated as: “A co-resident who is suffering,” and again, the training rule on associating which was stated thus:

“She may associate with a householder or a householder’s son,” and [the case of] one who, being addressed, “Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,” having consented by saying “Very well,” afterwards—
And the training rule stated as: "If she does not cause [the dispute] to be settled, it shall be an offense of immediate reprimand.

Furthermore, regarding the monastery and the invitation ceremony, there are two training rules stated as: "If one enters a monastery known to have monks without having asked permission," and "If one does not invite [for criticism] before both Sanghas on three grounds."
“Every half-month, two [things] from the community of monks” refers to the training rule stating, “Every half-month,
two matters must be requested by a bhikkhunī from the community of monks,” as well as the two training rules stating, “Having given the full admission to a co-resident,
she does not support her for two years,” and “Having given the full admission to a co-resident, she does not cause her to leave. “Following after the robe” means:
The two training rules stated as: “If you, noble lady, will give me a robe, I will ordain you,” and “If you, noble lady, will follow me for two years, I will ordain you.
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the *kathina* [rules].
262. "The three on the suspension of the *kathina*" refers to the first three training rules stated as: "When a robe has been finished and the *kathina* has been suspended by a monk.
"The bowl and medicine first" refers to the first bowl-training rule stated as "An extra bowl may be kept for ten days at most," and the training rule stated as "Medicines that are to be stored."

"Accekañcāpi sāsaṅkan" refers to both the training rule on the "urgent robe" (accekacīvara-sikkhāpada) and immediately following it, the training rule on "what is attended by risk" (sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada).
"Or two for one departing" refers to the two training rules stated in the Bhūtagāma-vagga: "When departing, he should not lift [the bedding]" and so forth.
"Successively to the residence" refers to: "Having gone to the nuns' residence, he should exhort the nuns," and "in successive eating" (paramparabhojana).

The two training rules stated as "an offense entailing expiation" (pācittiya) are: the two training rules stated as "not leftover" (anatiritta) and "being invited" (nimantita)—namely, "solid food or soft food that is not leftover" and "being invited and having already finished one's meal"—and the three training rules regarding "assigning at an improper time" (vikappaṃ rañño vikāle):
namely, "having oneself assigned a robe," "of a kṣatriya king," and "at an improper time [entering] a village."

The triad of training rules stated as “she should enter”; the two training rules stated as “standing in a manner that suggests she is waiting for him” and “in such forest lodgings, without having previously informed [the residents]”;
and the two training rules stated as “one who engages in litigation” and “one who should make a hoard of bowls.”
"Pure," "pacchā," and "vikāle": these refer to the triad of training rules stated as "Whatever bhikkhunī, having approached families before the meal...
and "having approached families after the meal... and "having approached families at an improper time...
"Pañcāhikā saṅkamanī" refers to "she should exceed the five-day limit for the movement of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi)" and "the robe that may be moved..."
And there are the two training rules stated as "he should keep [it]"; and furthermore, there are the two training rules stated together with the "dwelling" (āvasatha), namely:
"if he should use a dwelling-robes (āvasathacīvara) without having relinquished it," and "if he should set out on a journey without having relinquished the dwelling.
Thus, there are two training rules mentioned along with the dwelling.

The two training rules stated as: “She sits on a seat with her thighs [crossed]” (*pasākhe āsane cevāti*)—referring to both the rule concerning a boil born on the thigh (*pasākhe jātaṃ gaṇḍaṃ vā*) and the rule stating that “she should not sit on a seat in front of a bhikkhu without having asked permission.
263. Commentary on the Origin of the Sheep’s Wool:
“Two beds of sheep’s wool” refers to the training rule on sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*) and the two training rules regarding sleeping together (*sahaseyya*).
"Having struck [the bowl]" refers to the training rule on sitting on a stool with feet [protruding] and the training rule on eating almsfood at a residence.
"A group, at an improper time, and storing" refers to the triad of training rules concerning eating in a group, eating at an improper time, and causing food to be stored.
"With a tooth-stick, [or] naked" refers to the training rule on tooth-sticks and the training rule on being naked. "An army mobilized, a battle" refers to [the rule]: "An army mobilized..."
The triad of training rules stated as: "One should go to see an army," "one should stay with an army," and "or [watch] a battle rehearsal...
or go to see a military array"; the two rules concerning intoxicants: the training rule on drinking fermented liquor (*surāpāna*) and the training rule on bathing within half a month;

and the two offenses to be confessed (*pāṭidesanīya*) that remain after the statement regarding the three ways of disfiguring: the training rule on the three methods of disfiguring and the remaining two offenses to be confessed.

“Standing over one with garlic,” “dancing,” refers respectively to the training rule on garlic, the training rule stating, “One should not stand over a bhikkhu while he is eating, [offering] water or a fan,” and the training rule stating, “One should not go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music.
From this point onward, they write having omitted the Pāḷi text. However, as...
We shall explain the meaning; thus the sequence here is to be understood.

"Bathing, a rug, and a bed" refers to the triad of training rules stated as: "She might bathe naked," "They might lie down under one and the same cover," and "They might lie down on one and the same couch.
"Likewise within the country and outside" refers to: "Within the country, in a place considered risky..."
The two training rules stated as: “In a foreign kingdom considered dangerous”; and the two training rules stated as:
“During the rains, one should not set out on a journey to a pleasure-house,” or “...to see a royal palace, a picture-gallery, ... or a lotus pond. And [the rule]:
“One should not use a high couch or a long chair. “A shuttle for spinning thread. “One should not use a high couch or a long chair.”
The two training rules stated as "he should weave thread";
and the two training rules stated as "service with one's own hand," namely:
"He should perform service for householders, or he should give hard food or soft food with his own hand to a householder, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer."
"And by a residence without monks" means this was said with reference to: "One should spend the rains residence in a residence without monks.
"The sunshade, the vehicle, and the hip-belt" refers to the triad of training rules stated as: "One should carry a sunshade and sandals; one should travel by vehicle; one should wear a hip-belt.
"Adorned with ornaments and scented with perfumes" refers to: "One should wear female ornaments; [one should apply] powdered perfume..."
The triad of training rules stated as: “She may bathe; she may bathe with scented flour-meal.

By the words beginning with “a bhikkhunī,” the four training rules beginning with “she should have herself massaged” are stated. “An offense for not wearing an inner robe” refers to the offense stated thus:
“If she should enter a village without an inner robe, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). “Forty-four” means forty and four.
All these forty-four training rules have been stated.
[The phrase] "by body, not by speech and mind" means they originate from both body and body-mind, but not from speech and mind;
[the phrase] "not by speech and mind" means they do not originate from speech and mind. All of them are of two origins, and this applies equally to the rule concerning wool—this much is self-evident.

Commentary on the Offenses Originating from Teaching Word-by-Word (Padasodhammasamuṭṭhāna) 264. “Teaching word-by-word except when authorized”: this refers to the triad of training rules stated as: “If one should teach the Dhamma word-by-word to a woman with more than five or six words;

if one should exhort the bhikkhunīs without being authorized; [and] if one should teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words except when accompanied by a man capable of understanding.”
Likewise, "and when [the sun] has set" refers to this: it was said with reference to the rule, "One should advise when the sun has set.
"Two kinds of low arts" refers to the two training rules stated thus: "One should master a low art" and "One should teach a low art.
"And asking a question of one who has not given leave" refers to this: it was said with reference to the rule, "One should ask a question of a bhikkhu who has not given leave."
Commentary on the Origin by Way of Time (Addhānasamuṭṭhāna): 265.
Regarding the phrase "a boat on a journey is excellent": "If one should set out on a journey by way of a single road in company with a bhikkhunī, or board a single boat;
or if, being not ill, one should request and eat choice foods for one's own sake."
The three training rules already mentioned: (1) the rule concerning "concealing body hair with a woman," which refers to traveling in company with a woman;
and (2) the rule stating, "one should have body hair removed from the private parts. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "whether invited for grain":
this refers to both the rule, "having requested grain," and the rule, "if one should eat fresh or cooked food when invited or when the formal invitation has been extended."
And the training rule stated as, “...or should eat. And “eight” refers to the eight *pāṭidesanīya* offenses prescribed for bhikkhunīs.
266. Commentary on the Origin of the Rule concerning Traveling with a Caravan of Thieves:
“Traveling with a caravan of thieves” means traveling along a road together with a caravan of thieves after having made an appointment with them.

"And standing while eavesdropping. "And by requesting soup" refers to the solicitation of rice and curry. "The three rules concerning the night, concealment, and the place" refers to the triad of training rules stated thus:
"In the darkness of night when there is no lamp, in a concealed place, or in the open air, together with a man.
"The seventh by way of a carriage-road" refers to that which follows immediately after: "On a carriage-road..."
This was said with reference to the training rule concerning [a nun] who has come together with a man in an open space, at a crossroads, or at a place where three roads meet.
267. Regarding the commentary on the origins of the teaching of the Dhamma:
the eleven origins of the teaching of the Dhamma are indeed plain. Thus, first, is the mixed origin.
This should be understood. However, the "definite origination" (niyata-samuṭṭhāna) is threefold, and it pertains to each individual training rule (sikkhāpada).
To demonstrate that specifically, it was said: "The real arises through the body," and so forth; this is self-evident.
"In accordance with the Dhamma of the Net" means in conformity with the Dhamma of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The commentary on the section on origins is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the Intermediate Series of Questions and Answers.

271. Now, for the purpose of generating proficiency regarding the categories beginning with offenses, the *vibhaṅga* (analysis) is set forth by establishing a *mātikā* (matrix) in the manner of "How many offenses?

and so forth, followed by the exposition (*niddesa*) and sub-exposition (*paṭiniddesa*). Therein, "How many offenses? is the inquiry concerning the offenses as they appear in both the *mātikā* and the *vibhaṅga*. This same method applies to the second term as well.
However, here the offenses themselves are called "aggregates" (*khandha*) by way of a collection. "Matters of discipline" (*vinītavatthu*) refers to those [cases] of those very offenses.

The inquiry regarding the discipline (*vinayapucchā*): "Discipline is that which is disciplined, it is tranquility"—this is indeed one in meaning. Here, the word-meaning is that the very things disciplined are the bases of discipline (*vinītavatthūni*).
Now, in order to show those things in whose presence there are offenses and in whose absence there are none, there is the pair of inquiries beginning with "How many kinds of disrespect?
This inquiry regarding the discipline is, moreover, directed toward those who are disrespectful concerning the bases of discipline.
Since, however, those offenses are not called "failures" (vipatti) because they have already fallen into failure, the question "How many failures are there?
is an inquiry into the nature of the offenses as failures. "How many origins of offenses are there? is an inquiry into the origins of those very same offenses.
"Roots of dispute" and "roots of accusation" refer to those [offenses] that have come down as "formal acts of dispute" (vivādādhikaraṇa) and "formal acts of accusation" (anuvādādhikaraṇa).

"Disputes and accusations" refers to a question concerning their root. "Dharmas conducive to harmony" refers to a question concerning those dharmas that cause the absence of the roots of disputes and accusations.
"Bases for schism" refers to a question concerning the causes of schism as stated in such passages as "a legal issue leading to a schism.
"Legal issues" refers to a question concerning the dharmas that arise when the bases for schism exist. "Settlements" refers to [the means] for those very [legal issues].

The inquiry concerning the nature of tranquility. "Five offenses" is stated according to how they appear in the *Mātikā*; "seven" is according to how they appear in the *Vibhaṅga*. One delights far away from these, thus it is *ārati*;
or, intense delight is *ārati*. One delights without these, thus it is *virati*. One desists individually and individually, thus it is *paṭivirati*.
It destroys (*maṇati*) and eliminates (*vināseti*) enmity (*vera*), thus it is *veramaṇī*. By means of this, these aggregates of offenses [do not arise].
They are called *akiriya* because they are not being done. It is the non-doing that serves as the antidote to whatever category of offense (*āpattikkhandha*) might arise through their absence.
It is a "non-offense" (*anajjhāpatti*) because it is the opposite of committing a category of offense. It is a "limit" (*velā*) because of its boundary;

the meaning is that it marks a limit by causing movement [toward safety] or destruction [of faults]. It is a "bridge" (*setu*) because it binds together, fastens, or prevents [the flow of evil). This refers to the categories of offenses.

It is a designation. Because he is struck by means of this designation, it is called "the destruction of the bridge" (*setughāta*). This same method applies to the descriptions of the remaining training rules as well.

Regarding those who speak of disrespect toward the Buddha: one who does not go to attend upon the Buddha while he is still living; who, after his final *parinibbāna*, does not go to the site of the shrine or the site of the Bodhi tree;
who does not pay homage to the shrine or the Bodhi tree; or who remains at the shrine courtyard with an umbrella and sandals on—[is so described].
One who acts in such a way should be understood as having no reverence for the Buddha.

Furthermore, one who, though quite capable, does not go to hear the Dhamma, does not recite the scriptures, does not give a discourse on the Dhamma, leaves the assembly while it is hearing the Dhamma, or sits distractedly or disrespectfully, has no reverence for the Dhamma. One who [behaves thus] toward the elders, the novices, or those of middle standing...
He does not show respect; he displays physical immodesty in the Uposatha hall, the thought-chamber, the pavilion, and so forth;

he does not pay homage according to seniority; thus, he has no reverence for the Saṅgha. Furthermore, one who has undertaken the three trainings but does not train in them at all should be understood as lacking reverence for the training.
And while remaining in negligence and the absence of mindfulness, he [lacks] the characteristic of heedfulness.
One who does not encourage [others] in heedfulness should be understood as one who lacks respect for heedfulness.
Likewise, one who does not perform these two kinds of hospitality—hospitality with material things and hospitality with the Dhamma—should be understood as one who lacks respect for hospitality.
The meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated in the description of respect (*gārava*).

272. In the exposition of the roots of dispute, the meaning of such terms as "disrespect toward the Teacher" should be understood according to the method already explained regarding disrespect toward the Buddha.
"Lacking deference" means behaving without humility; it means one does not dwell making the Teacher his superior.
"Internally" means within one's own continuum or within one's own faction—the sense being "within one's own assembly. "Externally" means within the continua of others.
Or on the side of others. In that context, "for you" (*tumhaṃ*) refers either to one's own or another's continuum—whether within one's own group or another's group.
"You should strive for their abandonment" means you should strive for the purpose of abandoning them by means of such methods as the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*);

for by the method of cultivating loving-kindness and so forth, that [defilement] is abandoned both internally and externally. "For the sake of non-outflow" (*anavassavāya*) means for the state of non-occurrence.

*Sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*: one who clings to one's own view; one who grasps whatever position on a view has been adopted by oneself, thinking, "This alone is the truth. *Ādhānaggāhī*: one who holds firmly; one who grasps with obstinacy. 273.

Although the exposition of the roots of accusation is similar to the exposition of the roots of dispute, nevertheless, for those who dispute based on the eighteen grounds for schism, anger, resentment, and so forth are the roots of dispute. For those disputing in such a manner...

However, having fallen into one of the failures such as failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), others reproach them, saying, "Such-and-such a bhikkhu has fallen into such-and-such a failure," or "You have fallen into a *pārājika* offense," or "You have fallen into a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
For those who thus reproach, anger, resentment, and so forth are the roots of the reproach; this is the distinction here.
274. In the exposition of the qualities conducive to affection (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*): bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness is called "loving-kindly bodily action.

"Both openly and in private" means both in the presence of others and behind their backs. In that regard, acting as a companion to junior monks in matters such as the making of robes is called "loving-kindly bodily action in the presence [of others].
Furthermore, even acts toward senior monks consisting of washing their feet, fanning them, providing cooling breezes, and so forth—[are also included].
All acts of proper courtesy performed in person are called "loving bodily action in the presence.

When both parties have placed wooden articles and so forth down poorly, to put them back in order without showing contempt for them—just as if one had placed them down oneself—is called "loving bodily action behind one's back.
This too is a "conducive to harmony" (sāraṇīya) quality: this quality consisting of loving bodily action is to be remembered, meaning it generates mindfulness.
The intention is this: whoever performs it, and those for whom it is performed, they—possessing a clear mind—recollect him, thinking, "Oh, what a true person!

"One who acts with affection" means he makes that person dear to his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*). "One who acts with respect" means he holds that person in high esteem among his fellow celibates.
In the phrases beginning with "for the sake of gathering," the meaning is: for the purpose of being gathered together by his fellow celibates.
This leads to non-dispute with them, to concord, and to unity.
Regarding "loving verbal action" and so forth: speaking words such as "Venerable Deva" or "Venerable Tissa" in their presence is called loving verbal action in person.
However, when they are not present in the monastery, for one who inquires about them, saying, "Where is our Venerable Deva? [is also included].
“Where is our Elder Tissa? When indeed will he return?”—such words of possessiveness are called loving verbal action in the absence of the person.
Furthermore, opening one’s eyes, which are moist with the oil of loving-kindness, and looking upon him with a serene face is called loving mental action in the presence of the person.
[Saying], “May the Venerable Elder Tissa be free from illness, may he be free from affliction,”...
Directing the mind toward others with loving-kindness is what is called mental action of loving-kindness.
"One who shares enjoyments without partiality" means that one neither divides material goods nor individuals when eating;
for such a person does not think, "I will give this much to others and eat this much myself," or "I will give this much to so-and-so and to so-and-so."
One who, having divided [the alms-food], thinks, "I will eat this much myself," and then eats it, is called one who enjoys what has been individually apportioned (*paṭivibhattabhogī*).
However, this [monk] does not do so; rather, he gives the alms-food brought to him starting from the seat of the elders, and eats what remains after it has been taken.
Because of the words "by those possessing virtue" (*sīlavantehi*), it is even permissible for him not to give to one who is immoral; however, by one who fulfills the *sāraṇīya-dhamma*...

It is stated that "it must indeed be given to everyone. However, it is also permissible to give after making a distinction for those who are ill, those attending the sick, newcomers, those about to depart, and those occupied with robe-making and so forth.

For by one who gives after such discernment, no discrimination among individuals is made; rather, because such persons obtain [robes] with difficulty, a special consideration must indeed be made for them—this is what he does.

Regarding the terms *akhaṇḍa* (unbroken) and so forth: when one has violated a training rule either at the beginning or at the end among the seven classes of offenses, one's virtue is called "broken," like a garment torn at the edge.
When one has violated it in the middle, it is called "perforated," like a garment with a hole in the center. When two or three [rules] have been violated in succession, [it is called "stained"].

When a certain color different from its own arises on its back or belly, it is called "spotted" (*sabala*), like a cow whose body color is black, red, or otherwise variegated. When its precepts are broken here and there, it is called "mottled" (*kammāsa*), like a cow variegated with spots of colors different from its own appearing at intervals. But for one whose precepts are entirely unbroken in every respect, those [precepts]— [The text continues: ...are like a cow that is pure white throughout, without any blemish. For such a person, these precepts are called "pure" (*parisuddha*). Just as a cow that is pure white throughout, without any blemish, is called "pure," so too, for one whose precepts are entirely unbroken, they are called "pure. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has undertaken the training rules" (*sikkhāsamādāna-sampanna*). Why? Because they have undertaken the training rules and possess them. Moreover, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has fulfilled the training rules" (*sikkhāsampadā-sampanna*). Why? Because they have fulfilled the training rules and possess them. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has attained the goal" (*atthasiddhi-sampanna*). Why? Because they have attained the goal and possess it. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the goal" (*atthagamana-sampanna*). Why? Because they have reached the goal and possess it. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has crossed over" (*tiṇṇa*). Why? Because they have crossed over the flood of craving and possess that crossing. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has gone beyond" (*pāraṅgata*). Why? Because they have gone beyond the flood of craving and possess that going-beyond. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the further shore" (*pāramippatta*). Why? Because they have reached the further shore of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the ultimate" (*accuggata*). Why? Because they have reached the ultimate of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the summit" (*aggaṃ patta*). Why? Because they have reached the summit of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the pinnacle" (*aggaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the pinnacle of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the peak" (*aggaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the peak of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the highest point" (*aggaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the highest point of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the limit" (*koṭiṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the limit of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the boundary" (*sīmāṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the boundary of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the end" (*antaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the end of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the ultimate end" (*antantaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the ultimate end of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the finality" (*pariyantaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the finality of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the culmination" (*pariyosānaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the culmination of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the perfection" (*paripūraṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the perfection of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the completion" (*pariniṭṭhitaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the completion of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the fulfillment" (*paripuṇṇaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the fulfillment of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the fullness" (*puṇṇaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the fullness of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the abundance" (*bahulaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the abundance of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the greatness" (*mahantaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the greatness of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the vastness" (*vipulaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the vastness of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the breadth" (*vitthataṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the breadth of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the expanse" (*puthulaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the expanse of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the wide extent" (*pharusaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the wide extent of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the far-reaching" (*dūraṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the far-reaching of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the remote" (*vidūraṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the remote of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the distant" (*sudūraṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the distant of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the extreme" (*antikaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the extreme of the flood of craving and possess that reaching. Furthermore, when a person possesses these four kinds of precepts, they are called "one who has reached the very edge" (*paccantikaṃ patvā ṭhita*). Why? Because they have reached the very edge of the flood of craving and possess
The precepts are called "unbroken, flawless, unblemished, and untarnished. Furthermore, they are called "free" because they bring about the state of freedom;
they are "praised by the wise" because they are commended by the wise; they are "unadhered-to" because they are not clung to by craving or views;
and they are said to be "conducive to concentration" because they lead to either access concentration or absorption concentration.
“He dwells having attained commonality in virtue” means that he dwells with a virtue that has entered into a state of equality with those bhikkhus of good character who dwell in various directions.
“This view” refers to right view associated with the Path. “Noble” means faultless. “Leads out” means it is conducive to deliverance.
"Of one who acts thus": of him who acts in that manner. "For the destruction of suffering": for the purpose of the exhaustion of all suffering.
The remainder, up to the conclusion of the classification of serenity (*samatha*), is of plain meaning.

The Section on Questions from the Khandhaka:
Commentary on the Answers to the Questions 320.
"They will ask about ordination" means they will ask about the Ordination Khandhaka (Upasampadakkhandhaka). "Together with its introduction and its exposition" means...
I shall ask together with the introduction (*nidāna*) and the exposition (*niddesa*).
Regarding the "most excellent terms" (*samukkaṭṭhapadānaṃ*): how many offenses (*āpatti*) are there for those most excellent, supreme terms that have been stated therein?
In brief, how many offenses are there for those supreme terms? For by whichever term whatever offense was prescribed, that [is the offense].
For each respective word, an "offense" (āpatti) is spoken of. Therefore it was said: "How many offenses are there for the most excellent words? There are two offenses:
for one who confers full ordination on a person under twenty years of age, there is a *pācittiya*; for all the remaining words, there is a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding "Tisso":
[it refers to] performing the Uposatha with those whose primary aim is schism, thinking, "Let these perish, let these be destroyed; what use have you for them?"

There is a *thullaccaya* for performing the *uposatha* together with one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), a *pācittiya* for performing the *uposatha* together with one who has been suspended, and a *dukkaṭa* for the remaining cases;
thus, there are three offenses in the *Uposathakkhandhaka*. "One" refers to the single *dukkaṭa* offense in the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*. "Three" refers to:

a *thullaccaya* for one who intends to cause schism while performing the *pavāraṇā*, a *pācittiya* for performing the *pavāraṇā* together with one who has been suspended, and a *dukkaṭa* for the remaining cases; thus, there are also three offenses in the *Pavāraṇākkhandhaka*.
In the case of those who seize and kill a calf, there is a *pācittiya* offense; in touching the genitals with a mind of lust, there is a *thullaccaya*;
and for the remaining cases, there is a *dukkaṭa*. Thus, there are three offenses connected with hides.

Also, in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, there is a *thullaccaya* for [using medicine] within two finger-breadths [of the wound], a *pācittiya* for solid food (*bhojjayāgu*), and a *dukkaṭa* for the remaining cases. Thus, there are three offenses.

The *Kathina* [chapter] is merely a formal rule (*paññatti*); there is no offense therein. In the *Cīvara-saṃyutta*, for grass robes and bark robes, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); for an extra robe, a forfeiture offense (*nissaggiya*); and for the remaining cases, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—these are the three offenses.

In the *Campeyyaka*, there is only one offense of wrong-doing. In the *Kosambaka*, the *Kammakkhandhaka*, and the *Pārivāsikasamuccayakkhandhaka*, there is also only one offense of wrong-doing. In the *Samathakkhandhaka*, if one who gives consent (*chandadāyaka*) reviles, the one who reviles incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), while for the others there is an offense of wrong-doing.
These are two offenses. Under the *Khuddakavatthu* section: cutting off one’s own genitals is a *thullaccaya*;
shaving the pubic hair is a *pācittiya*; for the remaining cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*. These are three offenses. Under the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*:

disposing of valuable property belonging to the Saṅgha is a *thullaccaya*; ejecting someone from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha is a *pācittiya*; for the remaining cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*. These are three offenses.
There are these two offenses: a *thullaccaya* for those who cause a schism in the Saṅgha, and a *pācittiya* for eating in a group.
When it is said, "They will ask about the proper conduct," there is only one *dukkaṭa* offense in the *Vattakkhandhaka*.

That occurs through disrespect regarding all the rules of conduct. Likewise, there is a *pācittiya* for the suspension of the Pātimokkha. In the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*, there is a *pācittiya* for not inviting [the monks].
Regarding the "sesesu dukkaṭaṃ," there are two offenses. In the *Pañcasatika* and *Sattasatika*, only the Dhamma was compiled;
there are no offenses therein.
The commentary on the Khandhaka-pucchāvāra is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Single Items (Ekakavāra) within the Numerical Method (Ekuttarikanaya), [Section] 321:
Regarding the passage beginning with "The things that cause offenses should be known," there are six such things that cause offenses in this numerical method.
The origins of offenses (*āpatti-samudāna*). For it is by means of these that a person incurs an offense; therefore, they are called "those that cause an offense.
The seven principles for settling disputes (*satta samathā*) are called "those that do not cause an offense. Regarding "the offense must be known":

the offense stated in each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and in its analysis (*vibhaṅga*) is what must be known. Regarding "non-offense" (*anāpatti*): [it is explained] by such passages as, "There is no offense for a monk who does not consent," and so forth.

The non-offense (*anāpatti*) should be understood according to the method [of the texts]. "Light" (*lahuka*) refers to the fivefold offense that is purified by a light disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).
"Heavy" (*garuka*) refers to the offense of *saṅghādisesa*, because it is purified by a heavy disciplinary act;
and the offense of *pārājika*, because it is impossible to bring it to the state of non-offense in any way whatsoever. "With remainder" (*sāvasesa*), excluding...
The *pārājika* offenses are "without remainder" (*anavasesa*); that is, an offense involving defeat. Two categories of offenses are grave (*duṭṭhulla*); the remainder are not grave (*aduṭṭhulla*).

The dyad concerning offenses with remedies (*sappaṭikamma*) is similar to the dyad concerning offenses with remainder (*sāvasesa*). The dyad concerning offenses leading to confession (*desanāgāminī*) is included within the dyad concerning light offenses (*lahuka*).
The term "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) refers to the seven types of offenses when intentionally transgressed, as they constitute an obstruction to heaven and an obstruction to liberation.

They are called "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because they create obstacles. However, when committed by one who is ignorant, it is an offense that is a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajjāpatti*);

it neither obstructs heaven nor obstructs liberation, and is thus "non-obstructive" (*anantarāyika*). For one who has fallen into an obstructive offense, once he has confessed it so as to bring about purification and has emerged from it through the process of rehabilitation, he attains purity;
for him, as he stands on the level of a novice (*sāmaṇera*), the path to heaven and liberation remains unbarred.

"Proclamation of the blameworthy" refers to those things blameworthy according to worldly standards. "Proclamation of the blameless" refers to those things blameworthy by way of formal rule (paṇṇatti).

"Arising from action" means that one incurs an offense while performing an act, such as a *pārājika* offense. "From non-action" means that one incurs an offense while not performing an act, such as the offense of not formally designating (*anadhiṭṭhāna*) a robe.
"From both action and non-action" means that one incurs an offense both while performing and while not performing an act, such as the offense of building a hut (*kuṭikāra*).

"Previous offense" (*pubbāpatti*) means an offense committed first. "Subsequent offense" (*aparāpatti*) means an offense committed later by one who is already undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), etc. An "intermediate offense for previous offenses" (*antarāpatti*) is an intermediate offense for the purpose of purification of the root (*mūlavisuddhi*).

An "intermediate offense for subsequent offenses" is an intermediate offense for the purpose of purification by value (*agghavisuddhi*). However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: "A 'previous offense' is one committed first."

"An *aparāpatti* (a subsequent offense) is one committed at the time when one is subject to the *mānatta* penance. An *antarāpatti* (an intermediate offense) regarding previous offenses is one committed during the *parivāsa* probation.
An *antarāpatti* regarding subsequent offenses is one committed while practicing the *mānatta* penance"—so it is said. This too is consistent with one method [of interpretation].
"Confessed offenses that come into the reckoning" refers to those confessed after having laid down the burden [of the offense], thinking, "I shall not commit them again."
"Immeasurable" (agaṇanūpagā) means that which has been confessed with a mind that is not entirely pure and without having laid down the burden;
for even though it has been confessed, it does not enter into the count of what has been confessed. In the eighth case, it is a *pārājika* offense for the nun.
Regarding the nine points beginning with "The formulation (*paññatti*) must be known," the method is exactly as stated in the inquiry concerning the first *pārājika*.
The analysis should be understood as follows:
"Serious offenses" (*thullavajja*) refers to grave transgressions prescribed for major faults; "not serious offenses" (*athullavajja*) refers to light transgressions.
"Connected with householders" refers to the offense of the Elder Sudhamma, as well as the offense incurred in not fulfilling a lawful promise; the remainder [are connected with the Sangha].
They are not connected with householders. The commission of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*) is fixed; the rest are unfixed.

An "original perpetrator" (*ādikaroti*) is one who commits the act first, such as the Elder Sudinna and others. An "unoriginal perpetrator" (*anādikaroti*) is one who establishes a subsequent rule, such as the monkey-monk and others.

One who commits an offense "occasionally" (*adhicca-āpattika*) is one who falls into an offense only at certain times. One who commits an offense "frequently" (*abhiṇha-āpattika*) is one who falls into it constantly.
One who accuses is called a *codaka*, meaning one who accuses another on account of a matter (*vatthu*) or an offense (*āpatti*). One who is thus accused is called the *cuditaka*.
If, without being established in the fifteen [proper] qualities, one accuses another with a groundless matter, he is called an accuser of what is contrary to the Dhamma (*adhammacodaka*);

one who is thus accused by him is called the accused of what is contrary to the Dhamma (*adhammacuditaka*). By way of reversal, the accuser and the accused who act according to the Dhamma are to be understood.
One who is endowed with states fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness is "fixed" (niyata); the opposite is "unfixed" (aniyata).
Disciples are called "capable of falling away" (bhabbāpattika), whereas Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are called "incapable of falling away" (abhabbāpattika).

One who has undergone the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) is called "suspended" (ukkhitaka); one who has undergone the remaining fourfold types of formal acts, such as censure (tajjanīyakamma), is called "not suspended" (anukkhitaka). For this [person]...
One does not disrupt the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the enjoyment of the Dhamma, or the enjoyment of material goods.

One who has been expelled by means of the "expulsion" (nāsanā) through the imposition of the penalty of changing gender (*liṅgadaṇḍakamma*)—such as when it is said, "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā; a defiler must be expelled; the thorn-like novice monk must be expelled"—is called "one who has been expelled. All others are "not expelled. With whomsoever there is association for the Uposatha and so forth...
There is one who belongs to the same community (samāna-saṃvāsaka), and the other who belongs to a different community (nānā-saṃvāsaka). That person belonging to a different community is of two kinds:
one who differs by way of formal acts (kamma-nānā-saṃvāsaka) and one who differs by way of views (laddhi-nānā-saṃvāsaka).

"The setting aside should be understood" means that the setting aside of the Pātimokkha, as stated in the method beginning with, "Monks, there is one unrighteous setting aside of the Pātimokkha," should be understood.
The commentary on the section on single terms is finished.
Commentary on the section on pairs (322):

Among the pairs, an offense committed with one's own mind is "released by recognition" (*saññāvimokkha*); an offense not committed with one's own mind is "not released by recognition" (*nosaññāvimokkha*). For one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*)...

An offense called "reporting what is true" is an offense of reporting what has actually occurred; an offense called "reporting what is not true" is an offense of reporting what has not occurred to one who has not attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

Those connected with the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) refer to offenses such as reciting the words of the Dharma improperly; those connected with what is not the True Dharma refer to the offense of indecent speech.
Those connected with requisites refer to the use of an article subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) without first relinquishing it, as well as [the improper use of] bowls and robes.
An offense is incurred in such improper use as storing [garments], washing soiled robes, or failing to cook a bowl that has become stained.
An offense connected with another’s requisites is one to be incurred in cases such as spreading out communal beds, chairs, and so forth in the open air, or departing without asking permission.
An offense connected with a specific person is, for example, [the case of] "one with a soft backside and a hanging [organ] [using] the thigh..."

The offense described by way of the method beginning with "of one who oppresses" and so forth. That which is connected to another person refers to the offenses described in cases such as sexual intercourse, physical contact, or giving blows;

for example, one incurs a heavy offense when speaking the truth, saying, "I am a *sikharaṇī*," but incurs a light offense when speaking falsely, under the rule, "In intentional lying, there is a *pācittiya*.
When speaking falsely in reporting what has not occurred, it is a heavy offense; when reporting what has actually occurred, [it is a light offense].
“Speaking the truth lightly”:
one who sits down to one side within the boundary thinking, “I will perform a Saṅgha transaction that is invalid,” commits an offense if he is on the ground.
However, if he were to remain even a finger’s breadth in the air, he would not commit the offense; therefore it is said, “not while remaining in the air.”
One who sits down on a bed or a bench with detachable legs in an upper chamber is said to be "gone aloft.
However, if one were to spread it out on the ground and lie down, one would not incur [the offense]; therefore it is said:
"not having gone to the ground. One who departs without fulfilling the duties for those going on a journey is said to be "departing," but not...
Entering: A visiting nun who enters while failing to fulfill the duties of a visitor—doing so with her sunshade and sandals on—is said to commit an offense upon entering, not upon leaving.
Taking up: A nun is said to commit an offense when she takes up an excessively deep water-cleansing cloth for the purpose of disfiguring herself.
However, one who uses a robe without taking it up is said to incur an offense by not taking it up.
One who undertakes the practices of the non-Buddhist sects, such as the vow of silence, is said to incur an offense by undertaking them.

But those such as those on probation or those subjected to the *tajjanīya* (reproval) and other formal acts incur offenses by not undertaking their own duties; it is with reference to them that it was said: "There is an offense incurred by not undertaking."

“He incurs [an offense],” it is said. One who sews a robe for an unrelated bhikkhunī, or performs medical work, work as a storekeeper, work as a painter, and so forth, is said to “incur [an offense] by doing. One who fails to perform duties toward one’s preceptor and so forth is said to “incur [an offense] by not doing.
One who gives a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī is said to “incur [an offense] by giving. [The same applies to] one who [neglects] co-resident disciples and pupils.
One is said to "incur [an offense]" by not giving robes and so forth when they ought to be given. One is said to "incur [an offense]" by taking or receiving a robe from an unrelated nun.
One is said to "incur [an offense]" by not receiving the exhortation—not by refusing it—due to the statement: "Monks, the exhortation must not be rejected.
One is said to "incur [an offense] through use" by using an article that should have been relinquished without first relinquishing it. Regarding the five-day period...
One is said to incur an offense by not using [an item] when letting the time for wearing the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) pass.

One is said to incur an offense by sleeping together with a man during the night, but not during the day; one incurs it during the day, not at night, when dwelling in seclusion without having closed the door.
