Regarding the offenses mentioned for exceeding one night, three nights, seven nights, ten days, or a month:
one is said to incur the offense at dawn; one is not said to incur it at dawn when eating after having performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
One is said to "commit" [an offense] while repeatedly cutting both vegetation and the genitals; one is not said to "commit" [an offense] while not cutting hair or nails.
One is said to "commit" [an offense] while repeatedly concealing it; [the rule states]:
"One should come having covered oneself with grass or leaves; one must certainly not come naked. Whoever should come..."
One is said to "incur" this offense when one does not conceal it. One is said to "incur" [the offense] by repeatedly wearing garments such as those made of kusa grass.
One is said to "incur" the offense [of the bowl] when one does not keep it according to the rule: "This bowl of yours must be kept until it breaks."

“By oneself one makes oneself of a different communion”: when two Saṅghas are seated within a single boundary, if one sits on one side and adopts the view of the opposing side, one is said to make oneself of a different communion from those on the side where one is seated.
By becoming a completer of the quorum for those in whose presence one is seated—
He stirs up a dispute because he has not come within arm’s reach of the others. The same principle applies even among those of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka).
For those whose view he approves of, he is of the same communion; for the others, he is of a different communion. "Seven offenses, seven classes of offenses":
they are called offenses (āpatti) because they are to be incurred; they are called classes (khandha) in the sense of a heap. Thus, there are only two [categories].
The dyad is shown by way of names because "names exist. Regarding the phrase "either by formal act (kamma) or by the drawing of lots (salākaggāha)":
here, the motion (uddesa) and the formal act are one; the proclamation (vohāra), the announcement (anussāvana), and the drawing of lots are one;
the proclamation, the announcement, and the drawing of lots are the preliminary stages, while the formal act and the motion are the authoritative standard.
"One deficient in time" (*addhānahīna*) means one who is less than twenty years of age. "Deficient in limb" (*aṅgahīna*) means one belonging to the class of those with severed hands and so forth.
"Deficient in subject matter" (*vatthuvipanna*) means a paṇḍaka, an animal, and a hermaphrodite.

The remaining eight types of persons incapable [of ordination], such as those living in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), are called "those for whom there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*karaṇadukkaṭaka*). The performance of wrong-doing is *dukkaṭa*-action; [the result] occurs in this very same personal existence.
The meaning is that one has reached an impossible state because of one’s own past karma. "Incomplete" means having an incomplete set of bowl and robes.
"Does not ask" means does not ask for full ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding the phrase "of the shameless and the foolish":

even if he is shameless, if he is a master of the Three Pitakas (*tepiṭaka*), and even if he is foolish, if he is sixty years old—one should not live in dependence upon either of them. [Regarding] the foolish...
Regarding the phrase "and for one who is conscientious": here, even when commanding a fool, "Take formal support," the support must be granted;
however, for one who is conscientious, it is granted only when he asks. "With transgression" means with fault—that which, by practicing, one incurs an offense.
"Refusal by body" means refusal by means of gestures of the hand and so forth. "He acknowledges by body" means by means of gestures of the hand and so forth.
He acknowledges it. "Destructive" means causing harm. "Destructive to training" means the destruction of training. "Destructive to enjoyment" means the destruction of use;
herein, the three trainings should be understood as being "destructive to training" for one who does not train in them.
For one who uses what belongs to the Sangha or an individual in an improper manner, it should be understood as "destructive to enjoyment. Two...

*Venayika*: there are two meanings established by the Vinaya. "Laid down" (*paññatta*) means that which has been laid down throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka according to what is permissible and what is impermissible.
"In conformity with what is laid down" (*paññattānuloma*) is to be seen in the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*). "Destruction of the bridge" (*setughāta*) means the destruction of the condition;
the meaning is the non-arising even of that very mind by which one would make something impermissible. "Acting with moderation" (*mattakāritā*)...
"By measure" means by means of a standard; the meaning is "standing within the limit. "One commits through the body" means one commits via the door of the body;

that which pertains to the door of speech is committed by speech. "One emerges from it through the body" means that even without a formal confession (*desanā*), one emerges through the body alone in the case of the settlement by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*);
however, one who emerges after having confessed emerges through speech. Internal enjoyment...
"Consumption by swallowing" refers to eating. "External consumption" refers to things such as anointing the head.

"He bears the burden that has not yet come" means that, while being a *thera* himself, he bears the burden that must be borne by *theras*, such as fanning, taking up the fan, and seeking alms for the Dhamma;
he exerts energy in order to fulfill that task. "He does not bear the burden that has already come" means that the *thera* [does not neglect] the duty of a *thera*.

"He does not do it" means that he omits everything such as: "Monks, I allow the senior monk to either speak the Dhamma himself or to request another to do so; monks, I allow the Pātimokkha to be presided over by the senior monk.
"He feels remorse where there is no need for remorse" means that having felt remorse, he acts [only after having done so].
"Not being remorseful about what should be regretted" means that one does not act after having felt remorse for what should be regretted.

The meaning is that for these two [types of persons], the taints increase both by day and by night. The meaning of the subsequent dyad should also be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated.
The remainder is self-evident because it follows the method already explained in various places.
The commentary on the section on groups of two is finished. Commentary on the section on groups of three (Tikavāravaṇṇanā). 323.
Regarding the "groups of three": "There is an offense committed while the Blessed One is standing" means that there is an offense which one commits while [the Blessed One] is standing.

The meaning is that one incurs [the offense] against the Blessed One. This same method applies everywhere. In that regard, one incurs the offense of shedding blood while [the Buddha] is still present.
"But now, Ānanda, the bhikkhus address one another with the term 'friend' (āvuso);
after my passing, you must not address one another in this way. A junior bhikkhu, Ānanda, should address a senior bhikkhu as 'Venerable Sir' (bhante)..."

Because of the statement, "He should be addressed as 'Venerable' (āyasmā) or [by name]," one incurs an offense for addressing a senior elder with the term "friend" (āvuso) only after the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna,
not while he is still living. With the exception of these two offenses, all remaining ones are incurred both while the Blessed One is still living and after he has attained final Nibbāna.
One who, having performed the *pavāraṇā*, eats what is not left over, incurs an offense at the proper time (*kāla*), not at the improper time (*vikāla*).
However, one incurs an offense for eating at the improper time at the improper time, not at the proper time. All remaining [offenses] are incurred both at the proper time and at the improper time.

One incurs the offense of sleeping in the same dwelling as a woman at night; one incurs the offense of secluding oneself without closing the door during the day. The rest are incurred both at night and during the day.

If a fool who is incompetent establishes a following while thinking, "I am ten years [of standing], or I am more than ten years," he incurs an offense as one who is ten years, not as one who is less than ten years.
If a novice or one of middle standing establishes a following while thinking, "I am wise and competent," he incurs an offense as one who is less than ten years, not as one who is ten years.
As for the rest, they incur an offense both as those who are ten years and as those who are less than ten years.
One who is five years [of standing] but is foolish, incompetent, and living without dependence incurs an offense as one who is five years [of standing].

One who is newly ordained but considers himself wise and competent and lives without dependence incurs an offense as one who is less than five years [of standing]. The rest incur offenses both as those who are five years [of standing] and as those who are less than five years [of standing].
Teaching the recitation of the words of the Dhamma to one not fully ordained, or teaching the Dhamma to a woman—[these constitute offenses].

One commits such an offense with a wholesome mind; one commits [offenses] such as the pārājikas, emission of semen, bodily contact, lewdness, service for one's own sensual pleasure, corruption, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or striking with the palm or a clod of earth, etc., with an unwholesome mind; one commits [offenses] such as sleeping together in the same room unintentionally with an indeterminate mind;
whatever an Arahant commits, he commits it entirely with an indeterminate mind; and one who possesses pleasant feeling commits an offense such as sexual intercourse, etc.
One who possesses painful feeling encounters [kamma] such as that categorized by malice and hatred;
whereas one who possesses pleasant feeling encounters that very same thing while remaining neutral, thus encountering it as one possessing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Three rejections" refers to the three rejections of the Buddha, the Blessed One. "Great desire regarding the four requisites."
Lack of contentment is a failure to guard against the practice of the effacement of defilements; these three qualities were prohibited by the Blessed Buddha.
However, the three beginning with fewness of wishes were permitted by the Blessed Buddha; therefore it is said, "three were permitted.
One who presents himself to a community saying, "I have ten years [of seniority]," yet does not take formal dependence (nissaya) saying, "I have five years," incurs an offense of ignorance.

A wise person who, being less than ten years senior, represents an assembly as "I am competent" due to his great learning, and a wise person who does not take formal dependence (nissaya) while being less than five years senior, incur an offense that is not [an offense] for a fool;
the remainder are offenses incurred by both the wise and the fool.

One who does not enter the rains retreat incurs an offense during the dark fortnight, not during the bright fortnight; one who does not perform the Great Invitation (mahāpavāraṇā) incurs an offense during the bright fortnight.

One incurs [an offense] during the dark fortnight, but not during the light fortnight; for the remainder, one incurs [an offense] both during the dark and the light fortnights. Entering the rains residence is permitted during the dark fortnight, but not during the light fortnight;

the invitation at the Great Invitation ceremony is permitted during the light fortnight, but not during the dark fortnight; the rest that has been authorized is permitted both during the dark and the light fortnights.
While wearing the rainy-season robe that was set aside after being formally assigned on the first day following the full moon of the month of Kattikā:

One commits an offense in the winter. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "If one does not formally relinquish [the robe] on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, one commits an offense in the winter.
This too is well said, for it is stated: "One may determine [the robe] for four months, and beyond that, one may assign it [to another].
Thus, one who seeks [a robe] during the summer while more than a month remains, and one who puts it on while more than half a month remains, [commits an offense] in the summer.
"Enters upon" means: when one, while possessing a rain-cloak, lets the body be rained upon nakedly during the rainy season, one enters upon [the offense].
When the Saṅgha performs either the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* or the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*, it enters upon [the offense].

When a group (*gaṇa*) performs both the recitation of the Suttas and the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*, it enters upon [the offense]. When one alone performs the recitation of the Suttas and the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, [one enters upon the offense].
A person incurs [an offense] while performing [the act]. The same principle applies to the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).

The Sangha’s observance of the Uposatha and the Sangha’s invitation ceremony are appropriate only for the Sangha. The group’s observance of the Uposatha and the group’s invitation ceremony are appropriate only for the group.
The individual’s determination of the Uposatha and the individual’s determination of the invitation ceremony are appropriate only for the individual.
One who says, “I have committed a pārājika,” and so forth, conceals the *vatthu* (the underlying fact) but not the *āpatti* (the offense).

One who says, “I engaged in sexual intercourse,” and so forth, conceals the *āpatti* but not the *vatthu*. He who does not report either the *vatthu* or the *āpatti* conceals both the *vatthu* and the *āpatti*.
It covers, thus it is a "cover" (*paṭicchādi*). A sauna itself as a cover is a "sauna-cover" (*jantāgharapaṭicchādi*). The same method applies to the others as well.
It is permissible to perform the preparatory service while standing inside the sauna after closing the door.
This same thing is also permissible for one who has entered the water. In both cases, however, it is not permissible to chew food or eat. [This refers to] a cloth-cover (*vatthapaṭicchādi*).
Because it is made permissible in every respect, it is allowable to do everything while it is concealed. "Flowing" means they go forth or are carried away;
they do not incur blame or opposition. The lunar disk shines forth only when uncovered, being freed from clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and the *rāhu* demon;
it does not shine when covered by any one of those. Likewise the solar disk, and even the Dhamma and Vinaya, shine only when revealed.
He shines when teaching after having analyzed [the matter], not when it is concealed.

One who is ill incurs an offense by requesting one kind of medicine for the purpose of another; one who is not ill incurs an offense by requesting medicine for the purpose of medicine; as for the remaining offenses, both the one who is ill and the one who is not ill incur them.
"One incurs [an offense] within, not without" means that one who spreads his bedding intrusively incurs [an offense] within, not without; one incurs [an offense] without...
"Not inside" means that one who, having spread out a bed or other furniture belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air, departs, incurs the offense outside, not inside;
however, for the remainder [of the rules], one incurs it both inside and outside.

"Inside the boundary" means that a visitor, failing to perform the duties of a visitor, enters the monastery with his umbrella and sandals on, incurring the offense the very moment he steps across the precinct boundary (upacārasīma). "Outside the boundary" means...

A traveler departing without fulfilling the duties of a traveler—such as putting away wooden utensils and so forth—incurs an offense the very moment he crosses the boundary of the precinct (upacāra-sīma).
The remainder of such offenses are incurred both within the monastery boundary (sīmā) and outside it.
When there is an elder present, speaking the Dhamma without being requested does so in the midst of the Saṅgha; the same applies in the midst of a group or in the presence of an individual.

This is the method. "He emerges by means of the body" means he emerges by means of the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) method of settling. For one who confesses by speech without moving the body, he emerges by means of speech.
For one who confesses by performing a bodily act associated with speech, it is said that he emerges by means of both body and speech.
Even when the confession takes place in the midst of the Saṅgha, it leads to emergence; however, in the midst of a group or an individual...
She emerges only after she has undergone the formal act of confession (*desanā*). "He should intend for what is deep-seated" means he should intend for a state of firmness;

the meaning is that the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against one who does not fulfill the duties pertaining to one subject to an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and the like. And he is shameless and foolish.

Regarding the phrase "and one who is unattached" (*apakatatto*): here, one should not perform a formal act (*kamma*) merely because a fool is said to be "unattached" in the sense that he does not know what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, or because he does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense.
Rather, the meaning is that a formal act should be performed against one who has committed an offense rooted in foolishness or rooted in being unattached.
One who has failed in higher virtue (*adhisīla*) is called "one who has fallen away from virtue" (*sīlavipanna*) with respect to two classes of offenses.

"One who has fallen into [offense]" means one who has fallen into the five classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*). "One who has failed in conduct" means one who possesses extreme views (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*).
The formal act (*kamma*) must be performed against those very persons while they are still not seeing their offense, not making amends for it, and not relinquishing that view.
"Bodily dalliance" refers to improper conduct such as gambling with dice and the like; "verbal dalliance" refers to [improper speech] such as making lewd gestures with the mouth and so forth.
Improper conduct (*anācāra*): that which is called bodily and verbal improper conduct consists of various types such as dancing, singing, and so forth, and is improper conduct through both doors.

Bodily improper conduct means the transgression of training rules prescribed for the door of the body; verbal improper conduct means the transgression of training rules prescribed for the door of speech;
and bodily-verbal improper conduct means the transgression of training rules prescribed for both doors.
"By bodily injury" means by not training in the training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed for the door of the body;
for he who does not train in it brings about that injury, and therefore his non-training is called "bodily injury.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "By bodily wrong livelihood" refers to such things as sending messages on foot, and so forth.
"By means of medical treatment," such as by squeezing a boil and so forth; "by verbal means," such as by receiving instructions or making announcements;
the third phrase is stated by way of the combination of both.
"Enough, monk, no quarreling" means: "Enough, monk, do not engage in quarreling, do not engage in strife, do not engage in dispute."
The meaning is that he acts. "Not to be addressed" means that nothing should be said to him;
for even if such a person speaks, people consider his words unworthy of being heard.

"In no particular position" means that he should not be placed in any senior position, such as the head of a seed-vigil (*bījanaggāha*) or similar roles. "To one who is making an invitation" means: "Let the venerable one grant leave."
When one is asking for permission in this way, saying, "I wish to speak to him," [the other] should not grant the opportunity, thinking, "What will you do?
One should not give a reply, meaning one should neither accept the request nor listen to the words;
the meaning is that one should not go to the place where one intends to go after having accepted the invitation.
The Vinaya for a bhikkhu endowed with three factors is that which he himself knows;
that is what is called his Vinaya, and the meaning is that he need not be questioned. "No further inquiry should be granted" means that when he asks, "Is this allowable?
no opportunity for such a question should be given; he should be told, "Ask something else. Thus, he is neither to be questioned, nor is there to be an occasion for his questioning.

The meaning is "should be heard. "The Vinaya is not to be discussed" means that the question of the Vinaya is not to be debated; the discourse on what is permissible and what is impermissible is not to be deliberated upon.
"Without abandoning this" means without relinquishing this view, such as the claim of being a "professed celibate" (*brahmacāri*).

"A pure celibate" refers to a monk whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. "'He falls into the state of being drunk' (*pātabyataṃ āpajjati*)" means he falls into the practice of consuming that which is to be drunk.

But because of the statement, “Without abandoning this,” one should abandon that claim to being a celibate practitioner, ask forgiveness from the one whose taints are destroyed, saying, “I have spoken falsely;
forgive me,” relinquish the view that “there is no fault in sensual pleasures,” and perform purification of the destiny.
“Roots of the unwholesome” (akusalamūlāni) means both unwholesome and roots, or the roots of the unwholesome; thus they are the roots of the unwholesome.
The same method applies to the roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) as well. "Misconduct" (*duccarita*) refers to conduct that is wicked or deformed;
"good conduct" (*sucarita*) refers to conduct that is excellent or beautiful. Bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) is misconduct performed by means of the body acting as the instrument.
This same method applies everywhere. The remainder is self-evident, as it follows the method explained in various other places.
The commentary on the section on triads is finished.
Commentary on the section on tetrads (324):

Among the tetrads, "one commits [an offense] by one's own speech and emerges from it through another's speech" refers to that which pertains to the door of speech, such as the various types of *padasodhamma* and so forth.
"Having committed an offense, one who has gone to the place of the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) settlement is cleared by another’s formal act (*kammavācā*).

One commits [the offense] by another’s speech and is cleared by one’s own speech": this means that regarding the non-renunciation of a wicked view, one commits it by another’s formal act, but when confessing in the presence of the individual, one is cleared by one’s own speech. By one’s own speech...

"He commits through his own speech and emerges through his own speech" means that he commits an offense—such as the recitation of a verse (*padasodhamma*) and so forth—which is connected to the door of speech through his own speech;

even when emerging from it by confessing, he emerges through his own speech. "He commits through another's speech and emerges through another's speech" means that he commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense involving a formal act up to the third time through another person’s formal act (*kammavācā*); even when emerging from it...

One emerges from another’s offense through formal acts such as the *parivāsa* (probation). Beyond that, one commits an offense belonging to the door of the body by means of the body, or one emerges from it by means of speech while confessing.
One commits an offense belonging to the door of speech by means of speech, and one emerges from it by means of the body through the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass).

One commits an offense belonging to the door of the body by means of the body, and one emerges from that very same offense by means of the body through the *tiṇavatthāraka*. [An offense] belonging to the door of speech...
One falls into an offense by means of speech, and while confessing that very same offense, one emerges from it by means of speech.

When one has not spread one’s own bedding over a couch belonging to the Sangha, one falls asleep and incurs an offense involving a count of body hairs for physical contact, as well as the offense of sleeping in the same dwelling;
however, having woken up, knowing the state of having fallen into the offense, and confessing it, one emerges from it while awake. While tending [to the sick],...
But having committed [an offense] while lying down in the state of the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) method of settling, one commits it upon waking and emerges from it while asleep;
this is called "emerging while asleep. The latter two phrases should also be understood according to what has been stated.

One who is without consciousness commits an offense that is without consciousness; later, while confessing it, one who possesses consciousness emerges from it. Regarding an offense that possesses consciousness...
One is said to incur [an offense] with a conscious mind. When lying down in the place for the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka), one emerges from it without a conscious mind.
The remaining two cases should also be understood according to what has been stated. He who confesses a similar offense (sabhāga-āpatti) incurs a *dukkaṭa* due to the act of confessing;
while confessing that [offense], he may also incur one of the other categories, such as a *pācittiya*, and in doing so, he incurs a *dukkaṭa*. However, that...
One who incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense emerges from a *pācittiya* or similar offense; and one who emerges from a *pācittiya* or similar offense incurs that [same] offense.
Thus, it should be understood that this tetrad—"one who incurs an offense confesses it"—was stated with reference to a single individual and a single application of effort.
In the tetrad of formal acts (*kamma*), one incurs the offense of not relinquishing an evil view through a formal act; one emerges from it by confessing, which is not a formal act.

One incurs offenses such as neglect (*vissaṭṭhi*) without a formal act, and emerges from them through formal acts such as probation (*parivāsa*). One incurs the offense of formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*) only through a formal act, and emerges from it through a formal act.
The remainder are incurred without a formal act, and one emerges from them without a formal act.
In the tetrad of requisites, the first is one’s own personal requisite; the second belongs to the Saṅgha; the third is the property of a shrine (cetiyasantaka);

and the fourth is the property of a layperson. However, if it has been brought for the purpose of the bowl, robes, new construction, or medicine, it is permissible to place the lid inside to give it away.
In the tetrad concerning the presence [of the Sangha]: one incurs the offense of not relinquishing a pernicious view in the presence of the Sangha;
however, at the time of the formal resolution (*vuṭṭhāna*), since there is no further duty for the Sangha, one is resolved in their absence.

One incurs [offenses] such as "neglect" (*vissaṭṭhi*) in the absence [of the Sangha], but resolves them in the presence of the Sangha. "Formal admonition" (*samanubhāsana*) is incurred only in the presence of the Sangha.

One emerges [from the offense] in the presence [of others]. The remainder—consisting of the various types such as intentional lying and so forth—is incurred only in the absence [of others], and one emerges from it only in their absence.
The "tetrad of unknowing" is similar to the "tetrad of the mindless. Regarding "by the manifestation of gender":
while a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī is still sleeping, if a change of gender occurs, there is an offense for sharing a sleeping place [with the opposite sex].
"This is indeed said with reference to that. Furthermore, for both [sexes], an offense not common to both is cleared by the manifestation of the sex.

In the tetrad regarding simultaneous acquisition: when a bhikkhu’s sex changes, he simultaneously with the acquisition of the sex abandons the former male sex—by virtue of its being the first to arise and its being superior—and [assumes] the subsequent female sex.
It is established; the bodily and verbal intimation occurring by way of the appearance of a man or a super-man and so forth subsides; designations occurring as "bhikkhu" or "man" cease;
and regarding those forty-six training rules not shared with bhikkhunīs, there is indeed no offense for him. However, in the second tetrad, for whichever bhikkhunī...
The gender changes: she abandons the feminine gender, which had come later, was subsequently arisen, or had reached the status of being inferior, and is reckoned as "last";
she becomes established in the masculine gender, which has reached the status of being "prior" in the manner already described.
The communications that occurred in the opposite way—those occurring as "nun" or "woman"—subside.

They also cease with respect to the designation (*paṇṇatti*); that is, regarding those one hundred and thirty training rules (*sikkhāpada*) which are not shared by other monks, there is indeed no offense for them.
"The four exalted points" (*sāmukkaṃsa*) refers to the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), for these were established by the Blessed One himself when the matter had not yet arisen.
Because they are set aside by being lifted up and raised high, they are called "excellent" (*sāmukkaṃsā*). As for "enjoyments," these refer to edible enjoyments;
however, water is permissible even if not formally received, because it is not restricted by time.

It is not permissible to consume the various types of food, such as those to be consumed only at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), if they have not been formally received. The four great raw meats are permissible during the aforementioned times, because they are visible at that time.
"A lay follower who is virtuous" means one who guards the five or ten precepts.

Regarding the fourfold set beginning with "newcomers": when entering or wandering within a monastery while carrying a sunshade and wearing sandals, and with his head covered, only the newcomer incurs the offense, not the resident.
However, one who fails to perform the duties of a resident incurs the offense as a resident.
There is no offense for the visitor. Regarding the remaining offenses pertaining to the doors of body and speech, both incur them;

however, for an offense that is not common to both, neither the visitor nor the resident incurs it. In the tetrad concerning those departing, one who departs without fulfilling the duties of one departing incurs an offense, but the resident does not.
Conversely, one who fails to perform the duties of a resident incurs an offense, but the one departing does not.
The remainder both incur; neither incurs that which is not common to both.

In the tetrad concerning the diversity of the basis (*vatthu*), there is only a mutual diversity of the basis for the four *pārājika* offenses, not a diversity of the offense itself; for all of them are indeed the same *pārājika* offense.
This same principle applies to the *saṅghādisesa* and other offenses as well. Regarding the bodily contact between a monk and a nun: [the offense is incurred by both].

For a monk it is a *saṅghādisesa*, but for a nun it is a *pārājika*; thus there is a difference in the offense (*āpatti*), but not a difference in the basis (*vatthu*), for in both cases the basis is indeed physical contact.

Likewise, the application should be understood here according to this same method: "In the case of eating garlic, it is a *pācittiya* for a nun, but a *dukkaṭa* for a monk," and so forth. [This applies] to the four *pārājikas*.

With respect to the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses, there is both a diversity of bases (*vatthu-nānatta*) and a diversity of offenses (*āpatti-nānatta*). The same applies to the *saṅghādisesas* and so forth in relation to the *aniyata* offenses and others.
However, for monks and nuns who simultaneously commit the four *pārājika* offenses from the very beginning, there is neither a diversity of bases nor a diversity of offenses.
Even when they commit them separately, the remaining common offenses (*sādhāraṇāpatti*) [are treated similarly].
The same principle applies even when they are committing [the offense].

In the tetrad concerning the similarity of the basis (*vatthusabhāga*) and so forth: in the case of physical contact between a monk and a nun, there is similarity of the basis, but not similarity of the offense;
in the four *pārājika* offenses, there is similarity of the offense, but not similarity of the basis. This is the method.

Regarding the *saṅghādisesa* offenses and the rest: for a monk and a nun, there is both similarity of the underlying matter (*vatthusabhāgatā*) and similarity of the offense (*āpattisabhāgatā*) in respect of the four *pārājika* rules. This same method applies to all common offenses (*sādhāraṇāpatti*).

In the case of an uncommon offense (*asādhāraṇāpatti*), there is neither similarity of the underlying matter nor similarity of the offense. For that which was the first question in the preceding tetrad is here the second.
And he who is the second there is the first here. There is no difference between the third and fourth [cases].
In the tetrad concerning the preceptor, when the resident pupil fails to perform the duty that must be performed for the preceptor, the preceptor incurs an offense;
the resident pupil does not incur an offense for failing to perform the duty that must be performed for the preceptor.
There is no *upajjhāya* [offense]; the rest both incur, and both do not incur what is non-common. The same method applies to the fourfold set concerning the teacher (*ācariya*).

Regarding the fourfold set concerning taking [food], one who takes with his own hand a full portion or more than a full portion incurs a heavy offense; by commanding another, saying "Take less than a full portion," he incurs a light offense. By this method, the remaining three items should be understood. Regarding the fourfold set concerning those worthy of salutation:
first, among the bhikkhunīs, starting from the ninth bhikkhunī in the meal hall, even the *upajjhāya*...
They are worthy of salutation but not worthy of rising up. And in general, for a monk who has finished his meal, anyone who is senior is [worthy of rising].
Even for one who has been on probation for sixty years, a person ordained on that very day who comes into his presence is worthy of rising up, but not worthy of salutation.
In places where it is not prohibited, a senior is both worthy of salutation and worthy of rising up by a junior.
Furthermore, a junior is neither worthy of being saluted nor worthy of being stood up for by an elder.

The first phrase of the "fourfold set on being worthy of a seat" is identical in meaning to the second phrase of the preceding fourfold set, and the second phrase is identical in meaning to the first.

In the "fourfold set on time," one who eats after having invited [others] incurs an offense at the proper time, not at an improper time; [one incurs] the offense of eating at an improper time at an improper time.

[The first] is permissible only at the proper time; the remainder is permissible both at the proper time and at the improper time; that which is not shared is permissible neither at the proper time nor at the improper time.

Regarding the tetrad of what has been received: food received before the midday meal is permissible at the proper time, not at the improper time. A beverage is permissible at the improper time, but on the following day it is not permissible at the proper time.
That which is for seven days and that which is for life are permissible both at the proper time and at the improper time.

Furthermore, for each person, the three types of food that are "only during the proper time" (yāvakālika), as well as unallowable meat, whether already received or not yet received, are permissible neither at the proper time nor at the improper time.
Regarding the fourfold set of border regions: when one establishes a boundary in the ocean, it applies to the bordering provinces, but not to the central provinces.

When one confers full ordination with a group of five, one incurs the offenses of *guṇaṅguṇūpāhana* (sandals with many layers), *dhuvanahāna* (shoes with thick soles), and *cammattharaṇa* (leather mats) in the Middle Countries, but not in the Border Regions.
Regarding these four, even one who says, "These are not permitted here," incurs them in the Border Regions;
however, one who says, "These are permitted here," incurs them in the Middle Countries.
One incurs a remaining offense in both cases; one does not incur an uncommon offense anywhere.
In the second tetrad, all four types of matters, such as ordination by a group of five, are permitted in the border regions.
To illustrate that "this is permitted," it is permitted only there and not in the Middle Countries. However, to illustrate that "this is not permitted," it is [forbidden] in the Middle Countries.

It is allowable in the inhabited districts (janapada), but not in the border regions (paccanta). The remainder—beginning with "I allow you, monks, five kinds of salt"—which has been authorized, is allowable in both places.
However, that which is declared unallowable and prohibited is not allowable in either place. Regarding the fourfold set beginning with "inside":
one enters the offense of lying down inside [a dwelling] by intruding, not outside; as for the beds and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air...
When departing after having set it down, one commits an offense outside, not inside; the remainder [of offenses] are both inside and outside; the uncommon [offense] is neither inside nor outside.
In the fourfold group beginning with "inside the boundary," a visitor who fails to fulfill the duty commits an offense inside the boundary; a traveler commits an offense outside the boundary;
one commits an offense both inside and outside the boundary regarding lying and so forth; the uncommon [offense] is not...
In some cases: regarding the training rule (sekhiya-paññatti) connected with entering houses within a group of four villages, one commits it in a village, not in the forest.
A bhikkhunī, by causing dawn to rise [while staying overnight], commits it in the forest, not in a village. False speech and so forth are committed both in a village and in the forest;
that which is not common [to both] is committed nowhere at all.
Regarding the phrase "four preliminary duties," it is stated that the fourfold preparation consisting of "the broom, the lamp, water, and the seat" is called the *pubbakaraṇa*.

However, these—namely, the motion for the assembly (*chandapārisuddhi*), the declaration of the season (*utu-akkhāna*), the counting of the monks (*bhikkhu-gaṇanā*), and the exhortation (*ovāda*)—are to be understood as the "four preliminary duties.
Regarding the "four appropriate occasions," [it refers to] the Uposatha for as many...
And when the monks who have reached the stage for the formal act (kamma) have arrived, no similar offenses exist, and there are no persons to be avoided present—this is called "the time is right.

Regarding the four *pācittiya* rules concerning "nothing else" (*anañña*): these are those stated as "having made this very condition, [there is] a *pācittiya* offense, and nothing else," namely the training rule on lying down in encroachment (*anupakhajjaseyyā*) and the training rule on making a bed (*kappana*). "Come, friend... [etc.]
The training rule regarding "a village or a town," intentionally causing remorse, and standing to eavesdrop—these are the four.
The four formal permissions of the Saṅgha (bhikkhusammuti) are: "If a bhikkhu should stay apart from his three robes for even one night, except by permission of the Saṅgha;
if he should have a new rug made, except by permission of the Saṅgha."
“Furthermore, if he should stay apart for longer than that, except by the authorization of the monks, or if he should inform a person who is not fully ordained of a grave offense,
except by the authorization of the monks”— thus are the authorizations [mentioned], freed from the thirteen [types of] authorization as they have come down.
In the tetrad on the sick, if a sick person, out of greed, asks for something else when he has need of another medicine, he incurs an offense.
When one who is not ill requests medicine for the purpose of making it into a non-medicine, they incur an offense; when [requesting] lying and so forth, both incur an offense;
and neither incurs an offense regarding what is not common. The rest is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the section on the tetrads is finished.
**Commentary on the Pentads (Pañcakavāravaṇṇanā)** 325.
Regarding the pentads, the statement that "five persons are fixed" refers specifically to those who have committed the immediate offenses (*ānantariya*). The five offenses involving cutting are:
[exceeding the prescribed] measure for beds and chairs; for sitting cloths; for itch-covering cloths; for rain-cloaks; and for robes of the Sugata’s proportions.

And it should be understood [as follows]. "In five ways" means: lack of shame, ignorance, being overcome by remorse, the perception of what is improper as proper, and the perception of what is proper as improper—these are the five.
"Five offenses caused by lying" refers to the *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, *dukkaṭa*, *saṅghādisesa*, and *pācittiya* offenses.
"Going uninvited" means: going among families before or after a meal without having asked a monk who is present.
Regarding the phrase "he would incur [an offense]": this refers to the absence of having asked for permission before going on alms-round.

"Non-determination" (anadhiṭṭhāna): Determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is the act of determining the meal after having determined the occasion mentioned in the rule, "In eating in a group, except at the proper occasion.
Not doing so is non-determination. "Non-designation" (avikappanā): This is the non-performance of that designation which was prescribed in the case of eating in succession (paramparabhojana).
For these five [types of food] are already rejected by the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of eating only alms-food.
"Suspected and suspected of" means that he is both suspected and suspected of by those who see him and those who hear about him.
Even though he is of an unshakeable nature and his taints are destroyed, nevertheless, these improper resorts must be avoided; for by being seen among them, one might incur dishonor or censure.
Or it is discarded. *Sosānika* means that which has fallen in a charnel ground. *Pāpaṇika* means that which has fallen at the door of a shop.
*Thūpacīvara* means that which has been offered as a ritual oblation by encircling an anthill. *Ābhisekika* means a robe discarded either at a bathing place or at the site of a king’s consecration.
*Bhatapaṭiyābhata* means that which was brought back after having been taken to a charnel ground. The five great thieves...
These are spoken of in relation to superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

Regarding the five offenses that originate from the body: by means of the first origin of offense, one incurs five offenses—namely, those offenses stated in the intermediate section of the *Peṭaka* (the *Antarapeyyāla*), such as:
"A bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, builds a hut by means of begging."
"Five offenses by way of body and speech": by means of the third origin of offenses (*āpatti-samudāna*), one incurs five offenses;
these are the offenses stated in that very context: "A bhikkhu, perceiving it as allowable, builds a hut after making an arrangement.
"Those leading to confession" (*desanā-gāminiyo*) refers to all remaining offenses, excluding the *pārājika* and the *saṅghādisesa*.
"Five legal acts" means five: the four—*tajjanīya*, *niyassa*, *pabbājanīya*, and *paṭisāraṇīya*—and the threefold *ukkhepanīya* (act of suspension) as one.

"Five up to the third time" means: for a nun who follows one who has been suspended and does not relinquish her position after being admonished up to the third time, there are three offenses—*pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa*; and [similarly] in the cases of admonishing those who follow a schismatic and so forth.
An offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*); an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for not relinquishing an evil view. "Not given" means not given by another.
"Unknown" means unknown due to the absence of the intention [thinking], "I am receiving it.
"Unallowable" means that which has been made unallowable by the five monastic allowances (*samaṇakappa*), or whatever else is unallowable meat or unallowable food. "Not made into leftovers" means...

Having performed the *pavāraṇā*, [food] that has not been declared leftover (*atiritta*) is not permitted. "Giving for a festival" (*samajjadāna*) refers to giving for performances such as those by actors.

"Giving a bull" (*usabhadāna*) refers to releasing a bull among a herd of cattle. "Giving for wall-painting" (*cittakammadāna*) is permissible provided one builds a dwelling and has wall-paintings executed there;
however, this statement is made with reference to the giving of wall-paintings as a decorative offering (*paṭibhānacittakammadāna*). For although these five [types of gifts], even if...
In the world, these are considered meritorious, yet they are actually demeritorious and unwholesome.

Regarding the phrase "an arisen flash of inspiration" (*uppannaṃ paṭibhānaṃ*), here "flash of inspiration" refers to the desire to speak. "These five are difficult to dispel" means they are not easily dispelled;
however, the sense is that they can be dispelled by means of appropriate methods, reasons, reflections, instructions, and so forth.
"His own heart becomes serene": regarding this, there are these instances.

It is said that the Elder Phussadeva, who lived in Kaṭa-andhakāra, after sweeping the courtyard of the Cetiya and arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, looked upon the courtyard—its sand strewn evenly as if covered with *sinduvāra* flowers—and, giving rise to rapture and gladness directed toward the Buddha, [his heart became serene].
He stood there. At that moment, Māra, having become like a black monkey born at the foot of a mountain, went about scattering cow dung across the courtyard of the cetiya.
The Elder was unable to attain *arahantship*; he swept it up and departed.
On the second day as well, having become an old ox, he caused a similar disturbance. On the third day, [he became] one with crooked legs...
Having manifested the form of a human being, he went along walking about on his feet.
The Elder thought, "There is no such hideous person within the surrounding villages for a league’s distance; could this be Māra?
Having reflected thus, he said, "Are you Māra? "Yes, venerable sir, I am Māra; I was not able to deceive you now. "Have you been seen before?"
“By her, the Tathāgata? “Yes, he was seen before. “Māra is possessed of great power;
come now, fashion a body for the Blessed Buddha that is identical to his own body.
“It is not possible, Bhante, to fashion such a form; however, I shall fashion a likeness that resembles it.”
Abandoning his own natural form, he stood there with a body resembling that of the Buddha.

The Elder looked at Māra and thought, "If even this one, still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, shines so brightly, how much more must the Blessed One shine, being entirely free from lust, hatred, and delusion?
Having thus attained joy directed toward the Buddha, he intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship.
He attained it. Māra said, "I have been deceived by you, Bhante. The Elder replied, "What is there, O Death of Decay, that could deceive such as me?
While dwelling in the space between worlds, a young bhikkhu named Datta, having swept the courtyard of the cetiya and looking about, attained the white-kasiṇa.
He produced the eight attainments. Then, having developed insight, he—
He realized the threefold fruit.
Regarding the phrase "the minds of others were inspired with confidence," here are the instances:
A young bhikkhu named Tissa, having swept the courtyard of the Jambukola Cetiya, stood holding a refuse-broom in his hand. At that moment, the Elder Tissadatta—

Having disembarked from the boat named Nāva, while surveying the *caitya* courtyard, the Elder Nāgasena recognized it as a place well-swept by one whose mind was cultivated; thus he asked ten thousand questions, and the other answered them all.
Furthermore, in another monastery, the Elder had swept the *caitya* courtyard and finished his duties when four elders arrived from the realm of the Yonakas to worship the *caitya*.
Having seen the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyangaṇa*), one elder stood at the very door without entering within and recollected eight eons;
another recollected sixteen; another twenty; and another thirty eons.
Regarding the phrase "the deities were delighted," this is the story: it is said that in a certain monastery, a certain monk [was walking] around the courtyard of the shrine...
Having swept the circle of the Bodhi tree, he went to bathe.
A deity, with a mind full of faith, thinking, "Since this monastery was built, there has never been a monk who has performed the duties and swept it so well," stood there with a handful of flowers.
When the Elder returned, she asked, "Venerable sir, where do you dwell? He replied, "I dwell in such-and-such a village. She said, "Venerable sir, we live right here; regarding this monastery—"

"Venerable sirs, since there has been no monk who had previously been formally ordained (*sammā-ṭhapubba*) who fulfilled the duties (*vatta*) in this manner from the very moment of his ordination, we have stood here with flowers in our hands, having gained confidence in your conduct," said the deities.
Regarding the phrase "conducive to inspiring confidence," this is the story: it is said that [the Blessed One] saw a certain minister’s son and the Elder Abhaya...
With reference to this, the following conversation arose: "What if we were to look at both the minister’s son and the Elder Abhaya from one place? Are they indeed handsome?
The kinsmen, having adorned the minister’s son, went forth with the thought, "We shall have him pay homage at the Great Cetiya.
The Elder’s mother also had a beautiful robe made and sent it to her son, saying: "My son, having had your hair shorn..."
“Having put on this robe and surrounded by the community of monks, let him pay homage to the Great Cetiya.
The minister’s son, surrounded by his kinsmen, ascended the courtyard of the cetiya by the eastern gate;
the Elder Abhaya, surrounded by the community of monks, ascended the courtyard of the cetiya by the southern gate, met him there in the courtyard, and said: “What...?”
“Friend, after you had thrown away the rubbish in the place swept by the Elder Mahallaka Thera, you took up a position alongside me.
It is said that in a past existence, the Elder Abhaya was the Elder named Mahallaka;
while he was sweeping the courtyard of the shrine in the alms-village, a great lay devotee who was the son of a minister took the rubbish from the place he had swept and threw it away.
"The Teacher’s instruction has been carried out": this refers to the duty of sweeping, which has been praised by the Buddhas;
therefore, by one who performs it, the Teacher’s instruction is fulfilled. Here is an account of this:

it is said that the Venerable Sāriputta went to the Himālaya mountains and, without having swept a certain mountain cave, sat down and attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). The Blessed One, reflecting upon this—
Knowing that the Elder had remained seated without sweeping, he traveled through the air, showed his feet in the unswept spot before the Elder, and returned.
When the Elder emerged from his meditative attainment and saw the Blessed One’s feet, he established a powerful sense of shame and moral dread;
kneeling on his calves, he thought, "Alas, my Teacher has seen me sitting here without having swept!"
Thinking, "I shall now issue a formal charge against him in the midst of the Saṅgha," he went into the presence of the One of Ten Powers, paid homage, and sat down.
The Blessed One asked, "Where have you been, Sāriputta? and replied, "It is no longer fitting for you to sit without having swept the area while walking in a place close to me.
From that time forth, the Elder [would sweep] even the place where the gong was hung.
Standing, he stands only after sweeping away the refuse with his foot.
He does not grasp the limit of his own speech means that he does not set a limit to his own speech by thinking, "In this matter, so much sūtra is found;
there is so much exposition; I shall speak so much sūtra and exposition. Thus [he does not fix] the limit of his own speech.
He does not grasp it. One who does not grasp it in this way—namely, "This is the former statement of the accuser, this is the latter statement;
this is the former statement of the accused, this is the latter statement; so much is relevant, so much is not relevant"—is said not to grasp the limits of another's speech.
"He does not know the offense" means he does not know whether it is a *pārājika* or...
"Saṅghādisesa" means he does not know the distinction between the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
"Root" refers to the two roots of an offense, namely body and speech; he does not know those. "Origin" refers to the six origins of offenses (*āpattisamudaya*);
he does not know those. It is also said that he does not know the basis (*vatthu*) for the *pārājika* and other offenses.
"Cease": this offense ceases through confession; it is pacified by rising from it. Thus, one does not know the cessation of offenses.
Furthermore, one who does not know the seven principles for settling disputes does not know the path leading to the cessation of offenses.
Regarding the fivefold classification of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), "legal issue" refers to the four types of legal issues. The "root of a legal issue" is as follows:

There are thirty-three roots: twelve roots for a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), fourteen for a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), six for a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and one for a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*); these will be explained further on.

The "origin of legal issues" (*adhikaraṇasamudaya*) means the source of legal issues. A legal issue arising from a dispute arises in dependence upon the eighteen grounds for schism (*bhedakaravatthu*).

The meaning is that he does not know this classification: that a legal issue arising from an accusation consists of the four failures; a legal issue arising from an offense consists of the seven classes of offenses; and a legal issue arising from business consists of the four duties of the Saṅgha.

He does not know the cessation of legal issues means that he does not know the settlement through a formal decision, having proceeded root-to-root according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.

He is unable to bring it to resolution; one who does not know the seven methods of settling—such as, "this legal issue is settled by two, this by four, this by three, and this by one"—is said not to know the practice leading to the cessation of legal issues.
"He does not know the basis" means he does not know, for instance, "this is the basis for a *pārājika* offense, this is the basis for a *saṅghādisesa* offense," and so forth.
He does not know the basis for the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*). Regarding the "origin" (*nidāna*):
he does not know, "This training rule was laid down here among the seven origins; this one there. He does not know the "formulation" (*paññatti*):
he does not know the original formulation (*paṭhamapaññatti*) for each respective training rule. He does not know the "subsequent formulation" (*anupaññatti*): the repeated formulation.
"He does not know" means he does not know the sequence of the discourse by way of the sequence of the narrative and the sequence of the decision.
"He does not know the motion (*ñatti*)" means he does not know the motion in its entirety.

"He does not know the performance of the motion" means he does not know the function of the motion; for among the nine points such as reinstatement (*osāraṇā*), there is what is called the formal act of motion.

In formal acts consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) or one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), he does not know that [the candidate] stands having reached the stage of the formal act through the motion.
He is neither skilled in what precedes nor skilled in what follows; thus he does not know what should be said first and what should be said later.
He also does not know that the motion must be placed first and should not be placed later. And he is one who does not know the proper time.
He does not know the proper time; he speaks unasked and uninvited; he does not know the time for a motion (*ñatti*), the field for a motion, or the occasion for a motion.
"Through dullness and delusion" means that, solely due to ignorance and a state of bewilderment, he fails to understand the benefits of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"One of evil desires" means one who, by means of that forest-dwelling, hopes for the acquisition of requisites. "Seclusion" refers to seclusion of body, mind, and material possessions.
"Having this as its purpose" (*idamatthitā*): because this noble practice has this as its purpose, it is "having this as its purpose";

the state of having this as its purpose is "the fact of having this as its purpose. The meaning is that one relies solely on that fact of having this as its purpose, and not on any other worldly bait (*lokāmisa*).

"One does not know the *uposatha*" means one does not know the ninefold *uposatha*. "The *uposatha* ritual" refers to [rituals] divided by way of being contrary to the Dhamma, lacking a quorum, and so forth.
He does not know the fourfold Uposatha procedure. He does not know the *Pātimokkha*, which consists of the two Matikas.

He does not know the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, that is, the ninefold recitation of the *Pātimokkha* in its entirety. He does not know the Invitation (*Pavāraṇā*), that is, the ninefold Invitation.
The formal act of Invitation (*Pavāraṇākamma*) is exactly like the formal act of Uposatha.
In the *Apāsādikapañcaka*: "Unattractive" (*apāsādika*) refers to unwholesome action such as bodily misconduct; "attractive" (*pāsādika*) refers to wholesome action such as good bodily conduct.
"Excessively" (*ativela*) means having transgressed the proper time, spending too much time among families—this is the meaning.
"Entry" (*otāra*) is the penetration into the defilements. "Defiled" (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) refers to various types [of offenses], such as grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) and physical contact.
By including the prohibition within the group of five purifications (*visuddhipañcaka*), all nine kinds of invitation (*pavāraṇā*) should be understood. The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the section on the pentads is finished.
The commentary on the section on the hexads.
326. Regarding the wheels (*cakka*): the six proper conducts (*sāmīci*) are as follows: "That monk is not censured and those monks are worthy of praise;
this is the proper conduct therein"; "Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own welfare; let not your own welfare perish—this is the proper conduct therein";
"This bowl of yours is to be kept until it breaks—this is the proper conduct therein"; "Having taken it out from there..."
“It should be shared with the bhikkhus; this is the proper conduct therein. “It should be understood, inquired about, and investigated;
this is the proper conduct therein. “He who has [the need] shall take it away; this is the proper conduct therein.
These are the six rules of proper conduct (*sāmīci*) found in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha itself. As for the “six things to be cut off,” these are the five mentioned in the Pañcaka [Vagga].
There are six [offenses] together with the *udakasāṭikā* (bathing robe) for bhikkhunīs. "In six ways" means:

through lack of shame, through ignorance, through being overcome by anxiety (*kukkucca*), through perceiving what is improper as proper, through perceiving what is proper as improper, and through forgetfulness. Among these, one incurs an offense through forgetfulness in cases such as exceeding the limits of one day, three days, or seven days.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. "Six benefits for one who masters the Vinaya" is from the *Pañcaka*.
Including this [term] "the Uposatha is under his authority," there are six.
Regarding the "six maximums": "An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days; that monk must store that robe for a maximum of one month;
that monk may accept a robe from beyond that [period] as a maximum consisting of an inner and outer garment."
One should stand silently in attendance for no more than six meal-times. Furthermore, having had a new rug made, a monk must use it for six years;
it may be used for a maximum of six years. One may carry [robes] with one's own hands for a distance of up to three *yojanas*.
An extra bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days. Food stored for personal consumption may be kept for a maximum of seven days.
These may be used; that monk may be separated from that robe for at most six nights;

[the robe] may be taken up [as a patch] to a maximum of four *kaṃsa*-weights, or two and a half *kaṃsa*-weights, or a maximum of two finger-joints; the bed-leg support may be a maximum of eight finger-breadths;
the tooth-stick may be a maximum of eight finger-breadths—these are the fourteen maximums. Therein:
The first six constitute one set of six; then, having removed one from that, by adding it to each of the remaining [sets] in this manner, other sets of six should also be formed.

"Six offenses" refers to three sets of six mentioned in the *Antarapeyyāla*. "Six legal acts" refers to the acts of censure (*tajjanīya*), demotion (*niyassa*), banishment (*pabbājanīya*), and reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*).

There are four [offenses]: the two mentioned regarding the non-acknowledgment of an offense and the non-remediation of one constitute one, and the non-renunciation of a wrong view constitutes another, making six.
Regarding bathing, there is the offense for bathing within half a month. The two sets of six beginning with "uncompleted robe" are explained in the Kathina-khandhaka.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the section of sixes is finished.
Commentary on the Section of Sevens (Sattakavāravaṇṇanā) 327.
Regarding the sevens: "Seven kinds of proper conduct" refers to the six previously mentioned [cases] where "that nun has not been fully ordained... [and so forth].
And those nuns are to be censured; this is the proper conduct in that regard—having added this, seven [cases] are to be understood.
There are seven illegitimate procedures for acting upon a confession: "A monk has committed an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*);
when being accused of a *pārājika*, he confesses, 'I have committed a formal meeting offense (*saṅghādisesa*)'; the Saṅgha [then deals with him] by means of a *saṅghādisesa*..."
"He causes [an act] to be performed that is contrary to the Dhamma by means of a formal admission"—thus it is explained in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
Lawful procedures (*dhammika*) are also explained in that same place. "There is no offense for one who goes on a seven-day mission" is stated in the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*.
"Seven benefits for one who maintains the Vinaya" refers to these together with: "The Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies are under his authority."
The five mentioned in the *Pañcaka* become seven. Regarding the "seven maximums," those very same items mentioned in the *Chakka* should be applied according to the sevenfold set.
The two sevenfold sets beginning with "the robe is finished" (*katacīvara*) are specified in the *Kathina-kkhandhaka*. [The cases are:
"no offense is to be seen for the monk," "an offense is to be seen for the monk," and "for the monk..."
“There is an offense that must be expiated”—these are three sets of seven; two are non-Dhamma and one is Dhamma; all three of these are explained in the Campeyyaka [Khandhaka].
“Non-Dhamma” means the qualities of the wicked, or the qualities of those who are not good;
the meaning is that they are unattractive, base, and inferior. “True Dhamma” means the qualities of the virtuous, such as the Buddhas and others; or it means the qualities that are truly good.
"Beautiful" means "excellent. The rest is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the section of seven is finished.
The commentary on the section of eight.
328. Regarding the *Aṭṭhakas*—the eight benefits: “We will not perform the Uposatha together with this monk;
we will perform the Uposatha without this monk; we will not invite him to the Pavāraṇā;

we will perform the formal acts of the Saṅgha [without him]; we will sit on the seats [without him]; we will sit at the drinking of rice-gruel [without him]; we will sit in the dining hall [without him].”

“We shall dwell under one roof; we shall perform salutations, rising from our seats, joining our palms in reverence, and respectful service according to seniority, except for this one monk”—these are the benefits stated thus in the Kosambaka Khandhaka.
The same method applies to the second group of eight; for that too was stated in exactly the same way in the Kosambaka Khandhaka.

"Eight [offenses] that may be resolved at the third [formal act]" refers to the four among the thirteen [offenses] for monks, and the four not shared with monks among the seventeen [offenses] for nuns—
thus there are eight. "He corrupts families in eight ways" means he corrupts families by means of flowers,
or fruits, or face-powder, or clay, or tooth-sticks, or bamboo, or medical practice, or by running errands on foot.
It blows by means of these eight. Eight headings (*mātikā*) are stated in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*, and another eight are stated in the *Kathinakkhandhaka*.
"By the eight unrighteous qualities" (*aṭṭhahi asaddhammehi*) refers to gain and loss, fame and disrepute, honor and dishonor, evil desire, and evil friendship.
The so-called "eight worldly conditions" (*aṭṭha lokadhammā*) are: attachment to gain and aversion toward loss;
Thus, there is attachment to fame and notoriety, to praise and blame, to pleasure, and aversion toward pain.
"Eightfold false speech" means eightfold by way of the eight factors mentioned in the Pāḷi together with the phrase "having distorted perception.
"The eight factors of the Uposatha" are as follows:
One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given,
nor speak falsehoods, nor be a drinker of intoxicants;
one should abstain from unchastity and sexual intercourse.
One should not eat at night, nor at improper times.
One should not wear garlands, nor use perfumes;
one should lie on the ground itself, or on a spread, rather than on a bed.
“For this indeed is called the eightfold Uposatha, proclaimed by the Buddha who has reached the end of suffering.
Thus are the eight [factors] spoken of. Regarding the eight factors of a messenger: “In this case, monks, a monk is both a listener and a proclaimer...”

These [rules] regarding those who cause a schism in the Saṅgha have been stated by way of the passage beginning with "and so forth. The practices of the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiya-vatta) are explained in the Mahākhandhaka.
Both the rules concerning food that is not leftover and food that is leftover are explained in the Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada. Regarding the phrase "one must rise for eight":
this refers to senior bhikkhunīs in the dining hall, and seats must also be given to them alone. "Laywoman" (upāsikā) refers to Visākhā. There are eight benefits.

Regarding "one who holds the Vinaya": among the five mentioned in the *Pañcaka*, these three—"the Uposatha dependent on him," "the Pavāraṇā," and "a Saṅgha transaction"—should be added, making eight to be understood.
"The eight limits" should be understood by applying the previously mentioned limits according to the group of eight.
"One should conduct oneself rightly regarding the eight matters" refers to [not acting against] a regular monk...
"The Uposatha should be suspended, but the Pavāraṇā should not be suspended"—in this manner, [these matters] are explained among the eight [cases] pointed out in the Samathakkhandhaka.
The rest is clear throughout. The commentary on the section of eight is finished.
Commentary on the Ninefold Group (Navaka-vāravaṇṇanā) 329.
Regarding the ninefold group: - "The nine grounds for resentment" refers to the nine beginning with, "He has done me harm," and so forth.

- "The nine ways of removing resentment" refers to the nine beginning with, "He has done me harm; what can be gained from that? Thus one removes resentment," and so forth. - "The nine grounds for disciplinary action" refers to... [text continues]
“Non-restraint, abstention, refraining, and the destruction of the bridge [from the outflows] regarding the nine grounds for malice.
“The Saṅgha is split by nine”: “Upāli, when there are either nine or more than nine, there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a breaking of the Saṅgha.
“Nine supreme things” should be understood by applying the previously mentioned supreme things according to the category of nines. “Nine rooted in craving.”
Namely: dependent on craving (taṇhā) comes seeking (pariyesanā); dependent on seeking comes gain (lābha); dependent on gain comes decision-making (vinicchaya);
dependent on decision-making comes desire and lust (chandarāga); dependent on desire and lust comes attachment (ajjhosāna); dependent on attachment comes possessiveness (pariggaha);
dependent on possessiveness comes stinginess (macchariya); dependent on stinginess comes guarding (ārakkhā); and with guarding as the basis...
Taking up sticks, taking up weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech. The nine kinds of conceit are:
the conceit "I am better than one who is better," and so forth. The nine robes are those stated in such a manner as "the three robes" or "the rainy-season cloak," and so on.
They should not be assigned to others means that from the time they have been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita), they should not be assigned to others.
The nine unrighteous gifts are stated as follows: one dedicates what was intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a shrine (cetiyassa), or to an individual;
one dedicates what was intended for a shrine to another shrine, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual;
and one dedicates what was intended for an individual to another individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a shrine.
"Nine acceptances and uses" refers to both the acceptance and the use of these very same gifts. "Three lawful gifts" refers to these three:
giving what is intended for the Saṅgha to the Saṅgha itself; giving what is intended for a shrine to the shrine itself; and giving what is intended for an individual to that individual themselves.
Their "acceptance and use" likewise refer to the acceptance and use of those very same things.
And [there are] nine types of unrighteous reconciliation (*saññatti*). These are: an individual who speaks unrighteously, a plurality who speak unrighteously, and a Saṅgha that speaks unrighteously;
thus three triads are specified in the *Samathakkhandhaka*. Likewise, the righteous reconciliations are specified in that same place by way of "an individual who speaks righteously," and so forth.
Regarding unrighteous formal acts (*adhammakamma*), there are two sets of nine [cases] from the *Ovādavagga*.

In the exposition of the first training rule, those [offenses] are stated by way of *pācittiya*. The two new sets of nine [rules] regarding formal acts (*dhammakamma*) are likewise stated there by way of *dukkaṭa*. The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the section on the new [sets of rules] is concluded.
Explanation of the Decads (Dasakavāravaṇṇanā) 330.
Regarding the decads: "The ten bases for resentment" refers to the nine mentioned in the section on the Nines, together with the tenth, "or resentment arises toward what is unworthy," making ten.
The nine methods for the removal of resentment mentioned therein, together with "toward what is unworthy... [make ten].
Or else, when resentment arises, one dispels that resentment by thinking, "How could this be possible?"—these ten [grounds for resentment] should be understood in conjunction with this.
"Ten grounds for disciplinary action" (dasa vinītavatthūni) refers to the ten forms of abstention from the ten grounds for resentment.

"Wrong view with ten grounds" (dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi) should be understood by way of such statements as "there is no gift," and so forth; [right view] is by way of "there is a gift," and so forth.
Right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) should be understood as the view that grasps at extremes (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*), such as "the world is eternal," and so forth.
The ten forms of wrongness (*dasamicchatta*) consist of wrong view and the rest, ending with wrong liberation; they are the opposites of the right states (*sammatta*).
These were specified by means of voting sticks (*salākaggāha*) in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
“A bhikkhu endowed with ten factors should be appointed to a committee,” as stated in the *Samathakkhandhaka* by way of the passage beginning with “he is virtuous.
Ten dangers in entering a royal palace are specified in the *Rājasikkhāpada*.
The ten grounds for giving are: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, and dwellings.
"Lamp-offering. "The ten kinds of gems" refers to pearls, jewels, beryl, and so forth. "The ten kinds of refuse rags" are:

one from a charnel ground, one from a shop, one gnawed by rats, one gnawed by termites, one burnt by fire, one worn by a cow, one worn by a goat, one from a stupa, one from a royal consecration, and one brought as a gift for a meal;
regarding these, one who is fully ordained should make an effort [to obtain them].
Regarding the "ten robes" (*dasa cīvaradhāraṇā*): it is stated in the *Kurundi* commentary that there are ten according to the expression, "they wear robes that are entirely blue.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The 'ten' refers to the nine allowable robes (*kappiya-cīvara*) with either a bathing robe (*udakasāṭikā*) or a bodice (*saṅkaccika*) added to them."
Persons not to be saluted are specified in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*. The ten bases for abuse are specified in the *Omasavāda* [Sikkhāpada].

“There are, monks, eleven dangers for a person who is abusive and insulting, one who reviles the noble ones.

What are the eleven? [The first is] not attaining what has not yet been attained...”
He does not attain what has not been attained; he falls away from what has been attained; his faculties do not become purified in regard to the true Dhamma;
or he becomes overweening regarding the true Dhammas; or he leads the holy life without delight; or he commits some defiled offense;
or having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life; or he is afflicted by a severe illness; or he falls into madness.

And here, “the true Dhamma” is intended to mean the word of the Buddha.

"Vā. *Bahulīkatāya* means having been performed repeatedly. *Yānīkatāya* means having been made like a well-yoked vehicle.
