332. In the answering of the questions beginning with, “What is the beginning of the Uposatha transaction?”:

“Harmony is the beginning” means that for those who have assembled after purifying the boundary and bringing the consent and purity [of the monks], saying, “We shall perform the Uposatha,” bodily harmony is the beginning.
“The performance is the middle” means that after performing the preliminary duties, the performance of reciting the Pātimokkha is the middle. “The conclusion... [is the end].
The conclusion: "In this regard, all should train together in harmony, in mutual agreement, and without dispute"—this is the finality of the Pātimokkha, the conclusion.

Regarding the formal act of invitation (*pavāraṇā*), "harmony is the beginning" means that for those who have assembled after purifying the boundary and bringing the consent-invitation, physical harmony is the beginning. "The performance is the middle."
The motion for the invitation (*pavāraṇāñatti*) and the discourse on the invitation (*pavāraṇākathā*) constitute the middle;
the statement by the newest member of the Saṅgha, “If I see [an offense], I shall make amends,” constitutes the conclusion.

Regarding the acts of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and so forth, the "matter" (*vatthu*) is that matter by which one becomes subject to the legal act. The "person" (*puggala*) is the individual who committed that matter. The "conclusion" refers to the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
“The Sangha has performed the act of censure against the monk named so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Sangha, therefore it is silent;
thus do I understand this. Such is the concluding statement at the end of each formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the questions and answers regarding the Uposatha and so forth is concluded.
334. Regarding the commentary on the section on the purpose (*atthavasa*):
concerning the phrase "the ten purposes" (*dasa atthavase*) and so forth, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
It has been said. In such passages as "What is beneficial for the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha," each subsequent term is the meaning of each preceding term.
However, in the passage beginning with "A hundred meanings, a hundred phenomena," etc., having taken each of the ten terms as a root, [the text repeats] ten times...

A hundred phrases have been stated for the purpose of the application (*yojanā*). In that regard, a hundred meanings (*attha*) should be understood by way of each subsequent phrase, and a hundred phenomena (*dhamma*) by way of each preceding one.

Alternatively, there are ten purposes (*atthavasa*) depending upon which the Tathāgata prescribed the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) for his disciples; those [ten] were previously mentioned in the commentary on the first *pārājika* as: "In that regard..."
“Welfare of the Saṅgha” means the state of the Saṅgha being well;
it is the state of receiving one’s words, as in the case of saying “Very well, O King” where [the word] “well” occurs, or as in saying “Very well, Venerable Sir.

And for whoever receives the word of the Tathāgata, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, [this is said] so that the Saṅgha may receive my words by saying, “Very well, Venerable Sir.”

Having shown the disadvantage in not accepting and the benefit in accepting, and intending to reveal the meaning that [the Saṅgha] does not act by force or by overbearing means, he said: "For the welfare of the Saṅgha," and so forth.

Since these have been praised in this manner and occur here ten times, there are one hundred meanings; and by way of the words that illuminate those meanings, there are one hundred teachings (dhamma).
It should be understood as follows: now, by way of the etymologies (*nirutti*) that illuminate the meaning, there is one hundred etymologies;

and by way of the etymologies that consist of the phenomena (*dhamma*), there is another hundred etymologies—thus, two hundred etymologies. For the hundred meanings there is a hundredfold knowledge, and for the hundred phenomena there is a hundredfold knowledge;
thus, within the two hundred etymologies, there are two hundredfold knowledges, making four hundredfold knowledges in total. It should be understood in this way.
“There are one hundred and eight topics, one hundred states, two hundred etymologies,
and four hundred kinds of knowledge in this treatise on the purposes.
Thus, what was stated is said with reference to this.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāvagga within the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.

336. "Yaṃ taṃ pucchimhā" means that which we asked you. "Akittayī" means he spoke. "No" means to us. "Taṃ taṃ byākataṃ" means whatever was asked, each of those very things was explained. "Añaññathā" means it was explained without making it otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "ye duṭṭhullā sā sīlavipattī," although there is no question here specifically concerning what is called "failure in virtue" (sīlavipatti), this was nevertheless stated with the intention of answering the matter of "grave offenses" (duṭṭhulla).
For among the four types of failure, "grave offense" is [included] in one type of failure.
It is comprised [of offenses], and it is non-gross (aduṭṭhulla) insofar as it is comprised by the three failures (vipatti).

Therefore, having stated, "Those that are gross are failure in virtue (sīlavipatti)," he said, "The pārājika and the saṅghādisesa are called failure in virtue," in order to demonstrate that very point in detail.

Now, in order to show what is non-gross by way of the three failures, he said, "A thullaccaya," and so forth. In that context, the phrase "and whoever abuses with the intention of joking" is stated for the purpose of showing the basis (vatthu) for a dubbhāsita (wrong speech).
“They misrepresent” means that those who say, “I understand the Dhamma thus taught by the Blessed One,” misrepresent it.

Regarding that, the meaning of the verse "Pārājika" is as follows:

among the Pārājikas concerning persons, offenses, and training rules, that which is called an "offense of defeat" (*āpatti-pārājika*)—when a person incurs such an offense, they are defeated, have fallen into defeat, and have fallen away from the True Dhamma.
He is defeated, cast out, and excluded; as long as that person has not been reintegrated, there can be no communal living with him, such as the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies.
"Therefore this is so called" means: for that reason, this is called an *āpatti-pārājika*.
Here is the summary of the meaning: because he is defeated by it, therefore this is called a *pārājika*.
In the second verse as well, disregarding the literal phrasing (*byañjana*) and showing only the essential meaning (*atthamatta*), it is said: "The Saṅgha alone grants probation," and so forth.

Herein, the meaning is as follows: for one who has committed this offense and desires to emerge from it, regarding that emergence from the offense—at its very beginning, for the purpose of granting probation;
in the remainder following the beginning, in the middle, for the purpose of granting the trial period (*mānatta*); and through the sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*).
Or, because the Saṅgha must be sought at the beginning for the purpose of granting the *mānatta* penance and the *abbhāna* (rehabilitation) at the conclusion—

and because not even a single formal act (*kamma*) can be performed here without the Saṅgha— it is called a *saṅghādisesa*. Thus, it is a *saṅghādisesa* because the Saṅgha must be sought both at the outset and at the remainder [of the process].
Regarding the third verse, "indefinite" (*aniyata*) means not fixed; because it is not fixed, the meaning is that this class of offenses is indefinite.
For what reason is it not fixed? Because of the state of being non-exclusive; the meaning is that this training rule was established with non-exclusive intent.
How is it non-exclusive? By any one of three conditions; by any one of three factors.
For it is stated therein, "it must be dealt with"; therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (aniyata), and that class of offenses is called indeterminate.
And just as one of three positions [is specified], so too where one of two states is mentioned, that too is indeed indeterminate.

Regarding the fourth verse, "there is no transgression equal to that": among those transgressions that lead to confession (*desanāgāminī*), there is no transgression as grave as that; therefore it is said thus. Because of the gravity of the transgression, the meaning is that it is called a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Regarding the fifth verse, "having relinquished, one confesses": because it must be confessed after having been relinquished, it is called *nissaggiya* (to be relinquished); this is the meaning. Regarding the sixth verse, "it causes one to fall from the wholesome state":
for one who intentionally commits [an offense], it causes one to fall from what is reckoned as a wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*).
It causes a wholesome mind to fall away; therefore, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) because it causes the mind to fall.

Furthermore, as for that mind which it causes to fall, it transgresses against the Noble Path and becomes a cause for the delusion of the mind; therefore, it is described as "that which transgresses the Noble Path" and "a place for the delusion of the mind."

In the verses on the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses requiring confession), the passage beginning with "a monk who is a stranger" (*bhikkhu aññātako santo*) was stated specifically to show the reason for the state of being censurable (*gārayha*) mentioned in the phrase "I have committed a censurable matter, friend. However, because it must be confessed, that offense is called *pāṭidesanīya*.
In the verse on the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), all terms such as "transgressed," "failed," and "lapsed" are included within the expression "whatever *dukkaṭa*."
This is a synonym for what has been called "dukkaṭa. For that which is badly done or uglyly done is *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, this is "failed" (*aparaddha*) because it was not done as taught by the Teacher; it is "missed" (*viraddha*) because it proceeded having missed the wholesome;
and it is "slipped" (*khalita*) because one has not ascended the path of the noble conduct. Whatever a person does [in this regard]...

This, however, is an illustration by way of a simile. Its meaning is as follows: Just as whatever evil a person in the world does, whether openly or in secret, they proclaim it to be "misdeed" (*dukkaṭa*);
so too this is "evil" (*pāpa*) by virtue of its base nature, which is censured by the Buddha, and therefore it should be understood as a "misdeed."
In the verse regarding "ill-spoken" (*dubbhāsita*), "ill-recited" (*durābhaṭṭha*) means that which has been recited or spoken badly;
thus, it is "ill-recited. The meaning is: that which is ill-recited is "ill-spoken.
Furthermore, it is "defiled," in the sense that the word is defiled. Likewise, it is that which the wise censure.
And because wise people censure it—this is the meaning. "Therefore this is said" means that because of both its defiled nature and the censure of the wise, "this is said";
the meaning is that it is called "ill-spoken.
In the verse on the training rules (*sekhiya*), by the method beginning with "This is both the beginning and the conduct," it illustrates the state of belonging to one in training (*sekkha*).
Therefore, "this is for one in training" (*sekha*) means "this is a training rule" (*sekhiya*); this is the summary of the meaning here.

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of illustrating the meaning included by the word of entreaty, "Come, let us hear your words," which is not comprised within the questions beginning with "heavy and light."

The same method applies to the passage beginning with "It rains upon what is covered" (*channaṃ ativassati*). Therein, "it rains upon what is covered" means that first, a house that is not covered with grass and so forth is rained upon.
However, this "house," which consists of offenses (*āpatti*), is rained upon when it is covered;
for while covering over a root-offense (*mūlāpatti*), one incurs another new offense. "It does not rain upon what is open" (*vivaṭaṃ nātivassati*) refers first to a house that is not open.
What is well-covered does not leak excessively. But this "house" consisting of offenses, when uncovered, does not leak excessively:
for one who uncovers a root offense by confessing it as leading to confession (*desanāgāminī*), and having emerged from it via the path of emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*), becomes established in purity.
Restraining oneself in the future, one does not incur another offense. Therefore, "uncover what is covered" means for that reason.
While preaching that which leads to confession (*desanāgāminī*) and emerging from that which leads to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*), one should open what is closed.
"Thus it will not rain excessively upon you" means that if this [defilement] is opened up in such a way, it will not rain excessively.
"The forest is the resort of deer" means that for deer being pursued in the open air by tigers and other predators, the forest—the thicket of trees and so forth—is their refuge.
The forest is their destination and refuge; having reached it, they find comfort. In the same manner, space is the destination for birds.

Furthermore, in the sense of being inevitably approached, dissolution (*vibhava*) is the destination of phenomena (*dhamma*); indeed, the destruction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) is their destination.
For they are not able to remain without undergoing destruction. Even after remaining for a very long time, [they must pass away].
But Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant; the meaning is that for the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, the element of Nibbāna without residue is exclusively the destination.
The commentary on the first verse regarding socializing is finished. [Now follows] the classification of legal issues (*adhikaraṇabheda*).
340. Commentary on the Opening and Splitting, etc.:

Regarding the splitting of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), there are these ten openings. In order to demonstrate the opening of the methods of settlement (*samatha*) by means of reopening legal issues after they have been settled, he said:
"When one opens a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), how many methods of settlement does one open? and so forth.

In that regard, one who reopens a legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) reopens two methods of settling it: he reopens and prohibits both the presence of the accused (sammukhāvinaya) and the majority decision (yebhuyyasika);
this is the meaning of "he protests against. One who reopens a legal issue arising from an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) reopens four:

the presence of the accused, the verdict based on mindfulness (sativinaya), the verdict for one no longer insane (amūḷhavinaya), and the verdict of further penalty (tassapāpiyasika); these are the four methods of settling it.

"He reopens. When reopening a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), he reopens these three methods of settlement: face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*), acting according to what is admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*), and covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
When reopening a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), he reopens this one method of settlement: face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*).

341. In the response to the questions beginning with “How many kinds of reopening (ukkoṭa) are there?”, first, the three reopenings beginning with “an action not done” are found specifically in the second type of legal issue, the *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (legal issue of accusation).

The three beginning with “an action not settled” are found in the first type of legal issue, the *vivādādhikaraṇa* (legal issue of dispute). The three beginning with “not adjudicated” are found in the third type of legal issue, the *āpattādhikaraṇa* (legal issue of offense).

They are obtained. The three beginning with "unappeased" (avūpasanta) are obtained in the fourth category, the legal question (*kiccādhikaraṇa*); moreover, all twelve are indeed obtainable in each individual legal question.
Regarding the phrase "he reopens a legal question arising therein": in whichever monastery [one thinks], "My bowl was taken by this person," or "My robe..."
When a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) arises for the sake of the bowl, robes, and so forth,

according to the method beginning with the words "It has been taken," and the resident monks of that very monastery assemble and settle it through a decision outside the canonical texts— having persuaded their opponents with the words "Enough, friends"—
this is called a legal issue "arisen there" (*tatthajātaka*). The decision by which it was settled is also [to be understood].
There is only one [way], namely, through *samatha* (settling). For one who reopens this [case], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Regarding the phrase "the matter arising there has been settled": if the resident monks are unable to settle that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), then another monk learned in the Vinaya arrives and asks, "Friends, is the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā ceremony still pending in this monastery?"
If he asks about it, and when that reason has been stated by them, he settles that legal issue by means of a Sutta from either the Khandhaka or the Parivāra,
this is called a legal issue settled as "arisen on the spot. For one who reopens such a case,
there is likewise an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"On the way," means that those adversaries of his, thinking, "We will not stand by his judgment;
he is not skilled in the Vinaya. There are elder masters who are experts in the Vinaya living in such-and-such a village;
we shall go there and decide the matter," while traveling on the very path, perceive the grounds for their case and either convince one another or [inform] others.

Those monks cause them to reflect, and thus this matter becomes pacified. Whoever reopens a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that has been pacified on the way, for him there is likewise an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
"Pacified on the way" means not only through mutual reconciliation or by causing like-minded monks to reflect.
Or it becomes settled; moreover, a single Vinaya-holder coming along the opposite path sees them, asks, "Friends, where are you going?
and when they reply, "To such-and-such a village, for such-and-such a reason," he says, "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?
and settles that legal issue right then and there in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
This is what is called "settled on the way. Even for one who reopens this [case], it is indeed a *pācittiya*.

Regarding "having gone there": if, even when being told, "Enough, friend, what is the use of going there?", they nevertheless go, disregarding the words of the *vinayadhara* and saying, "We shall go right there and reach a decision," [then it is so].

Having gone, they report this matter to like-minded bhikkhus. Those like-minded bhikkhus, saying, "Enough, friend, for an assembly of the Saṅgha is a serious matter," have him sit right there, deliberate, and persuade him;
thus it becomes settled. Whoever reopens a legal issue that has been settled in this way after it has gone there, for him too there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In that context, "settled after being brought to the matter" means it is not settled merely through the persuasion of like-minded bhikkhus;
rather, having convened the Saṅgha, it is announced, and the experts in the Vinaya settle it in the midst of the Saṅgha—this is what is meant by "settled after being brought to the matter.
For one who reopens such a case, there is likewise an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one reopens a *sativinaya* (settlement by mindfulness) that was granted to one whose taints are destroyed, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The same principle applies to reopening a *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is not insane) granted to one who is insane, and to a *tassapāpiyasikā* (proceeding against one who is worse) granted to one who is malicious.

Regarding "reopening a *tiṇavatthāraka*" (covering over as with grass): when a legal dispute has been settled by the Saṅgha through the *tiṇavatthāraka* means of settlement, [to reopen it] means that an offense is said to be confessed by approaching a single monk, sitting in a crouching posture, and raising the joined palms in salutation.

"Even that which is called 'emergence from an offense' while one is sleeping—I do not approve of this," he who speaks thus is said to reopen a *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), and for him there is likewise a *pācittiya* offense.
One who proceeds with favoritism reopens a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*); even if he is a master of the Vinaya, if he [does so] for his own preceptor and others...
Having explained things such as "non-Dhamma is Dhamma" for the sake of some [personal] interest,

one who reopens a legal issue previously settled by means of any one of the twelve grounds for reopening (ukkoṭa) while proceeding with a biased motive (chandāgati) is said to "reopen the legal issue.
Furthermore, when one of two adversaries has developed resentment toward him in the manner of thinking, "He has done me harm," and so forth—
In order to bring about his defeat, one who— having explained "what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma" and so forth—
revives a legal issue previously settled by means of any one of the twelve grounds for reopening (ukkoṭana), thereby falling into error, is said to "reopen the legal issue.
However, one who is dull-witted or deluded, due to that very delusion, explains "what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma" and so forth, and in the manner already described...
One who reopens [a settled matter] while following a course of delusion is said to reopen a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). However, if between two adversaries,
one is supported by an unknown monk who is powerful, who holds wrong views, and who takes up improper bodily actions and so forth—
and thus that person is one whose support is improper, whose support is grasping, and whose support is powerful— then out of fear of him...

Thinking, "This person might cause an obstacle to my life or an obstacle to my holy life," one who, by declaring that "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma" and so forth, reopens a legal issue according to the method already described, and proceeds toward a course out of fear, is said to reopen a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
"One ordained on that very day": there was a certain novice who was competent and learned; having met with defeat in the formal decision, he—
Seeing the monks looking abashed, he asks, "Why are you abashed? They report that legal case to him.
He says to them, "Very well, venerable sirs, grant me full ordination; I shall settle that legal case.
They grant him full ordination. On the following day, having struck the gong, he [summons] the Saṅgha...
He convenes [the Saṅgha]. Then, when the bhikkhus ask, "By whom was the Saṅgha convened?", he says, "By me.
"For what purpose was it convened? "Yesterday a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) was wrongly decided;
I shall decide it today. "But where did you go yesterday? "I was not ordained (*anupasampanna*), venerable sirs; but today I am ordained (*upasampanna*)."
He should be told: "Friend, this training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One for those such as yourselves:

'If one who has been ordained that very day reopens [a settled legal issue], it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) for reopening. Go and confess the offense. This same method applies to a newly arrived monk as well.
A "decider" is a monk who, having resolved a legal issue together with the Saṅgha, has gone to his own cell after being defeated.
They say, "Venerable sir, why was this legal issue decided by you in this way? Should it not have been decided thus?

He then reopens that legal issue, saying, "Why did you not speak thus at the very beginning? Thus, for one who reopens [the matter], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for reopening. Regarding "one who gives consent": in the decision of a legal issue, one person...

Having given his consent, when he saw that the monks who were in agreement had arrived after suffering defeat and appeared dejected, he thought, "I shall decide this matter tomorrow," and convened the Saṅgha.
When they asked, "For what purpose have you convened us? he replied, "Yesterday the legal case was wrongly decided;
I shall decide it today. They then asked, "But where did you go yesterday?"
“I sat down after giving my consent. He should be told: “Friend, this training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One for those such as you:
‘If one who has given his consent revokes it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the revoker. Go and confess the offense.
[Commentary on the Origin and Basis of the Legal Issue]

342. Regarding the questions beginning with "What is the source of the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*)?", [the analysis is as follows]: that which has what as its source is "source-originated" (*kiṃnidāna*).

That which has what as its origin is "origin-originated" (*kiṃsamudaya*). That which has what as its birth is "birth-originated" (*kiṃjātika*). That which has what as its provenance is "provenance-originated" (*kiṃpabhava*).

That which has what as its equipment is "equipment-originated" (*kiṃsambhāra*). That which has what as its origination is "origination-originated" (*kiṃsamuṭṭhāna*). All of these [terms] are [to be understood in this manner].
These are indeed synonyms for the cause.

Regarding the phrase "the source of dispute" (*vivādanidāna*) and so forth: because dispute—consisting of the eighteen grounds for schism—is the source of this [matter], it is called "the source of dispute.
This is stated by way of the disputes that arise dependent upon [those] disputes. Because accusation is its source, it is called "the source of accusation" (*anuvādanidāna*).
This too is stated by way of an accusation arising based on an accusation. "The source of offenses" (*āpattinidāna*) means that which has an offense as its source.
This is stated by way of the offenses arising based on an offense, in the sense that one incurs four types of offenses due to a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
"The source of duties" (*kiccayanidāna*) means that which has duties as its source; it means that which has the fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha as its cause.

The meaning is as follows: this is stated with reference to the duties arising from the formal acts beginning with the third admonition for a nun who persists in following one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*).
This is the application of a single phrase to the resolution of all four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
Following this method, all the phrases should be applied accordingly.

In the answer to the second question, beginning with "the cause as source" (*hetunidāna*), the state of having a cause as source and so forth should be understood by way of the nine roots—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. In the answer to the third question, there is only a difference in phrasing;
for here, "cause" itself is stated as "condition."

343. Regarding the answer to the initial question: “twelve roots” refers to the twelve roots occurring within one’s own internal continuum, namely the six roots of dispute beginning with the pair of anger and enmity, the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
“Fourteen roots” means those same twelve plus bodily and verbal actions, making fourteen. “Six roots” refers to...
There are six origins, beginning with the body.

Regarding the answer to the question on origins: the eighteen grounds for schism are the origins, for [the schism] originates from these eighteen grounds for schism, or it originates by means of these factors acting as causes. Therefore, these...
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) are being stated. This same method applies everywhere.

344. Regarding the classification beginning with "the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) as an offense (āpatti)," this was stated to show by which legal issue they are settled—namely, by the legal issue of business (kiccādhikaraṇa)—and not because these [other issues] are exclusively settled by the legal issue of business alone.
They are settled. For there is no such thing as a *kiccādhikaraṇa* (a legal question concerning business) when one is confessing in the presence of an individual.

"By which means of settlement?"—it is not settled in the same way as an offense with remainder (*sāvasesāpatti*), for it is impossible to confess that [offense], nor can one, having emerged from it, be established in the state of purity.
348. The method beginning with "A legal question arising from a dispute becomes a legal question arising from an accusation" is already explained.

349. Following that, six pairs of questions are stated beginning with "where there is *sativinaya*," etc., without departing from *sammukhāvinaya*. Their meaning is elucidated by the very answers to those questions.

351. Regarding the answers to the questions on "associated" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) and so forth: at the very moment of the formal act (*kammavācā*) of *sativinaya* for one who is "associated," since both methods of settling the dispute (*samatha*) are established, these factors—namely, *sammukhāvinaya* and *sativinaya*—are associated.

They are not detached. However, because it is impossible to demonstrate their distinction by separating them—just as one cannot separate the layers of leaves from the trunk of a plantain tree—it is said:
"It is not possible, having repeatedly separated these phenomena, to point out their distinction.
This same method applies everywhere.
Commentary on the Seven Origins of Calm (Sattasamathanidānavaṇṇanā) 352.
Regarding the question "What is the origin? and its answer: that which has an origin as its origin is called "origin-origin" (*nidānanidāna*).

In this context, being in the presence of the Saṅgha, being in the presence of the Dhamma, being in the presence of the Vinaya, and being in the presence of the individuals—this is the origin of the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
One who has attained the fullness of mindfulness and whose taints are exhausted, having received formal praise, is the source for resolution by mindfulness (*sativinaya*).

A monk who is insane is the source for resolution because of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*). The presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom he confesses is the source for acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
The inability to settle a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) among those engaged in quarreling is the source for the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
A person who is full of evil is the source for the procedure of further penalty (*tassapāpiyasikā*).

Much un-monkish and transgressive conduct among those engaged in quarreling is the source for the "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*) procedure. The sections on causes and conditions have been explained in the same manner as before.

353. The answer to the question concerning the root is straightforward. Regarding the question concerning the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), although [it concerns] "of the seven methods of settling disputes..."

When it is asked, "What are the thirty-six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*)?", since *sammukhāvinaya* lacks an origin due to the absence of a formal act (*kamma*), only six origins are analyzed for the six methods of settling disputes (*samatha*).

In that context, "performance of the act" (*kammassa kiriyā*) should be understood as the motion (*ñatti*). "Doing" (*karaṇa*) is the laying down of that very motion at the time it is to be established. "Approaching" (*upagamana*)...
*Upagamanaṃ*: the act of approaching oneself; the meaning is that one performs that action by oneself. *Ajjhupagamanaṃ*: the approach through entreaty;
the meaning is the entreaty of another, such as a co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), saying, "Please perform this task.
*Adhivāsanā*: acquiescence, such as saying, "This is pleasing to me; let the Saṅgha do it"; the meaning is the giving of consent (*chandadāna*). *Appaṭikkosanā*: non-opposition.
"This is not proper; do not do so"—this is non-prohibition. Thus, by way of the six sets of six, thirty-six origins (samuṭṭhāna) are to be understood.
[End of] the commentary on the sevenfold diversity of pacification and so forth.
354. The response to the question concerning various meanings is straightforward. Regarding the response to the question concerning legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*):

"This dispute is not a legal issue"—this refers to disputes such as those between mother and son; because they consist of conflicting claims, they are called "disputes" (*vivāda*), but because they lack the quality of being something that must be settled by means of the methods of pacification (*samatha*), they are not "legal issues.
The same principle applies to accusations (*anuvāda*) and so forth. The rest...
"Everywhere it is indeed clear.
The commentary on the classification of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) is finished.
The second collection of verses (*gāthā-saṅgaṇika*).
Commentary on the Questions and Answers Regarding *Codanā* and Others, 359.
In the enumeration of the second verse: *codanā* (reproving) refers to reproving after having pointed out both the matter (*vatthu*) and the offense (*āpatti*).

*Sāraṇā* (reminding) refers to reminding of a fault. "For what purpose is the Saṅgha? means for what purpose is the assembly of the Saṅgha? But for what purpose is the act of deliberation (*matikamma*)?
"Reasoning" (*kāraṇā*) refers to the work of deliberation (*matikamma*), that is, the grasping of counsel; the meaning is: "for what reason?
"Accusation for the purpose of reminding" means an accusation of the kind already described, for the purpose of reminding the person being accused of the faults of the accuser.
"Reminding for the purpose of restraint" means that the reminding of faults is for the purpose of restraining that person. "The Saṅgha [acts] for the purpose of inclusion."
The Saṅgha assembles there for the purpose of determining and encompassing [the case];

that is to say, for the purpose of weighing what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, and for the purpose of knowing what has been well-determined and what has not been well-determined. As for "consultation" (matikamma), however, it is distinct:
it refers to the individual consultation of the Suttantika Theras and the Vinayadhara Theras, each separately, for the purpose of reaching a definitive determination in the legal process.

"Do not give way to resentment" means: do not generate anger toward either the one who has been censured or the one who censures. "If you, as an investigator" means: if you, being an expert in the Vinaya, are seated in the midst of the Saṅgha to adjudicate a legal issue that has arisen.
"Contentious speech" refers to speech proceeding in such a manner as: "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya," and so forth. "Unbeneficial" means:
do not speak such words as produce harm, which agitate and stir up the assembly. In the Sutta...
In the passages beginning with "in the Vinaya," *sutta* refers to the two *vibhaṅgas*; *vinaya* refers to the *khandhakas*; *anuloma* refers to the *parivāra*;
*paññatta* refers to the entire *Vinayapiṭaka*; and *anulomika* refers to the four great authorities (*mahāpadesas*).
"Listen to the conduct of application" means: listen to the conduct of diligent practice. "Done by one who is skillful and wise" means: done by one who is clever.
It was drawn out and established by the Blessed One, the wise one who has reached the perfection of knowledge.

"Well-spoken" means well-proclaimed. "In accordance with the training rules" means conforming to the training rules. This, first of all, is the word-meaning; this, however, is the brief explanation here including the underlying intention:
"If you are an investigator, do not speak hastily; do not speak contentious speech that is unbeneficial."

"But as for how the practice of application (*anuyogavatta*) was well-proclaimed by the wise and skillful Lord of the World among these suttas and so forth—being in conformity with all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)—listen to that; reflect upon it. Do not destroy your future destiny;
that is, do not fail to bring about a happy rebirth for yourself in the future life. Listen to the practice of application. For he who does not listen to it...
He pursues [them], and thus he destroys his own future destiny; therefore, the meaning is: "Listen attentively without complaining.
Now, in order to show that procedure for inquiry, he said, "seeking welfare," and so forth. Therein, "seeking welfare" means seeking and searching for what is beneficial; the meaning is:

having established loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. "At the proper time" means at the appropriate and fitting time; specifically, at the very time one is requested.
When your burden has been laid down, one should apply oneself to the goal.
"Do not hastily engage in legal proceedings" means: whatever legal proceeding these people undertake, whatever is spoken hastily—that do not engage in; do not take it up.

"Let it be done according to what is admitted through the sequence of the case" (*paṭiññānusandhitena*): here, "sequence" (*anusandhi*) refers to the sequence of the discourse; therefore, it means by way of the sequence of what is admitted.

"Kāraye": having observed the connection of the discourse (*kathānusandhi*), one should cause [the confession] to be made by means of a formal admission (*paṭiññā*); this is the meaning. Alternatively, "one should cause it to be made by means of both an admission and the connection of the discourse":
one should cause a conscientious person (*lajjī*) to make it by means of an admission, and an unconscientious person (*alajjī*) by means of the connection of the discourse;

this is the meaning. Therefore, he recited the verse beginning with "That very admission is for the conscientious. In that context, "one should cause it to be made by means of the connection of the discourse" refers to the connection of the discourse (*vattānusandhinā*).
"Let her cause [it] to be done": the meaning is that she should cause it to be done by means of that confession which accords with her conduct.
"Intentionally" (*sañcicca*) means she commits the offense while knowing it. "Conceals" (*parigūhati*) means she hides it; she does not confess it, nor does she emerge from it.
"I also know this" means: what you have said is true; I also know it exactly like that. "And another thing about her" means: I ask you something else concerning her.
"He does not know what precedes and what follows" means he does not know what was said before and what was said after.

"Unskilled" means unskilled in that sequence of what precedes and what follows. "He does not know the connection of the discourse" means he does not know the connection of the words in the narrative nor the connection of the words in the legal decision.
"He censures for failure in virtue" means he censures by means of two classes of offenses. "By conduct and view" means by failure in conduct.
And [there is] failure in view. One who reproves for failure in conduct reproves by means of the five classes of offenses;

one who reproves for failure in view reproves by means of both wrong view and the view of grasping at extremes. "One reproves even for livelihood" means one reproves by means of the six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood.
The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the second verse regarding socializing is finished.
The section on censure:
Commentary on the duties of the investigator.

360–361. Now, in order to show the duty that must be performed by the *vinayadhara* (one who maintains the discipline) when a charge has arisen in this manner, the passage beginning with "by the investigator" (*anuvijjakena*) is commenced.
Regarding that, the meaning of the verse beginning with "what is seen [is cleared] by what is seen" (*diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhena*) is as follows:
One person is seen leaving or entering a certain place together with a woman; he accuses him of an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), and the other [responds] to him...
He admits to having seen it; however, because he does not admit to an offense based on that seeing, nor does he confess to one, what was seen by him here accords with his statement "I have seen it.
But since the other does not confess to a fault based on that seeing, he is suspected of being impure.
The meaning is: "one who is suspected without basis. The Uposatha should be performed together with that person upon his declaration, "I am pure.
This same method applies to the other two verses as well. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the duties of the investigator is finished.
Commentary on the Answers to the Questions of the *Codaka-puccha* (362–363).

Regarding the answers to the questions beginning with "Who is the origin of the accusation?", it is stated: "In truth and in imperturbability. One should be established in truth and in imperturbability.
Whatever has been done or not done, that alone should be spoken; one should neither [speak falsely] to the accuser nor to the investigator.

Or anger should be aroused toward the Saṅgha. "One must know what has been plunged into and what has not been plunged into" means that one must know the speech that has been plunged into and the speech that has not been plunged into.

Herein, this is the method of knowing: one must know how much was the accuser’s prior statement, how much was his subsequent statement, how much was the accused’s prior statement, and how much was his subsequent statement. This is the measure for the accuser.
The measure of the one who has been censured must be taken; the measure of the investigator must be taken.
Even if the investigator does not fail by even a small amount, he should be told: "Friend, attend carefully and bring it straight.
The Saṅgha should proceed in this manner according to that Dhamma, according to that Vinaya, and according to that teaching of the Teacher.
Regarding the phrase "the legal issue is settled": here, "Dhamma" refers to the actual facts. "Vinaya" refers to both the formal accusation and the subsequent reminder.
"The Teacher’s instruction" refers to both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*).
For it is by means of this Dhamma, this Vinaya, and this Teacher’s instruction that the legal issue is settled; therefore, the investigator [should act] according to what is factual.

Having accused [the offender] by means of the basis for the charge and having reminded him of the offense, that legal dispute (adhikaraṇa) is to be settled through the perfection of the motion (ñatti) and the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvana);
this is how the investigator (anuvijjaka) should proceed. The rest here is self-evident. 364.
The questions and answers beginning with "For what purpose is the Uposatha? are also self-evident. Regarding the verses at the conclusion, among the elders...
And "he reviles" means that, acting with contempt, he reviles [others], thinking, "What do these people know?
He is "wounded" because he is wounded by himself through that inclination toward favoritism and through that reviling.
He is "one whose faculties are impaired" because his faculties, such as faith and the rest, have been impaired. "The witless one goes to hell, having no reverence for the training."
Thus, being scarred, with impaired faculties, and dull-witted due to the absence of wisdom, he does not train in the three trainings and lacks reverence for the training;
consequently, upon the breakup of the body, he goes only to hell. Therefore, one should not act out of dependence on material gain...
[as before] ...but should act according to the Dhamma. The meaning of this is: one should not act out of dependence on material gain toward those who have censured or are censuring [one].
For one who accepts material gifts such as robes given by another is acting in dependence on material things; he should not act in this way.

Nor should he act in dependence on a person, meaning that he should not act out of favoritism (*chanda*) and so forth toward a person by thinking, "This is my preceptor" or "This is my teacher," and so on; rather, having avoided both of these, [he should act].
"One should act exactly as the Dhamma stands.
"He whispers into the ear" means he counsels at the root of the ear, saying, "Speak thus; do not speak thus.
"He looks askance" means he seeks out faults. "He evades" means he avoids a formal decision. "He follows a wrong path" means he indicates an offense.

"He rebukes at the wrong time" means he rebukes even without an opportunity and without being asked. "He does not know what precedes and what follows" means he does not know both the preceding discourse and the subsequent discourse.
"He does not know the sequence of the words" means he does not know the speech by way of determining the sequence of the discourse. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Section on Rebuking is finished.
Cūḷasaṅgāma:
A Description of the Conduct of an Investigator 365.
In the Cūḷasaṅgāma, "a monk who has entered upon a legal dispute" refers to one who has entered into a dispute for the purpose of deciding a formal legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).

An assembly of the Saṅgha. For it is there that both those who are enemies of themselves and those who are enemies of the Teaching gather together, as did the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī, proclaiming a doctrine contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.
Whatever bhikkhu, having crushed the views of those adversaries, enters and plunges into that assembly for the purpose of proclaiming his own position and providing a definitive judgment—
He who causes [the Dhamma] to proceed is called a "warrior" (*saṅgāmāvacara*), such as the Elder Yasa.
When that warrior-monk approaches the Saṅgha, he should approach with a humble mind.
"With a humble mind" means having cast down the banner of pride, with a mind in which pride is subdued. "Equal to a dust-sweeper" means equal to a foot-wiper; just as a dust-sweeper...

Whether the feet being wiped are defiled or undefiled, there is neither lust nor hatred; thus, the meaning is that one should remain without attachment or aversion toward what is desirable or undesirable.

"On a suitable seat" means that having recognized a suitable seat, one should sit in the place where it reaches oneself, without showing one's back to the elder bhikkhus. "Without engaging in various kinds of talk" means...

By not engaging in various kinds of such useless talk. By one who does not engage in frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*) means by one who does not speak of frivolous talk concerning what has been seen, heard, or sensed, such as talk about kings and so forth.

"Or the Dhamma should be spoken by oneself" means that in the place where the Saṅgha has assembled, [the Dhamma] should be spoken based on what is allowable and what is unallowable, or based on the analysis of form and the formless, the methods of tranquility (*samatha*), the methods of insight (*vipassanā*), standing, sitting, and the observances (*vatta*), and so forth.
Or "Dhamma" refers to a discourse. Such a Dhamma should either be spoken by oneself or requested from another.
If a bhikkhu is capable of delivering such a discourse, he should be told: "Friend, when a question arises in the midst of the Saṅgha, you should speak.
Or, the noble silence should not be despised; for noble ones sit in silence.
They do not sit like foolish worldlings; rather, they sit only after taking up a particular meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, silence by way of attention to a meditation subject is called "noble silence. That should not be despised;
it should not be disregarded with the thought, "What is the use of devotion to a meditation subject? Rather, one should take up a meditation subject suitable for oneself.
The meaning is that one should sit down.
"The preceptor should not be questioned" means one should not ask, "What is your preceptor’s name? This same method applies in all cases.
"Birth should not [be questioned]" means one should not ask about birth in such a way as, "Are you of kṣatriya birth? Are you of brāhmaṇa birth?"
"By way of tradition" (*āgama*) means that one should not ask, "Are you a reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*? Are you a reciter of the *Majjhima Nikāya*?

"By way of family and lineage" (*kulapadesa*) should be understood as being by way of the Kṣatriya caste and so forth. "Affection or aversion toward him" means that toward this person there may arise either affection or aversion due to one or another of these aforementioned reasons.
"By one who conforms to the assembly": one should not be a conformist to the assembly or a follower of the crowd;
the meaning is that one should not speak by merely deliberating and conforming to whatever pleases the assembly. "No hand-gestures should be shown":
no movement of the hands should be made for the purpose of giving a signal regarding what should or should not be spoken.

"Adapting oneself to the meaning" means that one should sit while observing the penetration of the legal decision (*vinicchaya-paṭivedha*) itself, reflecting thus: "This discourse is found; regarding this legal decision, I shall say this.

"And one should not rise from one's seat" means that one should not rise from one's seat and wander about the assembly circle (*sannipāta-maṇḍala*), [but remain] with the holders of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*).
When [the teacher] has risen, the entire assembly rises. "It should not be bypassed" means that the formal decision (*vinicchaya*) must not be omitted.
"One should not follow a wrong path" means that an offense (*āpatti*) should not be pointed out. "One should be non-violent" means one should not act with violence;
the meaning is that one should not speak words spoken impulsively. "Patient in speech" means having a disposition to endure ill-spoken words.
"Surrounded by those who wish him well" means that one who desires his welfare and seeks his benefit should maintain both compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion;
this is the intended meaning of both these phrases. "Not with what is unrefined" means not with what is unrefined. "Unrefined speech" refers to unpleasant words characterized by contentious talk;
the sense is that such should not be spoken. "The self should be guarded" means [it should be guarded] in order to discern...
"One will be able to pacify it or not?"—in this way one should examine oneself;

the meaning is that one must know one's own capacity. "The other should be examined" means: "Is this assembly modest? Is it possible to persuade them, or not?"—in this way the other should be examined.
“The accuser is to be examined” means he is to be examined thus: “Is he one who accuses in accordance with the Dhamma, or not?
“The accused is to be examined” means he is to be examined thus: “Is he one who is accused in accordance with the Dhamma, or not?
“One who accuses contrary to the Dhamma is to be examined” means his authority must be known. The same method applies to the others as well. It was said: “without letting go.”
"By not letting go of the words spoken by those who have been reproved. "By not revealing what has not been said" means by not disclosing a matter that has not come forward.
"The dull-witted one should be encouraged" means the dull and bewildered person should be uplifted;

having inspired him with the thought, "Are you not indeed a son of good family?", and having had him speak on the course of training (*anuyogavatta*), his application should be undertaken. "The timid one should be reassured."
If someone experiences timidity because they have never before entered the midst of the Saṅgha or the midst of a group, one should say to such a person, "Do not be afraid;
speak freely; we shall be your support," and then have them recite the formal procedure (*anuyogavatta*).
One who is fierce should be restrained—that is, he should be reproved and threatened. One who is impure should be made to reveal it.

Having made the shameless one confess, he should be made to acknowledge the offense. "With straightforwardness and gentleness" means that a monk who is upright, virtuous, and free from crookedness of body and so forth should be treated with gentleness alone.

Regarding the phrase "toward both teachings and persons," it should be understood that only he who values the teaching and does not value the person is one who is equanimous toward both teachings and persons.

Regarding the phrases "for the purpose of reconciling the *sutta*" and so forth: it should be understood that when the *sutta* and other texts have been recited by an investigator who is dear, pleasing, respected, and venerable to his fellow celibates, [the investigation is] for the purpose of reconciling the *sutta*; that is, for the purpose of reconciling offenses and non-offenses.
"The simile is for the purpose of illustration" means the simile is for the purpose of showing the meaning. "The meaning is for the purpose of making it known."
The purpose is for the sake of making known. "For the sake of setting aside by way of counter-question" means that the questioning is for the purpose of setting aside the person.
"The act of granting leave is for the sake of reproving" means for the purpose of reproving regarding either the matter or the offense.

"Reproof is for the sake of reminding" means for the purpose of causing one to remember what is faulty or faultless. "Reminding is for the sake of making compliant" means for the purpose of making one compliant through the reminder of what is faulty or faultless.
“‘To serve as an obstacle for the sake of being subject to admonition’ means: ‘Do not depart from this residence beyond [this point]’—thus it serves as an obstacle.
‘An obstacle for the sake of reaching a decision’ means: for the purpose of bringing about a formal determination. ‘A decision for the sake of investigation’ means:
for the purpose of investigating and weighing what is faulty and what is faultless. ‘Investigation for the sake of determining what is possible and what is impossible’ means:”

"For the purpose of knowing what is an offense, what is not an offense, and what offenses are grave or light. "For the purpose of the Saṅgha’s thorough examination and acceptance" means for the purpose of accepting the formal adjudication (*vinicchaya*), and for the purpose of knowing whether the adjudication is well-done or poorly-done.
"Those who stand as individuals and do not deceive" means those who stand in positions of authority, sovereignty, leadership, and primacy, and who do not deceive in their positions.
And they are established; the meaning is that they are not to be disparaged.

Now, in order to close off the opportunity for those who are dull-witted and of weak intelligence to say, "For what purpose is the Vinaya?", he said, "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," and so forth.
In this context, "the Vinaya is for the sake of restraint" refers to the entire formulation of the Vinaya.
It is for the sake of restraint regarding the doors of body and speech. It is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for virtue culminating in purification of livelihood;

the meaning is that it is a condition (*paccaya*). This method applies everywhere. Furthermore, in this context, "non-regret" (*avippaṭisāra*) is the absence of mental regret with respect to what has been done or not done, whether evil or meritorious.
"Gladness" (*pāmujja*) is weak, nascent joy (*pīti*). "Joy" (*pīti*) is strong, abundant joy. "Tranquillity" (*passaddhi*)...
The subsiding of bodily and mental distress. "Happiness" refers to both bodily and mental happiness, for both of these are the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for concentration.
"Concentration" is one-pointedness of mind. "Knowledge and vision according to reality" is nascent insight;
this is a designation for the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). For one-pointedness of mind is the decisive support condition for nascent insight.
Disenchantment (*nibbidā*) is powerful insight leading to emergence that has reached its culmination. Dispassion (*virāga*) is the noble path (*ariyamagga*).
Liberation (*vimutti*) is the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala*); for even the fourfold noble path serves as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the fruit of arahantship.
Knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimutti-ñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of reviewing. "Knowledge and vision of liberation for the sake of final nibbāna without clinging" means...

It is for the sake of final nibbāna without remainder (apaccaya-parinibbāna). For that [discipline] is the condition for final nibbāna without remainder; when that has been attained, one must necessarily attain parinibbāna.
"This is the purpose of the talk" means that this discourse on the Vinaya has this as its purpose. "Counsels" (mantanā) refers specifically to the Vinaya counsels.
"Proximate cause" (upanisā) refers also to this successive conditionality, beginning with: "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," and so forth.
"For this purpose. "Attentive listening" means attentive listening to this discourse on the chain of dependent conditions.

The knowledge that arises from hearing this discourse is also for this purpose. "That is to say, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging" refers to that liberation of the mind—consisting of the fruit of Arahantship—which occurs by not clinging to the four types of clinging. That too [is for this purpose].
"For this purpose"; the meaning is "for the sake of final nibbāna without remainder.
Regarding the verses on the duties of inquiry (anuyogavatta), the first verse has its meaning already explained.

As for the terms "basis" (vatthu) and so forth, it is said that one who is unskilled in the basis, the failure, the offense, the cause (nidāna), and the mode (ākāra) does not know the sequence of what precedes and what follows.
The connection is with the word “does not know. The connection of the word “unskilled” (akovida) is with the phrase “he is indeed such a one.
Therefore, the construction here is as follows: that monk who does not know the basis for the *pārājika* offenses and so forth;
who does not know the fourfold failure (*vipatti*); who does not know the sevenfold offense (*āpatti*); [and who does not know] “this training rule concerns such-and-such a case...”
He does not know the origin [of the teaching], thinking, "It was laid down in the city"; he does not know the sequence, thinking, "This is the earlier statement, this is the later statement";

he does not know what has been done and what has not been done, thinking, "This has been done, this has not been done. And by "the same" means by that very same ignorance consisting in not knowing the sequence; thus it is said, "he does not know what has been done and what has not been done."
Thus, first of all, the connection with the word "does not know" (na jānāti) should be understood.
As for that which was stated, "unskilled in modes" (ākāra-akovida), therein "unskilled in modes" means unskilled in what is a cause and what is not a cause.
Thus, he who does not know even the basis (vatthu) and so forth, and is unskilled in the mode—such a bhikkhu indeed is called "one who is not to be rejected."
The connection of the terms *kamma* (action) and *adhikaraṇa* (legal issue) is also with the term "does not know.
Here is the construction: "In that very same way" refers to one who does not know the action, does not know the legal issue, and is unskilled even in the sevenfold settlement;
moreover, he is stained by lust and so forth, being corrupted, deluded, and [driven] by fear.
He proceeds out of fear; he proceeds out of delusion and confusion; moreover, due to passion and malice, he proceeds out of desire and hatred;
because of his inability to persuade others, he is not skilled in conciliation; because of his inability to discern what is right and wrong, he is unskilled in reconciliation;
and because he has obtained a following from an assembly similar to himself, he is one who has gained a faction.
One who lacks a sense of shame due to being devoid of moral dread is "shameless" (*ahirika*). One who is endowed with dark deeds is "one of dark karma" (*kaṇhakamma*).

Because of the absence of respect for the Dhamma and for persons worthy of respect, such a person is "disrespectful" (*anādara*). Indeed, such a bhikkhu is called "not to be rejected. The meaning is that he should not be rejected, nor should he be looked upon;
having been formally appointed, he should not be placed in a position of authority, sovereignty, leadership, or seniority. This also applies to the verses of the white side (*sukkapakkha*).
The method of construction should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The commentary on the Cūḷasaṅgāma Sutta is finished.
The Mahāsaṅgāma Sutta.
Commentary on what must be known by one who is conversing (368–374).

Regarding the "Great Battle": as for the phrase "from basis to basis," it means that having said, "I have seen or heard the matter of the first *pārājika*," when questioned again or pressed further, [one says], "I did not [see or hear] the first *pārājika*..."
“The basis was seen, not heard; the basis for the second *pārājika* was either seen or heard,” he says.
In this same manner, the transition between remaining bases, the transition from one failure to another failure, and the transition from one offense to another offense are to be understood.
However, as for one who says, “Neither was it seen by me, nor was it heard,” and later [says], “This indeed was seen by me...”
Or he says, "I have seen it or heard it," and having said, "I have seen it or heard it," he later says, "I have neither seen it nor heard it.
This should be understood as one who, having denied, affirms; having affirmed, denies.
This very act is called "evading with one thing another" (*aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati*).

375. Regarding "praise and blame": this refers to the training rule on sexual intercourse with a woman of pure intent (*sukkavissaṭṭhi-sikkhāpada*), according to the praise or blame of her complexion, such as blue-black and so forth. Regarding "the giving of messages":
this refers to acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*). The three [offenses] beginning with physical contact are stated in their own form.
Thus, these five should be understood as the preliminary stage and the preliminary application of sexual misconduct (*methunadhamma*).

376. "The four *apalokana*-karmas" refers to those performed by an incomplete assembly (*vaggādi*) through illegality (*adhammena*). The same method applies to the remaining [categories] as well. Thus, there are sixteen [karmas] consisting of four sets of four.
379. Commentary on the "unrighteous course not to be followed":
"He practices for the harm of many people" means that, in a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), the one who upholds the Vinaya has thus proceeded according to the inclinations of desire and so forth.
When that dispute was settled, the Saṅgha in that monastery split into two factions. The nuns who lived under their instruction also became divided into two groups.
Likewise, the laymen, the laywomen, the boys, the girls, and even the protective deities of those [monastics] split into two factions.
Then, starting from the earth-deities up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmās, they all likewise became divided into two.
Therefore it was said: “He practices for the harm of many people... for the suffering of gods and humans.

(382) “Dependent on what is uneven” means dependent on uneven bodily actions and so forth. “Dependent on a thicket” means dependent on a thicket consisting of wrong view and extreme views. “Dependent on the powerful” means dependent on powerful and well-known bhikkhus.
(393) “Disregarding him” means disregarding his words. Or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is “disregarding that [person].”
394. “Yaṃ atthāya” means for whatever purpose. “Taṃ atthaṃ” means that purpose. The remainder is entirely obvious throughout.
The commentary on the Mahāsaṅgāma [Sutta] is finished. [Now follows] the classification of the Kathina.
**Commentary on the Eight Subjects of Kathina (Kathināṭṭhatādivaṇṇanā)** 403.

Regarding *kathina*: "The eight headings" refers to the eight beginning with *pakkamanantika* (the end of the robe season by departure), as stated in the Khandhaka. The obstacles (*palibodha*) and the benefits (*ānisaṃsa*) have also already been explained previously.
404. Regarding "of the procedure": this refers to the fetching of water and so forth, which is for the sake of the sevenfold preliminary work (*pubbakaraṇa*), such as the washing of the robes.
An application is performed; [the question concerns] that application. "Which phenomena are conditions by way of the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*)?

means: having become proximate by way of the future, which phenomena serve as conditions? "By way of the immediate condition (*samanantara-paccaya*)" means: by way of a thoroughly immediate condition;
he asks while making the proximity condition itself even more immediate. "By way of the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*)"...
The meaning is: "Which phenomena act as conditions by having approached the state of being a support or a basis for the process that is arising?
By "through the decisive support condition" (*upanissayapaccayena*) means through a support condition that has become proximate;

he asks this having made the support condition itself more immediate. By "through the prenascence condition" (*purejātapaccayena*), [he refers to] the state of being a condition for that which has arisen first.
He asks. By the phrase "by way of post-nascence condition" (*pacchājāta-paccayena*), he asks about the state of being a condition for that which arises subsequently.
By the phrase "by way of co-nascence condition" (*sahajāta-paccayena*), he asks about the state of being a condition for those things arising neither before nor after one another.

"Of the preliminary preparation" (*pubbakaraṇassa*) refers to the preliminary preparation such as washing and so forth. "Of the relinquishment" (*paccuddhārassa*) refers to the old outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the other requisites.
Of the relinquishing. Of the determination: of the determination of the *kaṭhina* robe-cloth. Of the spreading: of the spreading of the *kaṭhina*. And of the matrices and the obstacles:
of the eight matrices and the two obstacles. Of the material: of the *kaṭhina* material such as the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth;
the rest is according to the method already stated.

Thus, having asked about everything that is obtainable and what is not, he now provides the answer by way of the method beginning with "The preliminary task of the application," etc., in order to show exactly what is obtainable for each case. Its meaning is as follows:
regarding what was stated, "Which factors are of the application," and so forth—it is said therein: "The preliminary task of the application."
It is a condition by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), contiguity-condition, support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), and decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

For the sevenfold preliminary preparation of the practice is a condition by these four conditions, because that practice is performed for the sake of the preliminary preparation that is to be accomplished by that practice. However, in the case of the prenascence-condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), this...
Among the dhammas enumerated, one does not obtain even a single dhamma [as a condition for it];

rather, the preliminary action (*pubbakaraṇa*) itself is its pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), because when there is the effort (*payoga*), the preliminary action comes to fruition. Therefore it was said:

"The effort is a condition for the preliminary action by way of the pre-arising condition. However, it obtains the post-arising condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*); therefore it was said: "The preliminary action..."
“Application is a condition for the subsequent by way of postnascence-condition. For that application is performed for the sake of a prior action that arises subsequently.

However, excluding the fifteen states consisting of the matrix, the obstacles, and the benefits, not even one other state among those such as application is found; for it is only those fifteen [that function as the postnascent condition].
The states, being accomplished together with the spreading of the *kaṭhina*, arise simultaneously; thus they are mutual *sahajāta-paccaya* (co-nascent conditions).
Therefore it is said: "Fifteen states are a condition by way of co-nascence. In this manner, all the answers to the various terms should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the analysis of the preliminary rites, the introduction, and so forth.

Commentary on the Analysis of What Should Be Known Regarding the Kathina and Other Matters (412). In response to the question, “What is to be known regarding the *kathina*? and so forth:

“Of those very phenomena” refers to the collection or combination of those phenomena—such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest—in the presence of which there is what is called the *kathina*. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with “a name, a naming act,” and so forth...
“*Kathina*” is merely a name for many phenomena; it shows that there is no single phenomenon existing in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
“By twenty-four modes” refers to the reasons previously stated, beginning with “not by mere scratching.
“By seventeen modes” refers to the reasons previously stated, beginning with “the *kathina* is spread when [the cloth] is unwashed. Regarding the formal acts (*nimitta-kamma*) and so forth...
Everything that ought to be said has been stated in the commentary on the Kathina Khandhaka.
416. "Arising together and ceasing together" means that when they arise, they arise together, and when they cease, they cease together.
"Arising together and ceasing separately" means that when they arise, they arise together, but when they cease, they cease separately.
What is meant? All [the factors] arise together with the *atthāra* (spreading out), for when there is an *atthāra*, there is what is called "lifting" (*uddhāra*).
However, here, the first two, while ceasing, cease together with the *atthāra* and reach the state of being lifted.
For the cessation of the *atthāra* and the state of these [two] being lifted occur at the same moment; the others [cease] separately.
They cease. Even when they have reached the state of being lifted, the application (atthāra) remains in force. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the explanation of the Kathina-bheda in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.

[Now begins] the commentary on the Anissitavagga, the "Upāli-pañcaka."

417. In the *Upālipañhā*, this is the connection to the question, "By how many [factors], venerable sir? It is said that the Elder, having gone into seclusion and reflected upon all these groups of five, thought:
"Now, having questioned the Blessed One, I shall establish a formal rule for the purpose of residing [in dwellings] and so forth based on these.
Thus, he approached the Blessed One and asked, "By how many, venerable sir? and so forth.
He asked questions according to the method. Regarding their answers: "He does not know the Uposatha" means he does not know the ninefold Uposatha.

"He does not know the Uposatha ritual" means he does not know the fourfold Uposatha ritual, which is divided into [procedures] such as those performed contrary to the Dhamma or by an incomplete assembly.
"He does not know the Pātimokkha" means he does not know the two Matikas. "He does not know the recitation of the Pātimokkha" means...
He does not know the ninefold recitation of the Pātimokkha—fivefold for monks and fourfold for nuns.

"He does not know the invitation (pavāraṇā)" means he does not know the ninefold invitation. "He does not know the formal act of invitation" means he does not know the fourfold formal act of invitation, which is divided according to whether it is contrary to the Dhamma, lacking a quorum, and so forth.
"He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense" means he does not know the offense and the non-offense as specified under each respective training rule.

"Having fallen into [an offense] and having had a formal act (kamma) performed against him": this means that having fallen into an offense, a formal act has been carried out by the Saṅgha on account of that very offense.
420. Regarding the phrase "the formal act is not to be suspended":

since he does not abide in the conduct in accordance with the Dhamma (*anulomavatta*), his formal act must not be suspended; the meaning is that he should be released only after having paid a fine (*sarajjuka*).

421. "If, Upāli, the Saṅgha performs acts that require unanimity"—that is, if it performs acts such as the Uposatha that must be done by a unanimous assembly—then no support should be given while the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or other such formal acts are being carried out.
For if the Saṅgha effects reconciliation after having caused an offense to be confessed, or [performs] the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass) method of settling a dispute;...
Having performed [the preliminary rites], he carries out the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā; such is called a legal act that must be performed in concord.
In that regard, if a monk does not consent to such a legal act, even after having made his view known, he should nevertheless attain such concord;
thus, one should not take a contrary position. However, where there is a teaching contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Teacher’s dispensation...
They illuminate [the matter]; in that case, the disclosure of one's view (*diṭṭhāvikamma*) is not permitted; one must depart after having resisted [the accusation].
"One who speaks with exalted words" (*ussitamantī*) is one who utters speech saturated with greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit—black-tongued and indicative of what is harmful.
"One who prattles dependently" (*nissitajappī*) is one who is unable to speak according to his own natural disposition in a manner consistent with excellence; rather, [he speaks] thinking, "By me..."
"He spoke thus with the king; such-and-such a high official spoke thus;
my teacher or preceptor named so-and-so, who is a master of the Three Piṭakas, spoke thus with me"—in this way, he prattles by relying on others.
Furthermore, he is not skilled in the sequence of speech, being unskilled both in the sequence of the discourse and in the sequence of its analysis.
"Not according to the Dhamma, not according to the Vinaya" means that he does not accuse or remind [another] of an offense by means of a factual basis.
"He exalts" means that he exalts some [persons] in such a manner as: "Our teacher is a master of the Great Piṭaka, a supreme preacher of the Dhamma," and so forth.
In the second phrase, he disparages some [persons] in such a manner as: "How could he not know the offense? and so forth.
“He takes up what is contrary to the Dhamma” means he takes up the side that does not lead to liberation. “He opposes the Dhamma” means he opposes the side that leads to liberation.
“He speaks much idle chatter” means he speaks much useless talk.
“He proceeds by force” means that, even when unasked and when no burden has been assigned to him, he simply overcomes others out of mere conceit.

"One who speaks without authority" means one who speaks without having been granted permission. "Having caused the formal act of not granting permission to be performed" means that he speaks without having had the formal act of granting permission performed.
"He does not declare according to his own view" means that he does not declare while placing his own personal view foremost;
rather, having set aside his own conviction, he speaks as one who holds the conviction that what is not truly real—such as non-dhamma—is indeed dhamma and so forth. This is the meaning.
Commentary on the Vohāravagga 424.
“He does not know the application for an offense” means he does not know: “This offense is through bodily application; this is through verbal application.
“He does not know the settlement of an offense” means he does not know: “This offense is settled by confession; this is by rehabilitation.”
"He does not know this [matter] either by way of the teaching or by way of the formal resolution.
"He is not skilled in the adjudication of offenses" means he does not know, "In this matter, this is the offense," and he is unable to extract and establish the offense in accordance with its fault.
"He does not know the origin of legal issues" means, "This legal issue arises based on the eighteen grounds for schism..."
He does not know: "This arises from the four failures; this arises from five or seven classes of offenses;
this arises in dependence upon the four duties of the Saṅgha. He does not know the application: "This legal issue has twelve root-applications;
this has fourteen root-applications; this has six root-applications; this has one root-application."
He does not know. For the applications (payoga) of legal issues (adhikaraṇa) have their respective roots; the meaning is that he does not know any of those.

"He does not know how to settle" means he does not know: "This legal issue is settled by two methods of settlement (samatha), this by three, this by four, and this is settled by one method of settlement. He is not skilled in adjudication.
"He does not know what 'occurs' means" refers to his inability to reach a settlement after having adjudicated a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
"He does not know the formal act" means he does not know the seven types of formal acts, such as the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) and so forth.
"He does not know the performance of the formal act" means he does not know that "this formal act must be performed in this manner. "He does not know the subject matter of the formal act" means...
He does not know: "This is a matter for censure (*tajjanīya*); this is for demotion (*niyassa*), and so forth. Regarding the duties (*vatta*):
among the seven formal acts (*kamma*), he does not know the eighteen-fold duty for the first four acts, nor the forty-three-fold duty for the three types of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*).
He does not know the settling of a formal act (*kamma-vūpasama*)—namely, [the case of] "a monk who, having performed the duties, makes a request..."
He does not know that "his offense must be settled and his transgression must be confessed.
He does not know the *vatthu* (basis) means he does not know the basis for the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*). He does not know the *nidāna* (origin) means he does not know:
"This training rule was laid down in this city; that one in that [city]. He does not know the *paññatti* (formulation)...
