“He does not know” means that he does not know the threefold *paññatti* (conceptual designation) by way of *paññatti*, *anupaññatti*, and *anuppannapaññatti*.
“He does not know the sequence of words” means that he does not know the word that ought to be uttered in its proper order;
for instance, when it should be said “the Buddha, the Blessed One,” he instead joins the words in reverse order, saying “the Blessed One, the Buddha.”
And he is unskilled in the Vinaya means that he is unskilled in both the Vinaya Piṭaka and its commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
"He does not know the motion" (ñatti): in brief, there are two kinds of motions—those specifically designated as "this is the motion," and those not so designated.
Of these, that which is not so designated is called a "formal act motion" (kamma-ñatti). That which is so designated...
That is called a "motion that is a part of the formal act" (*kammappādāñatti*); it does not know the motion in its entirety.

"It does not know the performance of the motion" means it does not know the performance of the motion as a formal act (*kammāñatti*) in nine instances, and [it does not know] the performance of the motion as a part of the formal act (*kammappādāñatti*) in two instances.
"The proclamation following the motion" means it does not know: "For this motion there is one proclamation; for this [other], there are three."

“He does not know the settlement by means of a motion (*ñatti*)” means that these four kinds of settlement—namely, resolution through recollection (*sativinaya*), resolution because of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*), further penalty (*tassapāpiyasikā*), and covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*)—do not occur without a motion; he does not know that this is “settlement by means of a motion.
“He does not know the pacification by means of a motion” means that whatever legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is pacified by these four kinds of settlement through a motion...
He does not recognize that settlement as "this settlement was effected by means of a motion.
"He does not know the Sutta" means he does not know the Ubhatovibhaṅga. "He does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta" means he does not know the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa).
"He does not know the Vinaya" means he does not know the Khandhaka and Parivāra. "He does not know what is in accordance with the Vinaya" means...

He does not even know the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*). Furthermore, being "unskilled in what is possible and what is impossible" means he is not skilled in what constitutes a valid reason and what does not.
"He does not know the Dhamma" means, setting aside the *Vinayapiṭaka*, he does not know the remaining two Piṭakas.

"He does not know what is in accordance with the Dhamma" means he does not know the four great authorities within the Sutta Piṭaka. "He does not know the Vinaya" refers specifically to the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra*.
“He does not know. Regarding the phrase “he does not know what is in accordance with the Vinaya,” this means he does not know the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
Here, however, the two Vibhaṅgas are not included; therefore, that which is stated in the *Kurundi*—“he does not know the entire Vinaya Piṭaka”—should not be accepted.
Furthermore, “he is not skilled in the sequence [of the text]” refers to being unskilled in both the preceding discourse and the subsequent discourse.
And he is unskilled. The remainder is self-evident, as it is to be understood everywhere by way of the opposites of what has been stated, and because it has already been explained previously.
The commentary on the *Anissita-vagga*, the *Nappaṭippassambhana-vagga*, and the *Vohāra-vagga* is finished.
The commentary on the *Diṭṭhāvikamma-vagga*.
425. In the section on the manifestation of views (*diṭṭhāvikamma-vagga*): "Manifestation of views" means the manifestations of views;
this is a designation for disciplinary acts (*vinaya-kamma*) consisting of the confession of offenses (*āpatti-desanā*), which are the explanations of one's own tenets (*laddhi*).

"He manifests a view regarding what is not an offense" means he confesses that very non-offense as an offense. "Regarding what does not require confession" means he manifests a view regarding a grave offense (*garuka-āpatti*).
The meaning is that he confesses both a *saṅghādisesa* and a *pārājika*. "When it has been confessed" means that even when a light offense has been confessed, he reveals his view;
the meaning is that he confesses again what has already been confessed.
"With four or five [people]" means he reveals his view in such a way that it becomes revealed by four or five people.
The meaning is that four or five people confess an offense together. "With mind and intention" means he reveals his view with an intention termed "mind";
the meaning is that without making a verbal utterance, he confesses the offense by means of the mind alone.

"In the presence of one who belongs to a different communion" means in the presence of one who belongs to a different communion either by way of holding different views or by way of a formal act (*kamma*). Regarding the view:

"Discloses" means he confesses an offense. "In another boundary" means that even for one who belongs to the same community, it is not permissible to disclose an offense in the presence of someone standing in a different boundary.

For instance, it is not allowed for one standing within the *māḷaka* boundary to confess an offense to one standing in the *sīmantarikā* (intermediate) boundary, nor for one standing in the *sīmantarikā* boundary to confess an offense to one standing in the *avippavāsa-sīmā* (non-separation) boundary. "Of one who has been made subject to disciplinary action" refers to one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
Or, the meaning is that one confesses in the presence of someone for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been suspended.

430. "Not capable of making an *okāsa* (granting leave)" means not being fit to do so; the meaning is that it should not be done. Here too, this refers to one who is not integrated into the Saṅgha (*apakatatta*), one who is suspended (*ukkhitaka*), and one for whom the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have been suspended. "With the intention of causing to fall away" means desiring to cause him to fall away from the Teaching (*sāsana*). 432.
"Through dullness and delusion" means that due to a state of dullness and a state of extreme delusion, one is incapable of knowing even what has been explained.
He asks like one who is mad, merely manifesting his own state of utter delusion.
"One of evil desires" asks with an evil desire, thinking, "In this way people will hold me in high regard. "Desiring to bring about contempt" asks while wishing to instill contempt.
This same principle applies to the other modes of answering as well. The rest is clear throughout. [End of] the Attādāna-vagga.
And whatever needs to be said regarding the Chapter on the Ascetic Practices (dhutaṅga) has already been stated above.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Manifestation of Views is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on False Speech begins.
444. In the Chapter on False Speech (*Musāvādavagga*): "One who goes to a *pārājika*" means one who reaches the state of a *pārājika* offense;

this is the meaning. The same principle applies to the others as well. In that context, false speech consisting in proclaiming non-existent superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) leads to a *pārājika*;
false speech consisting in groundless accusation of a *pārājika* offense leads to a *saṅghādisesa*. [As for] "he who dwells in your monastery," and so forth...

It should be understood that for one who speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it leads to a *thullaccaya*; for one who does not know, it leads to a *dukkaṭa*; and for one who speaks a deliberate falsehood, it is stated as "an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for a conscious lie," thus it leads to a *pācittiya*.
"By not seeing" means by the non-seeing of a Vinaya-expert (*vinayadhara*). For when doubt arises regarding what is permissible and what is impermissible, one [seeks] a Vinaya-expert...
Having seen [the distinction], one should inquire about what is allowable and what is unallowable, and having abandoned the unallowable, one should perform what is allowable;
however, not seeing it, one commits an offense by treating even the unallowable as allowable.

Thus, one does not commit an offense that ought to be committed through the sight of one who holds the Vinaya, but rather through not seeing him; therefore it is said, "by not seeing. "By not hearing" means...

However, even while living in a single dwelling, one certainly incurs [an offense] if one goes to attend upon a Vinaya-master but does not inquire about what is allowable and what is unallowable, or if one does not hear what is being said to others;
therefore it is said, "by way of not hearing. "By way of sleeping" means by the state of being asleep.
For one incurs [the offense of] sleeping together in the same house even through the condition of being asleep, due to the perception of what is unallowable as allowable.
But when one commits [an offense], one does so perceiving it as such. Through forgetfulness, one commits what ought to be committed by means of exceeding one night, and so forth.
The rest is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the Chapter on False Speech is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on Exhorting Bhikkhunīs (Bhikkhunovādavagga) 450.
In the section on bhikkhunīs: "For the sake of non-acquisition" means for the purpose of not obtaining the four requisites;
the meaning is that she strives and exerts herself in such a way that they do not obtain the requisites. "For the sake of harm" means for the sake of harm, which is the teaching of the Kali age.
"Attempting to move her" means she tries to go away. "For the sake of non-residence" means for the purpose of making her leave the village territory where she lives.
"He consorts with her" means he consorts with her for the purpose of practicing what is not the true Dhamma.
(451) "Venerable sir, with how many factors must a bhikkhunī be endowed for a formal act to be performed against her?"—he asks this referring to any one of the seven types of formal acts.

454. "One should not engage in discussion" means that the path of discourse—consisting of the distinctions between what is allowable and what is unallowable, the analysis of name-and-form, serenity, insight, and so forth—should not be expounded.
However, because a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed does not speak deceptively, he speaks as the master of such a path of discourse, whereas another does not;
therefore, after first rejecting [the idea that it could be spoken by] one who is "not yet perfected" (*asekha*) in the first pentad, [the text continues].
In the second pentad, the passage beginning with “by one who is beyond training” (asekkhena) is stated.

“One who has not attained the analytical knowledge of meaning” (na atthapaṭisambhidāpatto) means that, according to the commentary, he has not attained the analytical knowledge [of meaning], that is, he has not attained the knowledge that has reached its differentiation.

“One who has not attained the analytical knowledge of phenomena” (na dhammapaṭisambhidāpatto) means that he has not attained the analytical knowledge regarding the Dhamma of the Canon (pāḷidhamma). “One who has not attained the analytical knowledge of language” (na niruttipaṭisambhidāpatto) [means...]
He has not attained analytical knowledge regarding conventional expression and terminology.

"He has not attained the analytical knowledge of inspired eloquence" means that he has not attained analytical knowledge regarding those knowledges known as inspired eloquence, such as the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and so forth.
"He does not review his mind as it is liberated" means according to the fourfold liberation of the fruits [of the path].
The mind has not been reviewed by means of the nineteenfold reviewing. The remainder is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Section on Advice to Bhikkhunīs is finished.
The commentary on the Section on the Committee of Arbitration.
455. In the section on the *ubbāhika* (formal legal procedures): "Not skilled in the meaning" means not skilled in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*); he is not adept at extracting the meaning.
"Not skilled in the Dhamma" means, because it was not mastered from the mouth of a teacher, he is not skilled in the Canon (*pāḷi*), nor is he bold regarding the Canon.
"Not skilled in etymology" means not skilled in the linguistic usage of different languages. "Not skilled in phrasing" means [not skilled] by way of the lax, the emphatic, and so forth.
He is not skilled in arranging the phrasing (*byañjana*) in a rounded manner; the meaning is that he is not proficient in the delimitation of syllables.

"Not skilled in what precedes and what follows" means he is not skilled in the sequence of meaning, the sequence of Dhamma, the sequence of etymology, or the sequence of phrasing, nor is he skilled in prior discourses and subsequent discourses.
The terms beginning with "one who is prone to anger" are stated because one who is overcome by anger and the like does not know what is a cause and what is not a cause, and is unable to judge;
therefore they are so described. "One who causes forgetfulness, not one who causes remembrance" means he is a deluder, not a producer of mindfulness;

the meaning is that he deludes and conceals the speech of both the accuser and the accused, rather than causing them to remember. The rest here is self-evident from the section on the committee (ubbāhika-vagga).
The commentary on the Ubbāhikavagga is finished.
Commentary on the Adhikaraṇavūpasamavagga 457.
Regarding the Adhikaraṇavūpasamavagga: "One who respects individuals" refers to those such as "This is my preceptor; this is my teacher," and so forth.
Having reflected thus and desiring his victory, he proclaims what is contrary to the Dhamma as being the Dhamma.
"He is one who values the Saṅgha" means that by deciding cases without abandoning either the Dhamma or the Vinaya, he is called one who values the Saṅgha.

One who decides cases while accepting robes and other requisites is called one who values material things; one who decides according to the Dhamma without accepting those things is called one who values the true Dhamma.
458. “By five ways, Upāli, means by five causes the Saṅgha is split:
by a formal act (*kamma*), by a recitation (*uddesa*), by speaking (*voharanta*), by a proclamation (*anussāvana*), and by the taking of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).

Here, ‘by a formal act’ means by any one of the four formal acts, such as the act of information (*apalokana-kamma*) and so forth. ‘By a recitation’ means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. ‘By speaking’ means...”
Speaking thus, he was pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "non-Dhamma is Dhamma," by means of various rebirths.
Regarding the phrase "by proclamation": [he said], "Do you not indeed know my noble birth, my state of having gone forth, and my great learning?
Would anyone like me ever even conceive the thought of causing you to accept a teaching that is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya?"
[He did so] by whispering into their ears in this manner: "Is it fitting? Is Avīci cool for me like a grove of blue lotuses?

Do I not fear the states of misery? and so forth. "By the taking of voting tickets" means: having thus made the proclamation, having steadied their minds, and having rendered them incapable of turning back, [he said], "Take this voting ticket," and thus by the taking of the voting tickets.

And here, the action (*kamma*) itself is the description or the authority; however, the formal announcement, the proclamation, and the taking of the voting sticks (*salākā*) are the preliminary stages.

For even when they have been announced there for the purpose of generating consent while explaining the eighteen grounds, and the voting sticks have been taken, the Saṅgha remains undivided. But when, having thus caused four or more to take the voting stick...

When he performs either an exclusive formal act (*āveṇika-kamma*) or a proclamation (*uddesa*), then the Saṅgha is said to be "split. Thus, regarding what we stated in the commentary on the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka*:

"In this way, having illustrated any one of the eighteen grounds, and having persuaded [the monks] by various reasons saying 'Accept this, approve this,' and having had voting tickets (*salāka*) distributed, when a separate formal act of the Saṅgha has been performed..."
“The Saṅgha is split. However, in the *Parivāra*, it is stated: “Upāli, the Saṅgha is split in five ways,” and so forth.
There is no difference in meaning between that [passage] and this definition of a schism in the Saṅgha given here.
We shall demonstrate that lack of difference in its own context; thus, it has been explained.
"Paññattetaṃ" means this has been laid down. Where was it laid down? In the *Vattakkhandhaka*. For there, the fourteen duties for the *khandhakas* were laid down. Therefore he said:
"Upāli, this 'duty for incoming bhikkhus' has been laid down by me," and so forth.
Even so, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha; for to that extent there is merely a rift in the Saṅgha.
It exists, yet there is as yet no schism in the Saṅgha; however, the meaning is that this fissure in the Saṅgha, gradually increasing, leads to a formal schism.
"According to the night" means in accordance with the measure of the night; the meaning is "according to the seniority.
"Having made a separation" means having established a distinct division. "Performing legal and illegal acts" refers to performing various formal acts of the Saṅgha one after another.

Depending on [the circumstances], they perform both minor and major legal acts (*kamma*). The rest here is also self-evident, as in the Chapter on the Settlement of Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇavūpasamavagga*).
Commentary on the Two Chapters on Schism in the Sangha (*Saṅghabhedavagga*): 459.

Regarding the two chapters on schism in the Sangha—“having set aside [one’s] view by means of a formal act” (*vinidhāya diṭṭhiṃ kammena*)—among those [categories] such as "not-Dhamma" and so forth, [it refers to] "not-Dhamma" and so forth.
"Thus" means that having held such a view and having set aside that very view, one explains those factors by way of the Dhamma and performs a separate ritual act.

Thus, the five factors consist of the ritual act performed while having set aside the view, together with that very act of setting aside the view; "Upāli, it is by these five factors"—this refers to one [case].
There is an application of the meaning in the *Pañcaka* [Vagga]. By this method, all the *pañcakas* are to be understood.

Here too, the triad of factors beginning with "conventional expression" (*vohāra*) is stated by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) alone; however, incurability (*atekicchatā*) is to be understood by way of the assignment of kamma (*kammuddesa*).
The rest is clear everywhere; there is nothing here for which the method has not already been stated previously.
Commentary on the Chapter on Residents (Āvāsikavagga): 461.
Regarding the phrase "placed as it was brought" (*yathābhataṃ nikkhitto*) in the Chapter on Residents:

it means placed after having been carried there. 462. "Explanations of the Vinaya" (*vinayabyākaraṇā*): these are the answers to questions concerning the Vinaya. "He transforms" (*pariṇāmeti*) means he determines, illustrates, or explains. The rest here is self-evident.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Spreading of the Kathina, 467.
In the Chapter on the Spreading of the Kathina: "One who has gone into the dark" means one who has entered darkness;
for if he were to bow to him, his forehead might strike even the legs of the bed or other furniture. "Not attending" means not attending to the act of bowing because he is preoccupied with some duty.
"Sutta" means one who has fallen asleep. "Ekāvatta" refers to one who has turned away from [the Sangha] and stands on the side of an enemy—an adversary or a person of a different class;
such a person is not to be saluted. For if he were being saluted, he might even strike with his foot. "Aññavihita" means one who is thinking of something else.
"Khādanta" means eating flour-cakes and the like. "Uccārañca passāvañca karonto" (while voiding excrement and urine) is because of having no other place to go.
"One not to be saluted" (*avandiyo*): one who has been suspended by any of the three kinds of acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) is "one not to be saluted.
However, the four types of persons subjected to acts such as censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) are to be saluted. The *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* ceremonies may also be performed together with them.
Regarding those described as "not to be saluted" from the beginning, an offense occurs only for one who salutes a naked person or one who has been suspended; but for the others...
Veneration is prohibited on account of its unsuitability and for the reasons stated in the interim.

Hereafter, even the ten types of persons beginning with those who have received full ordination later than oneself are not to be venerated solely because they constitute grounds for an offense. For one who venerates them, there is necessarily an offense.
Thus, among these five sets of five, there is no offense for one venerating thirteen persons; however, there is an offense for venerating twelve.

468. “The teacher is to be venerated”: the teacher of going-forth, the teacher of full ordination, the teacher of dependence, the teacher of recitation, and the teacher of exhortation—this fivefold teacher is to be venerated. The rest is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Spreading of the Kathina is finished.
And the commentary on the Five Questions of Upāli is completed.
Commentary on the Origin of Offenses (Āpatti-samudāna-vaṇṇanā): 470.

Regarding the phrases "one commits [an offense] unintentionally" and so forth: one who commits an offense that is a formal rule-offense (*paṇṇattivajja*), such as sleeping in the same bed with another, unintentionally commits it;
when confessing it, one emerges from it intentionally. One who commits any [other offense] intentionally commits it intentionally.

One who resolves by means of the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) emerges without mental intention (*acittaka*). As previously stated, one who resolves by means of the "covering over as with grass" commits an offense without mental intention and emerges without mental intention.
One who teaches the other [methods] commits an offense with mental intention (*sacittaka*) and emerges with mental intention.
When one performs the recitation of the *Padasodhamma* and so forth, thinking, "I am giving the gift of Dhamma," one commits an offense with a wholesome mind (*kusalacitta*).
One who teaches with an uplifted mind, thinking, “I am carrying out the instruction of the Buddhas,” emerges with a wholesome state of mind (*kusalacitta*).

One who teaches while being depressed emerges with an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*). One who emerges from sleep by means of the “covering over as with grass” (*tiṇavatthāraka*) emerges with an indeterminate state of mind (*abyākatacitta*).
One who teaches with joy, thinking, “I am carrying out the teaching of the Buddhas,” after having performed such acts as causing terror, [emerges] with an unwholesome state of mind.
One falls [into an offense] with a wholesome mind and emerges with a wholesome mind. When confessing while feeling mental distress, one emerges with an unwholesome mind;
when emerging by means of the "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*) in the manner already described, one emerges with an indeterminate mind.

At the time of waking from sleep, one who enters a shared dwelling falls [into an offense] with an indeterminate mind; however, here too, it should be understood that "one emerges with a wholesome mind," and so forth, according to the method already stated.
"How many origins (samuṭṭhāna) does the first *pārājika* have? and so forth—this is self-evident because it follows the method already explained previously.
Regarding the questions "How many origins do the four *pārājikas* have? and so on, everything that applies to each respective origin, according to the maximum limit, has already been stated.
The commentary on the origins of offenses (*āpatti-samuṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
Aparadutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇikaṃ (1):
Commentary on the Offenses of Body, etc. 474.
In the response to the verses beginning with “How many offenses are bodily? it is stated that there are six offenses that are bodily (*kāyikā*) within the *antarapeyyāla*.

By means of the fourth origin of offenses, one incurs six offenses—namely, those stated in the sequence beginning with, "If a bhikkhu engages in sexual intercourse, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). These are called bodily because they originate at the door of the body.
Or, by means of the fifth origin of offenses in that same intermediate section, one incurs six verbal offenses.
He incurs offenses—namely, those offenses described in the manner beginning with, “The bhikkhu is of evil desire, overcome by desire. For one who conceals them, there are three:
for a bhikkhunī who conceals a fault, it is a *pārājika*; for a bhikkhu’s concealment of a *saṅghādisesa*, it is a *pācittiya*;
and for concealing one’s own grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*), it is a *dukkaṭa*. There are five conditions for physical contact with a bhikkhunī.

There are these five offenses conditioned by physical contact: a *pārājika* for [sexual] physical contact; a *saṅghādisesa* for a monk [touching a woman]; a *thullaccaya* for [touching] what is connected to the body with the body;
a *dukkaṭa* for [touching] what is connected to the body with an article that must be relinquished (*nissaggiya*); and a *pācittiya* for tickling with the fingers.
Regarding "Tissa at dawn," there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense based on the transgression of one night, four nights, seven nights, ten days, or a month.

In the case of a bhikkhunī’s staying apart at night, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense: "If she conceals it during the first watch, or conceals it during the second or third watch, the offense is concealed when the sun rises;
whoever conceals it must be made to confess a *dukkaṭa*. Thus, at sunrise, one incurs these three offenses.
"Two that require a formal act up to the third time" means that there are eleven [offenses] known as those requiring a formal act up to the third time.

By way of formal designation (*paññatti*), however, there are two: those involving a third admonition for monks (*bhikkhu-yāvatatiyaka*) and those involving a third admonition for nuns (*bhikkhunī-yāvatatiyaka*).
Among these, the one called "the eight matters" (*aṭṭhavatthuka*) belongs to the nuns alone; it is this single category within this Teaching known as the eight matters.
By the single introductory summary (*nidānuddesa*), namely, "Whosoever has an offense, let him reveal it," there is a complete inclusion of all [the rules].
There is a compendium of all training rules (sikkhāpada) and all recitations of the Pātimokkha.
"The two roots of the Vinaya" refers to body and speech. "Two heavy [offenses] are mentioned" refers to the Pārājikas and Saṅghādisesas.
"Two concealments of what is grave" refers to the Pārājika for one who conceals a fault (vajjapaṭicchādikā) and the Saṅghādisesa for one who conceals another.
“An offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*): these two are called offenses for concealing a grave matter (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*).
Regarding ‘four within a village’: if a monk makes an appointment with a nun, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if he enters the vicinity of another village, it is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*); while the nun is going from one village to another, if the village is enclosed...”
In the first step, there is a *thullaccaya*; in the second step, a *saṅghādisesa*. For an unenclosed area, in the first step upon entering the vicinity, there is a *thullaccaya*;
in the second step, a *saṅghādisesa*. These are the four offenses—*dukkaṭa*, *pācittiya*, *thullaccaya*, and *saṅghādisesa*—in relation to the interior of a village.
Regarding the four conditions for crossing a river: "A monk makes an appointment with a nun..."
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); if he boards a boat, it is an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).

For a nun crossing to the other side of a river, at the time of crossing, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for the first step, and an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*) for the second step—these are the four.
Regarding "a grave offense for one kind of meat," this refers to human flesh. Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing for nine kinds of meat," this refers to the remaining types of unallowable meat.
"Two verbal [acts] at night": if a bhikkhunī, standing within arm's reach of a man in the darkness of night where there is no lamp, converses with him, it is a *pācittiya*;
if she stands beyond arm's reach and converses, it is a *dukkaṭa*. "Two verbal [acts] by day":
if a bhikkhunī, standing within arm's reach of a man in a concealed place during the day...
If one speaks while within arm’s reach, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if one speaks after having moved beyond arm’s reach, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, with the intention of death, one gives poison to a human being saying, “Tissa is giving,” and that person dies because of it, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);
if one gives it to a *yakkha* or a *peta*, and they die, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya); if one gives it to an animal, and it dies, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"For giving a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). For one giving in this manner, there are three offenses:

if she accepts [the gift] with four [limbs], such as by taking the hand or taking the braid, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa); if she grasps the organ with the mouth, it is an offense involving defeat (pārājika);
for accepting a robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya); [and so too] for one who is lustful toward one who is lustful.
For one who receives solid food or soft food from the hand, there is a thullaccaya offense; thus, in the case of receiving, there are four classes of offenses.
(2) Explanation of those offenses entailing confession, etc.

475. "Five that lead to confession" refers to the five light offenses. "Six that require remedial action" refers to all except the *pārājika*. "One here that requires no remedial action" refers to the single *pārājika* offense.
"Two are said to be grave in the Vinaya" refers to the *pārājika* and the *saṅghādisesa*.

"And those pertaining to body and speech": all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) pertain to body and speech; there is not even a single training rule prescribed for the mind-door. "One [offense] at the wrong time."

"Grain-juice" refers to salted sour gruel (*soṇḍikā*). For this alone is the one grain-juice permitted at improper times. "One formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations" refers to the authorization for an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
For this alone is the one authorization permitted by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations.
"Two offenses involving defeat pertaining to the body" are the offense of sexual intercourse for bhikkhus and the offense of physical contact for bhikkhunīs.
"Two grounds of common affiliation" means either one makes oneself a member of the same communion as oneself, or a harmonious Saṅgha reinstates one who has been suspended.
In the *Kurundi*, however, these two grounds of common affiliation are stated as "the ground of common affiliation and the ground of different affiliation.
"The breaking of the two nights" refers to [the interruption] for one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) and for one who is undergoing the penance (*mānatta*).
And they are prescribed. "Two finger-breadths" means two prescriptions regarding finger-breadths:
one is "it should be taken with at most two finger-joints," and the other is "two finger-breadths or two months.
"Having struck herself twice" means that a bhikkhunī, having struck herself, incurs two offenses; she strikes herself.
If she weeps, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if she strikes her but does not weep, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"The Saṅgha is split by two means" refers to both formal acts (kamma) and the drawing of lots (salākaggāha). "There are two first offenses here" means that throughout the entire Vinaya, there are two types of first offenses according to the way they were prescribed for both [monks and nuns].
Otherwise, however, there are nine for monks and nine for nuns, making eighteen.

They exist. "By means of the motion (ñatti), two things are performed" refers to two functions of the motion: the formal act (kamma) and the basis for the formal act (kammapādaka). In nine instances there is the formal act, while in two instances it exists by way of being the basis for the formal act.
Regarding the taking of life, there are three cases: "If one digs a pit without specifying [the victim], and a human dies, it is a *pārājika*; [if a *yakkha* or a *peta* dies...]"
“There is a thullaccaya for causing death; there is a pācittiya for causing the death of an animal”—these are the three. Regarding the three who commit a pārājika by speech:
the concealer of an offense, the one who follows a suspended monk, and the one who claims eight grounds [for superhuman states].
However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: “By command, in the case of taking what is not given, in the case of human death, and in the case of claiming superhuman states.”
Three have been stated. Regarding "three illuminations": when one speaks in praise or dispraise specifically referring to the anus or the urinary passage, it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
when speaking in praise or dispraise referring to the area below the collarbone but above the kneecaps—excluding the anus and the urinary passage—it is a *thullaccaya*;
when speaking in praise or dispraise referring to the area above the collarbone but below the kneecaps, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [The same applies] regarding acting as a go-between.
"Or she herself": if he accepts it, examines it, and returns it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if he accepts it and examines it but does not return it, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); if he accepts it but neither examines it nor returns it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
These are the three classes of offenses based on the act of matchmaking as the cause.
"Three persons should not be ordained": one deficient in duration, one deficient in limbs, and one who has failed in the subject matter;

their distinctions have already been stated. Furthermore, in this context, those who are incomplete in bowl and robes, as well as those who possess them but do not ask for them, are included within the category of "deficient in limbs.
Likewise, matricides and others who commit offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—namely, those classified as eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and animals—are also included.

It should be understood that it is included by way of the failure of the subject matter (*vatthu*) alone. This method is stated in the *Kurundi*. There are three ways of including formal acts (*kamma*):

the performance of a motion (*ñattikappanā*), the individual completion of what was left unfinished (*vippakatapaccattaṃ*), and the making of what has passed (*atītakaraṇa*). Among these, the performance of a motion consists of the distinctions such as "he should give" or "he should perform";

the individual completion of what was left unfinished consists of the distinctions such as "he gives" or "he performs"; and [the making of what has passed] consists of the distinctions such as "given" or "performed."
“Past performance” (*atītakaraṇa*)—by these three, formal acts (*kamma*) are subsumed. Furthermore, formal acts are also subsumed by another three:

the matter (*vatthu*), the motion (*ñatti*), and the proclamation (*anussāvana*). For a formal act that is complete in its matter, complete in its motion, and complete in its proclamation is indeed called a formal act;
therefore it is said: “There are three ways of subsuming formal acts. The three who have been expelled are Mettiya... [and so on].
"A bhikkhunī is to be expelled; a violator is to be expelled; a novice endowed with ten factors is to be expelled;

expel the thorn-like novice"—thus, three types of those who have been expelled should be understood by way of the formal act of punishment (daṇḍakamma) for expulsion regarding the status of the religious emblem (liṅga) and communal residence (saṃvāsa).
Regarding "the three [acts] by a single proclamation": "I allow you, monks, to perform two or three [acts] by a single proclamation."
Regarding the words: for three persons who have the same preceptor but different teachers, a single formal proclamation (*ekānussāvanā*) is permissible.
Regarding taking what is not given: if it is three *pādas* or more than three *pādas*, it is a *pārājika*; if it is more than a *māsaka*, it is a *thullaccaya*;
if it is a *māsaka* or less than a *māsaka*, it is a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the four conditions for sexual intercourse: if it is unbroken, it is a *pārājika*; if it is mostly...
If it is swallowed, there is a *thullaccaya*; if the mouth is opened wide, there is a *dukkaṭa*; if it is in a *jatumaṭṭhaka* (a medicinal preparation), there is a *pācittiya*.
Regarding "for one cutting, three": for one cutting a forest tree (*vanappati*), there is a *pārājika*; for [cutting] a living plant (*bhūtagāma*), there is a *pācittiya*;

for [cutting] the sexual organ (*aṅgajāta*), there is a *thullaccaya*. "Five conditions for discarding": if one indiscriminately discards poison and a person dies because of it, there is a *pārājika*.

In the case of *yakkhas* and *petas*, it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*); in the case of an animal, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); in the case of discarding [waste] where there is no one to clean it up, it is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*);

and in the case of the training rules regarding the discarding of feces or urine on green vegetation, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). These are the five offenses based on the condition of discarding.

Regarding the phrase "the offense of wrong-doing is made by means of the offense of expiation": this refers to the ten training rules in the Chapter on the Instruction of Bhikkhunīs, which are offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*).

The meaning is: "Together with the *dukkaṭa*, they are committed. Regarding the statement "four novices are mentioned here," the meaning is that in the very first training rule (*sikkhāpada*), four novices are mentioned:
two in the case of an illegal formal act (*adhammakamma*) and two in the case of a legal formal act (*dhammakamma*). "And with the robe for two" means:
there is a *pācittiya* offense for one giving a robe to a person who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of monks, and [there is a different offense] in the presence of nuns.
"For one giving to a fully ordained nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*": this means that for one giving a robe to two nuns, an offense occurs by reason of the robe [being given].

"The eight *pāṭidesanīyas*" are indeed those transmitted in the Canon. "By the *pācittiya* for eating raw grain, the *dukkaṭas* are included": for one who eats after requesting raw grain, the *dukkaṭas* are indeed included along with the *pācittiya*.
Regarding "for one going": for a monk who travels having made an appointment with a nun or a woman, it is a *dukkaṭa*;

upon entering the vicinity of a village, it is a *pācittiya*. For a nun who goes alone from one village to another, as she enters the vicinity of the village, there is a *thullaccaya* at her first step, and a *saṅghādisesa* at her second step—this is for one who is going.
These are the four offenses. "And for one who stands, it is likewise" means that for one who stands, there are exactly four [offenses].
How so? If a bhikkhunī stands within arm's reach of a man in the dark or in a concealed place out of friendly intimacy, it is a *pācittiya*;
if she stands having left the arm's reach, it is a *dukkaṭa*; at the time of sunrise...
If she stands while leaving the reach of the second nun’s hand, it is a *thullaccaya*; if she stands after having left [the reach], it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
There are four offenses for one who is sitting. For one who is lying down as well, there are just as many: for even if she sits or lies down, she incurs these same four offenses.
(3) Commentary on the Pācittiya Rules: 476.

Regarding the "five pācittiyas": having received five medicinal substances, if they have been placed in various containers or in a single container without being mixed, and that bhikkhu exceeds the seven-day period, he incurs all five pācittiyas.
One incurs various bases [of offenses] simultaneously; it cannot be said, "This one was incurred first, this one later.

Regarding the nine *pācittiya* rules: whichever monk, having requested the nine kinds of refined food, mixes them together into a single mouthful, puts it into his mouth, and swallows it beyond the throat—this constitutes the nine *pācittiya* offenses.
One incurs all [five] offenses simultaneously based on different grounds; it cannot be said, "I have incurred this one first, and that one later.
"One should confess in a single utterance" means: "Venerable sir, having accepted five kinds of medicine and having exceeded the seven-day limit, I have incurred five offenses;
I confess them all before you"—in this way, one should confess in a single utterance.
They are indeed taught; there is no need for two or three verbal utterances. In the second response as well, one should say:
"Venerable sir, having requested nine kinds of choice food and eaten them, I have incurred nine offenses; I confess them in your presence.
Having declared the matter, one should confess: "Venerable sir, having accepted five kinds of medicine for seven days..."
“...I have transgressed; I confess that matter to you exactly as it occurred. Having thus confessed the matter, the offenses are indeed confessed;
there is no need to mention the name of the specific offense. In the second response as well:
“Venerable sir, having requested nine kinds of fine food, I ate it; I confess that matter to you exactly as it occurred.”
One should say, “I confess.
Regarding the offense of the third time: for Tissā, it is a *pārājika*; for those who follow the schismatic Kokālika and others, it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
and for Caṇḍakāḷikā, a nun who does not relinquish a wicked view, it is a *pācittiya*.
These are the three offenses that extend up to the third [repetition]. "Six offenses on account of trade" means that one incurs six offenses on account of speech used for the purpose of trade.
How so? For the sake of livelihood, for the sake of a livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by desire speaks of a non-existent, unreal superhuman state;
this is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*). For the sake of livelihood, for the sake of a livelihood, one acts as a go-between...

If one enters [into such a state], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. If, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, one says of someone dwelling in that monastery, "He is an *arahant*," there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.

If, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, a monk requests fine foods for his own use and eats them, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. [If] a nun, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood...
If one requests exquisite foods for one's own sake and eats them, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
If, for the sake of livelihood and as a cause for livelihood, one who is not ill requests either soup or boiled rice for one's own sake and eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding eating: for human flesh, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); for the remaining types of unallowable meat, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For a bhikkhunī, there is an offense of expiation regarding garlic. Regarding the five conditions for food:

having taken food from the hand of a lustful man who is himself lustful, and having requested human flesh or garlic for her own use right then and there, she takes those fine foods and mixes them with the remaining unallowable meat, crushing them together into a composite mixture.
While swallowing, one incurs these five offenses on account of food: a *saṅghādisesa*, a *thullaccaya*, a *pācittiya*, a *pāṭidesanīya*, and a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the "five grounds": [the case] of a nun who follows one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*) and does not relinquish her position despite being admonished up to three times...

“By the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); by two proclamations, a grave offense (thullaccaya); at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

In cases such as striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa); in not relinquishing a wicked view, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Thus, all [these] proceed through five stages up to the third time. “And of the five offenses”: as for the term “offense” (āpatti):

It pertains to five who share the same Dhamma; therein, for two [of them], it is indeed an offense in the literal sense (*nippariyāya*), but for those undergoing training (*sikkhamānā*), female novices (*sāmaṇerī*), and male novices (*sāmaṇera*), it is not permitted because of their unfitness.
According to this method, an offense of theirs should not be made to confess, but rather a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*) should be performed against them.
"And by means of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) of the five" means that the legal issue belongs only to these five.
For it is precisely for the sake of these five things—bowl, robes, and so forth—that the term *vinicchaya-vohāra* (legal adjudication) is called *adhikaraṇa* (a legal issue);
however, for laypeople, this is known as *aḍḍakamma* (litigation).
"There is an adjudication of five" means that there is indeed an adjudication only among those who share the same Dhamma. Of the five...
"By means of pacification" (vūpasamena) means that the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) of these very five [cases] is called "settled" (*vūpasanta*).
"And there is no offense for the five" means that for these very five, there is what is called "no offense" (*anāpatti*).
"It shines by three grounds" means it shines by the three causes beginning with the Saṅgha. For a person who has committed a transgression...

Having remedied an offense that requires remediation—whether in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual—one becomes of upright conduct and restored to normalcy;
therefore, it is said that one shines by means of these three factors.
Two bodily [offenses] are "throughout the night": when a bhikkhunī stands, sits, or lies down within arm's reach of a man in the darkness of night.
If she makes her arrangements, it is a *pācittiya*; if she makes her arrangements such as standing while remaining within arm’s reach, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Thus, at night, she incurs two offenses arising from the door of the body. "Two bodily [offenses] by day"—by this same method, during the day, she incurs two offenses in a concealed place. "For one who gazes, there is one offense": "And you, monks... [as follows].
“One who is lustful should gaze at the private parts of a woman. Whoever should so gaze, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one who gazes, this is the single offense. Regarding the single condition of almsfood: “And, monks, the face of the giver of food should not be looked at.
Herein, there is an offense of wrong-doing even for one giving as little as rice-gruel or a curry sauce.
For even for a novice monk who looks up at [a nun’s] face, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
“If one eats almsfood that has been prepared by a nun—[even] if it is a single portion of almsfood—it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Regarding the eight benefits, these are the benefits mentioned in the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*. It is said that three types of those who have been suspended (ukkhitaka) have been described.
"Regarding the non-seeing of an offense, the non-mending of it, and the non-renunciation of an evil view.
"The forty-three modes of right conduct" refers to the observance of these very rules of conduct by those who have been suspended.
"Lying in five instances" means lying in five categories: those reckoned as *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, and *dukkaṭa*.
False speech is included. "It is said that fourteen are the maximum" refers to what was stated above regarding the rule of the ten-day maximum and so forth.
"Twelve *pāṭidesanīya* rules" means four for monks and eight for nuns.
"And by the confession of the four" means by the confession of the four transgressions. But which are they? They are the murderous plots instigated by Devadatta.
The confession of transgression: the confession of transgression by the attendant of the Elder Anuruddha, the confession of transgression by Vaḍḍha the Licchavi,
and the confession of transgression by the monks who had come after a *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) was carried out against the Elder Vāsabhagāmiya—
this is called the "confession of transgression" for these four.
The eightfold false speech consists of eight factors beginning with "first he thinks, 'I will speak a falsehood'" and ending with "having set aside his perception.
The factors of the uposatha are likewise stated in the same manner as "he does not kill living beings," and so forth.
The eight factors of a messenger are stated as: "Here, monks, a monk is both a listener and a proclaimer," and so forth.
The rules regarding one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha are stated according to the *Naya* method.
The eight duties of a non-Buddhist ascetic (*titthiya*) are stated in the *Mahākhandhaka*. "Ordination by means of eight proclamations" refers to the ordination of bhikkhunīs.
"One should rise for eight" means that in the dining hall, one should rise for the other [bhikkhus] when eight bhikkhunīs arrive and offer them seats. [Regarding] the instructor of bhikkhunīs...
"Endowed with eight qualities": a bhikkhu endowed with these eight factors should be appointed as an exhorter of the bhikkhunīs.

Regarding the verse "The cutting belongs to one person": among the nine types of people, the cutting [of the Saṅgha] belongs only to him who, having distributed voting tickets (*salāka*), causes a schism in the Saṅgha;
like Devadatta, he incurs a *pārājika* offense. For the four followers of the schismatic, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
As in the case of Kokālika and others, there is no offense for the four who speak according to the Dhamma. Furthermore, both these offenses and non-offenses have the same basis for all:
they are based solely on the schism of the Saṅgha.

Regarding the verse "The nine grounds for resentment," the word "by nine" means that the Saṅgha is split by nine monks. "By a motion, nine" means that the formal acts (kamma) to be performed by a motion number nine. The rest is self-evident.
(4) Commentary on Persons Not to be Saluted, etc. 477.
“Ten persons are not to be saluted” refers to the ten individuals mentioned in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.

“And with joined palms in respectful service” means that one should neither perform the gesture of joined palms nor the act of respectful service toward them, such as asking for water or taking up a fan.
The meaning is that they should be shown the duties regarding the Khandhakas, but they should not be made to raise their joined palms in salutation.
"An offense of wrong-doing for ten" means that for those same ten [persons], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs for one who acts in this way.
"Wearing of robes for ten" means that the wearing of an extra robe for ten days is permitted.
"Robes should be given here to those who have completed five years of residence"—this means they should be given in the presence of five who are fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
"In the presence of seven"—this means that even in the absence [of the recipient], it may be given to these seven:

those who have gone abroad, the insane, the mentally deranged, those overwhelmed by pain, and the three types of those suspended (ukkhepakā), provided there is a suitable person to receive them. Of the sixteen...
"It should not be given" means it should not be given to the sixteen types of persons mentioned in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, such as the paṇḍakas and others.
"Having concealed a hundred katis of offenses for a hundred nights" means having concealed a hundred kati offenses for a hundred nights.
"Having concealed a thousand dasas of offenses for a hundred nights" means having concealed a thousand dasa offenses for a hundred nights.
This is the meaning in brief: suppose someone commits one hundred Saṅghādisesa offenses each day and conceals ten of them each day;

by that, one hundred nights and one thousand offenses have been concealed. Having requested probation for all those offenses as being concealed for ten days, and having lived through ten nights, he would be released as one who is on probation (pārivāsika).

It is said that there are twelve faults of formal acts (*kammadosā*). These are stated by taking three types for each formal act—namely, *apalokanakamma*: illegal and with an incomplete assembly, illegal and with a complete assembly, and legal and with an incomplete assembly—and likewise for *ñattikamma*, *ñattidutiyakamma*, and *ñatticatutthakamma*.
Thus, by applying these three to each individual formal act, the twelve faults of formal acts are stated.

The four successful legal procedures (*kamma-sampatti*) are: a procedure by way of notification (*apalokana-kamma*) that is lawful and performed by a unanimous assembly; likewise for the remaining three. Thus, the four successful legal procedures have been stated.

The six types of legal procedures (*cha kammāni*) are: an unlawful procedure by an incomplete assembly (*adhammena-vagga-kamma*); an unlawful procedure by a unanimous assembly (*adhammena-samagga-kamma*); a semblance of a lawful procedure by an incomplete assembly (*dhamma-patirūpakena-vagga-kamma*); a semblance of a lawful procedure by a unanimous assembly (*dhamma-patirūpakena-samagga-kamma*);
a lawful procedure by an incomplete assembly (*dhammena-vagga-kamma*); and a lawful procedure by a unanimous assembly (*dhammena-samagga-kamma*). Thus...

Six formal acts (kamma) have been mentioned. Regarding the phrase "one here has been performed legitimately" (dhammikā katā): the meaning is that one among these has been performed as a legitimate act (dhammika) by a unanimous assembly (samagga).
In the explanation of the second verse as well, this very same [act] is the legitimate one.

Regarding the phrase "which have been taught" (yaṃ desitā): those which have been taught, spoken, and revealed. In the phrases beginning with "by the Infinite Victor" (anantajinena), [the term is used] because of being devoid of any limitation or boundary.

The "Infinite" (ananta) refers to Nibbāna. That has been conquered, won, attained, and reached by the Blessed One—just as a king, having crushed his host of enemies, wins his kingdom—after he had crushed the host of defilements. Therefore, the Blessed One is called the "Conqueror of the Infinite" (Anantajina).

He is "Such" (tādi) because of his lack of perturbation toward the desirable and the undesirable; [he possesses] what is known as the seclusion consisting of suppression, substitution, eradication, tranquillization, and escape.

"One who sees seclusion" (*vivekadassī*) means one who has seen the fivefold seclusion. By that Conqueror of the Infinite, the Tathāgata, who sees seclusion, those categories of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) were taught and spoken.
"In this case, even a single [offense] is settled without the methods of settling" (*ekettha sammati vinā samathehi*); this is the connection between the words here.
Of those seven categories of offenses taught by the Teacher, therein even a single offense [is settled] without the methods of settling.

It is not settled; rather, all these factors—the six principles for settling and the four categories of legal issues—are settled by the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and reach a state of reconciliation.
However, in this context, the *sammukhāvinaya* alone settles [the matter] even without the other principles for settling;
it attains the status of a principle for settling (*samatha*). For there is no case where its resolution is impossible without another principle for settling.
Therefore it was said: "In some cases, there is settlement here even without the methods of pacification" (*samatha*). This is the meaning stated in the commentaries according to this intention.

We, however, taking the word "without" (*vinā*) as having the mere sense of negation, [interpret] "In some cases, there is settlement here even without the methods of pacification" to mean that among these seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), one class—the class of offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*)—is settled here even without the methods of pacification.
We would approve of this meaning: that it is settled (*sammati*) without the methods of settling (*samatha*). For it has also been said:
"Regarding that offense which is *anavasesā* (inexhaustible), by which legal question (*adhikaraṇa*), in what place, and by which method of settling is that offense settled?
[And: "Sixty-four and a half," Upāli, means: "In this case, Upāli, a monk proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma; in that regard, there is a view of non-Dhamma..."
In a case of schism, there is a view of non-Dhamma; in that case of schism, there is a view of Dhamma; in that case of schism, one is doubtful while having a view of non-Dhamma;
in that case of schism, one has a view of Dhamma while having a view of non-Dhamma; in that case of schism, one is doubtful while having a view of Dhamma;
in that case of schism, one is doubtful while having a view of non-Dhamma; in that case of schism, one is doubtful while having a view of Dhamma.
“Being doubtful about that [matter], he is doubtful about the schism. Thus, by way of the eighteen grounds for schism mentioned in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka, there are eighteen groups of eight;
by way of these, one hundred and fifty-four who go to states of misery (āpāyika) should be understood. As for the eighteen who do not go to states of misery (anāpāyika):
“Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and he holds the view that it is Dhamma regarding that [matter]...”

If, while there is a schism, one proclaims a view regarding the Dhamma without setting aside one's own view, without setting aside one's own preference, without setting aside one's own inclination, and without setting aside one's own disposition, and distributes voting tickets, saying: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction;
take this, approve of this," then, Upāli, such a person is indeed a schismatic of the Saṅgha, yet he is not bound for the states of misery, nor bound for hell.

"Neither one who lasts for an eon (*kappaṭṭha*), nor one who is incurable (*atekiccha*). Thus, by assigning one person to each case, eighteen individuals are mentioned at the conclusion of the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka*.
These eighteen groups of eight are already mentioned in the "Bestowal of One Hundred and Fifty Less Six" (*Chaūnadiyaḍḍhasatavissajjana*).
(5) Commentary on the Sixteen Formal Acts (*Kamma*) and so forth.
478. The explanations for all the verses beginning with "How many kamma-s? are indeed straightforward.
The commentary on the second supplementary collection of verses is finished.
The Sweat-Inducing Verses.
(1) Commentary on the Questions on Non-Separation: 479.
Regarding the verses on the shedding of sweat, "non-residence" (*asaṃvāsa*) means not being in residence through the communal acts such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā.

"Partaking" (*sambhoga*)—the phrase "certain [partaking] is not obtained there"—means that improper partaking (*akappiya-sambhoga*) is not permitted; this refers to [prohibited] care such as bathing, feeding, and so forth.
However, it is permitted for one to do so only with one’s own mother. “There is no offense because of not being separated” means there is no offense due to sleeping in the same house.
“This question was thought out by the skillful” means this question was contemplated by wise and skillful people.
Its answer should be understood from the nun who was the mother of the child, for this was said with reference to her son.
The "unreleased verses" were spoken with reference to heavy goods; however, their meaning has already been explained in the *Garubhaṇḍavinicchaya*.
"I do not speak of ten persons" refers to the ten persons mentioned in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
"Eleven to be avoided" refers to those eleven persons to be avoided who were mentioned in the *Mahākhandhaka*; these too I do not speak of. This...
The question regarding the "naked" monk was spoken with reference to a certain monk.

How is it that he is "not common to the training"? This question was spoken with reference to a monk who was formerly a barber; for he is not permitted to carry a barber's kit, whereas others are permitted to do so; therefore, he is not common to the training.
"Whom do the Buddhas call 'that person'?"—this question was spoken with reference to the emanated Buddha (*nimmitabuddha*).
"Avoiding below the navel" means having avoided that which is below the navel. This question refers to that headless trunk which has eyes and a mouth upon its chest.
"A monk [builds] a hut by means of begging" is a question stated with reference to a hut roofed with grass. The second question is stated with reference to a hut made entirely of clay.
"He would incur a grave offense involving defeat" is a question stated with reference to a nun who conceals a fault.

[The previous] was stated. The second question refers to persons such as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) who are incapable [of spiritual progress]. For even those eleven [types of persons] incur a *pārājika* offense only while still in the state of a householder.

"Speech" means not speaking with speech. "And one should not utter a word to others" means that, thinking "these people will hear it," one should not even emit a sound with reference to other persons.
This question concerns one who does not confess an existing offense, which constitutes a deliberate lie (*sampajānamusāvāda*).
This was said with reference to this false speech. For that monk, while sitting in silence after having made an unrighteous admission, there is no such thing as an offense at the mind-door.
However, because he does not disclose what ought to be disclosed, it should be understood that this offense arises from non-action at the door of speech.
Regarding the question "the four *saṅghādisesa* [offenses]," this was stated with reference to a nun who has entered the far bank of a river within the boundaries of another village at dawn.
For she, having departed from her own village at the time of early morning, has merely reached the aforementioned far bank of the river at the moment of sunrise;
thus, by the characteristic of being separated from the group of nuns at another village across the river during the night, [she incurs the offense].
One incurs four *saṅghādisesa* offenses all at once.
As for the question, "Could there be different offenses?"—this was stated with reference to two nuns who were ordained by the same group (*ekatoupasampannā*).
For in their case, if one takes the hand of one ordained by the same group from the presence of monks, it is a *pācittiya*; [but] from the presence of nuns...
For one who takes [an object] from the hand of a person who has received full ordination in one’s presence, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding "four persons having made an agreement": the teacher and three pupils stole goods worth six māṣakas;
for the teacher, it was three māṣakas by his own hand, and for the others, it was likewise three by command; therefore, he incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya).
For the others, there was one [offense] for each through physical action, and five through command; therefore, they incurred a *pārājika*.
This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the commentary on the "Agreement and Theft" (*saṃvidāvahāra*) section of the *adinnādāna-pārājika*.
(2) Commentary on the Questions concerning the *Pārājikas* and so forth.
480. "There is no hole in that house"—this question was spoken with reference to the *dussakuṭi* (rag-robe hut) and so forth, as well as the section on bedding (*santhata-peyyāla*).
The verse beginning "Oil, honey, and molasses" was spoken with reference to the change of gender (*liṅga-parivatta*).

The verse beginning "By means of what is relinquished" (*nissaggiyena*) was spoken with reference to the act of dedication (*pariṇāmana*). For [the monk] who [takes] from a gain dedicated to the Saṅgha...
If one dedicates two robes—one for oneself and one for another—under a single transaction, saying, "One is for me;
give the other to him," one incurs both a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* and a *suddhika-pācittiya* simultaneously.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "That action would be subject to dispute on account of a quorum," this question is stated with reference to village boundaries within cities such as Bārāṇasī, which measure twelve *yojanas*.
"The mere taking of a step" is said with reference to acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*), and its meaning is also explained specifically in the commentary on acting as a go-between.
"All those are to be forfeited" (*nissaggiyāni*): this question is stated with reference to having a nun who is not a relative wash [robes].
For if one takes hold of the ear of even all three robes when they are soiled by crow-droppings or smeared with mud...
If a bhikkhunī washes with water, the [offenses] pertaining to the body of the bhikkhu become *nissaggiya*.

Since he does not even have the going for refuge, he lacks the full admission (*upasampadā*) by way of going for refuge. However, this question was stated with reference to the full admission of Mahāpajāpatī.

"He might kill a lowly person" means that he might kill a woman or a man who is ignoble (*anariya*). This question was stated with reference to a father who has changed gender and become female, and a mother who has changed gender and become male.
“By that he does not immediately touch” (Na tenānantaraṃ phuse)—this question was spoken with reference to the animal parents, such as those of the Migasiṅga ascetic, Sīha Kumāra, and others.

“Without having charged” (Acodayitvā)—this verse was spoken with reference to ordination by means of a messenger. “Having charged” (Codayitvā)—this verse was spoken with reference to the ordination of paṇḍakas and others.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: “The first verse refers to the eight types of non-face-to-face legal acts (*asammukhākamma*).”
The second [statement], "there is no offense," is said with reference to an action performed against one who is innocent;
thus it is recorded. Regarding "an offense for one who cuts": for one cutting down a forest tree, it is a *pārājika*; for one cutting grass, creepers, and so forth, it is a *pācittiya*;
for one cutting off the genitals (*aṅgajāta*), it is a *thullaccaya*. Regarding "no offense for one who cuts": in the case of hair...
There is no offense for one who cuts his nails. "An offense for one who conceals" means for one who conceals his own offense or the offense of others.
"No offense for one who conceals" means there is no offense for one who conceals houses and so forth.
Regarding the verse "Speaking the truth," when one speaks the truth, saying, "You are a *sikharaṇī*, you are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanā*"), it is a grave [offense].
In the case of intentional lying, however, one incurs a light offense when speaking falsely; in the case of reporting what is untrue, one incurs a heavy offense when speaking falsely;
and in the case of reporting what is true, one incurs a light offense when speaking the truth.
(3) Commentary on the Questions concerning the *Pācittiya* and other rules.
481. The verse beginning with "Adhiṭṭhitaṃ" was spoken concerning one who uses a robe that has been relinquished (*nissaggiya*) without having first formally relinquished it.
The verse beginning with "Atthaṅgate sūriye" was spoken concerning one who chews the cud (*romanthaka*).

Regarding the verse beginning with "Na rattacitto," this is the meaning: one with a lustful mind (*rattacitta*) incurs the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) through sexual intercourse; one with a thieving mind...
The offense of defeat (*pārājika*) for taking what is not given; the offense of defeat for one who intends the death of another regarding a human being;
however, the schismatic of the Saṅgha has neither a mind of lust nor a mind of theft, nor does he intend the death of another.

Yet, for the one giving the voting-ticket (*salāka*), there is an offense involving expulsion; it is an offense of defeat. For the one receiving the voting-ticket who follows the schismatic, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*).
“May he go half a *yojana*”—this question was spoken with reference to the foot of a tree belonging to a single family, such as the well-established *nigrodha* tree.
“Bodily [actions]”—this verse was spoken with reference to one who grasps the hair or the fingers of many women together.
“Vocal [actions]”—this verse was spoken with reference to one who speaks lewdly in the manner beginning with, “All of you are *sikharaṇīs*.”
"Three women, he does not engage in sexual intercourse with them": three women are mentioned; even among them, he does not engage in that which is called sexual intercourse. "Three men":
having approached even these three men, he does not engage in sexual intercourse. "Three ignoble eunuchs":
having approached these six persons—namely, the three ignoble ones reckoned as hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjana*) and the three eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*)—he does not engage in sexual intercourse.

"He does not consort with her. "And he does not practice sexual intercourse with a woman" means that he does not practice sexual intercourse even according to the *anuloma-pārājika* (the preliminary offense).
"'There may be a cutting off on account of the act of sexual intercourse' means there may be a *pārājika* offense on account of the act of sexual intercourse.

This question was stated with reference to the eight bases [of the *pārājika* offenses], for it refers to physical contact (*kāyasamsagga*), which is the preliminary stage to the act of sexual intercourse.
For one who strives to commit an act on account of sexual intercourse, there is the penalty of cutting off (*chejja*).

The verse beginning with "A robe for one's mother" was spoken with reference to the occasion when, at the end of the rainy season, one arouses mindfulness for the sake of a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭika*). Its detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*), however, has already been stated in the commentary on the training rule regarding the rain-cloak.

The verse beginning with "An angry man becomes a winner" was spoken with reference to the conduct of the non-Buddhist ascetics (*titthiya*); for a non-Buddhist ascetic, while fulfilling his own prescribed conduct...
When the praise of the *titthiyas* (heretics) is being recited, one who becomes angry is an "offender" (*ārādhaka*);

when the praise of the Triple Gem is being recited, one who becomes angry is "blameworthy" (*gārayha*). The detailed explanation for this has been stated right there. The second verse was also spoken with reference to that very same matter.
As for the verse beginning with "an offense involving suspension" (*saṅghādisesa*), it refers to a lustful nun receiving almsfood from the hand of a lustful man.
It was said with reference to one who, having taken human flesh, garlic, or the remains of fine food, chews them together with unallowable meat and swallows it.
The verse beginning "One is ordained, one is not ordained" was spoken with reference to one who has gone into the air;
for if, between two novices, one sits having left the earth by even a hair’s breadth through psychic power (*iddhi*), he is "not ordained."
It is so called. Even the Saṅgha, while sitting in the air, must not perform a formal act for one who is on the ground; if it does so, it is invalid.
The verse beginning with "Akappakataṃ" was spoken concerning a monk whose robe has been stolen. Furthermore, a detailed explanation regarding that very training rule is also stated therein.
"Neither gives nor receives" means that neither the one who sends [the robe] gives it, nor does the one sent receive it from her hand.
"There is no receiving by that means" means: for that very reason, there is no receiving from the hand of the one who incited [the gift] by the one who was incited.

"She incurs a grave offense" means: even though this is so, she incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense by inciting the taking of almsfood from the hand of one who is lustful. And "on account of its consumption": furthermore, regarding that offense...
One incurs [an offense] by using that which has been offered;
for at the conclusion of her meal, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the one who made the offer. The second verse was spoken with reference to the offering of water and tooth-wood (*dantapoṇa*).
"A nun shall not touch what is blameworthy" refers to having incurred any one of the seventeen offenses.
Even if a bhikkhunī conceals [an offense] out of disrespect, she does not incur an offense on account of that concealment; she does not commit another new offense.
Whether the offense was concealed or unconcealed, she receives only a *mānatta* discipline for a half-month.
However, this [case] is not even a bhikkhunī; having committed a grave offense with a remainder and having concealed it, she incurs an offense.
"It does not touch. "This question has been pondered by the wise," he said. This question, it is said, was spoken with reference to a monk who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*).
Since there is no formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) against him, therefore, even if he commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense and conceals it, he does not "touch" the fault.
The commentary on the *Sedamocanagāthā* is finished.
The commentary on the fifth chapter, the *Kammavagga*.
482. Regarding the section on formal acts (*kamma*), the distinction between the four types of formal acts has already been stated in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
Nevertheless, although it has been stated there, this exposition of formal acts (*kammavinicchaya*) becomes clear when explained from the beginning;
therefore, we shall state what is to be said here starting from the very beginning. "Four" is a term defining the numerical limit of the formal acts.

“Kammāni” (deeds) is a designation for delimited deeds. A *ñatti-kamma* (formal act consisting of a motion) is a deed that must be performed by announcing it three times with the consent of a unanimous Saṅgha, after having cleared the Saṅgha residing within the boundary and having brought the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it, in accordance with the method already stated.
A *ñattidutiya-kamma* (formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation) is likewise [performed] with the consent of a unanimous Saṅgha... by means of one [proclamation].

A formal act to be performed by means of a motion (*ñatti*). A "formal act with a motion as the second member" (*ñattidutiyakamma*) is a formal act to be performed by means of a single motion and a single proclamation (*anussāvanā*), following the consent of a united Saṅgha in the manner already described; thus it is a formal act to be performed by means of a motion as the second member.
A "formal act with a motion as the fourth member" (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is [the same] in the manner already described, following the consent of a united Saṅgha by means of a single...
"By a motion and three proclamations"—thus, an act that is to be performed by three proclamations following a motion is a "motion-and-fourth" (*ñatticatuttha*) act.
Among these, an act of mere notification (*apalokanakamma*) must be performed simply by notifying; it is not to be performed by way of a motion or other formalities.

An act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) must also be performed by establishing a single motion; it is not to be performed by way of an act of notification or other formalities. An act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*)...
However, there are also formal acts (*kamma*) that must be performed after seeking permission, as well as those that must not be performed.

Among these, the following six formal acts are weighty; it is not permissible to perform them merely by seeking permission: the demarcation of a boundary, the abolition of a boundary, the offering of the *kaṭhina* robe-material, the removal of the *kaṭhina*, the designation of a site for a hut, and the designation of a site for a monastery. These require a formal motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

These [five] must be performed by means of an announcement (*sāvetvā*). As for the remaining thirteen formal acts of authorization (*sammuti*)—namely, the authorizations for the assignment of lodgings, the distribution of robes, and so forth—these light formal acts may be performed even by means of a mere motion (*apaloketvā*);

however, they must not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*). When performed by way of a *ñatticatutthakamma*, it is more firm; therefore...
Some say it should be performed; however, if that were the case, there would be a confusion of formal acts (*kamma-saṅkara*), and therefore it is rejected as something that should not be performed.

But if there is a missing syllable, a missing word, or a poorly uttered phrase, it is permissible to repeat it again and again for the purpose of correcting it. This constitutes the strengthening of an unshakable act.
In the case of a formal act that is subject to failure, it remains a formal act [only if performed correctly].

A formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*) must be performed only after having announced both the motion and the three proclamations; it must not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of mere intimation (*apalokanakamma*), etc. "It fails in five ways" means it fails due to five causes. 483.
