Regarding the phrase:

"A formal act that ought to be done in the presence of those concerned is done in their absence; this is a formal act deficient in its subject matter (*vatthu*) and is an illegal act (*adhammakamma*). Here—

There is an action that must be performed in the presence [of the accused]; there is an action that need not be performed in their presence. In this regard, "not to be performed in their presence" refers to:

ordination by messenger, overturning of the bowl, restoration of the bowl, the authorization for a mad monk to be considered mad, the authorization for those in training regarding families, the imposition of the *brahmadaṇḍa* on the monk Channa, and the formal act of proclamation against Devadatta.
The formal act of non-prostration (avaṇdanīyakamma) to be performed by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs against a bhikkhu who displays what is untrustworthy is eightfold;
all of that should be understood according to the method explained in the respective places.
This eightfold formal act, when performed in the absence [of the accused], is well-performed and irreversible.
All remaining legal procedures must be performed in the very presence [of the parties].
They must be carried out by applying this fourfold *sammukhāvinaya*—namely, presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals.
For when performed in this way, they are well-performed; but when not performed in this way, these [procedures] are known as lacking *sammukhāvinaya*.
Because they are performed without the proper basis (*vatthu*), they are called "deficient in basis" (*vatthuvipanna*). Therefore it was said:
"A formal act that ought to be done in the presence [of the Sangha] is done in their absence; this is an illegal act (*adhammakamma*) deficient in basis.
In the case of acts that ought to be done with interrogation (*paṭipucchākaraṇīya*) and so forth, the interrogation itself is the basis; because they are performed without that basis...
Their failure regarding the basis (*vatthu*) should also be understood. Here, however, is merely the literal meaning of the words:

"He does what should be done after interrogation (*paṭipucchā*) without interrogating" means that he performs what ought to be done by asking, accusing, and reminding, yet he does it without asking, without accusing, and without reminding.
"He does what should be done with admission (*paṭiññā*) without admitting" means having made an admission according to the admission as it was given.
It should be performed. For one who acts without having obtained consent, while he is speaking incoherently, [the Sangha] acts by force.

"Worthy of settlement through recollection" (*sativinayāraha*) refers to one like the Elder Dabba Mallaputta, whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Worthy of settlement because of past insanity" (*amūḷhavinayāraha*) refers to one who is insane, like the monk Gagga.
"Worthy of the legal act of further penalty" (*tassapāpiyasikākammāraha*) refers to one whose evil has increased, like the monk Upavāḷa. This same method applies in all cases.
"He performs the *uposatha* on every *uposatha* day" means that he performs the *uposatha* on each and every *uposatha* day. A "day for *uposatha*" refers to:
(1) the day of reconciliation for a split Saṅgha during the remaining eleven months, excluding the month of Kattika;
and (2) the fourteenth and fifteenth days as previously mentioned. Apart from these three types of *uposatha* days, on any other day...
One who observes the Uposatha on a day that is not the Uposatha day is said to be performing the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day.

For instance, when those quarreling over some minor matter regarding bowls, robes, or other such things suspend either the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā ceremony, then once that legal dispute has been settled, they may perform an interim Uposatha for the sake of concord, thinking, "We have become united. It is not [permissible] otherwise.
They obtain [the merit]; by those who perform it, even on a day other than the Uposatha, it is said that the Uposatha has been performed.
"He performs the Pavāraṇā" means he performs it on the day of the Pavāraṇā; the day of the Pavāraṇā refers to two full-moon days:
the day of reconciliation for a split Saṅgha within a single Kattika month, and the day established by postponement.
Thus, having set aside the four kinds of *pavāraṇā* days, if one performs *pavāraṇā* on another day, it is called performing *pavāraṇā* when there is no *pavāraṇā*.
Here too, they are not permitted to perform a *sāmaggī-pavāraṇā* (a communal *pavāraṇā*) for the sake of settling a minor dispute;
if they do so, a *pavāraṇā* performed when there is no *pavāraṇā* has been carried out. Furthermore, [if one admits] someone under twenty years of age or one who has committed an *antimavatthu*...

Or, even when one ordains someone who has previously committed an offense or any one of the eleven types of persons incapable [of higher ordination], it is an illegal act (adhammakamma) because the basis (vatthu) is deficient.
Thus, legal acts fail by way of the basis.
484. Regarding failure by way of the motion (ñatti), "he does not touch upon the basis" refers to the person for whom he performs the act of higher ordination and so forth.
He does not misrepresent that person, nor does he take their name. When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this Dhammarakkhita desires the full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
[he] desires the full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita"; thus he does not misrepresent the subject matter.
"He does not misrepresent the Saṅgha" means he does not seize upon the name of the Saṅgha. When one should say, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me;
this is Dhammarakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable sirs, let [the venerable] hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita";
in this way, he does not misrepresent the Saṅgha.
"He does not misapprehend the person" means that he does not misapprehend the preceptor of the one seeking full ordination;
he does not take his name. When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this Dhammarakkhita seeks full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this Dhammarakkhita seeks full ordination."
He speaks; thus he does not misapprehend the person.
"He does not misapprehend the motion" means he does not misapprehend the motion in every respect.

In a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), having set aside the motion, he performs the act of proclamation twice by means of the ritual formula alone. In a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) as well...
Having omitted the motion (*ñatti*), he performs the formal act of proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*) by means of the ritual formula (*kammavācā*) four times; thus, he does not touch upon the motion.

Or, "he places the motion afterwards" means that after first performing the formal act of proclamation with the ritual formula, he says, "This is the motion," and then says, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this"; thus [he places] the motion afterwards.
He sets it aside. Thus, by these five ways, formal acts fail due to the motion (*ñatti*).
485. Regarding failure due to the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the basis and other factors should be understood in the same manner as already stated. However, their non-appropriation occurs thus:
at the first proclamation, [one says] "Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me," and at the second proclamation...

"I speak this matter; for a third time I speak this matter. Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me"—in these second and third proclamations, when it should be said, "This Dhammarakkhita is desirous of full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," if one says instead, "Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me, [from] the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he is said to have missed the subject.

When it should be said, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita,” if one says instead, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita,” one is said not to have misapprehended the Saṅgha. When it should be said, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita [acting] for the Venerable Buddharakkhita,” if one says instead, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is... [Dhammarakkhita]” [omitting the reference to the other], one is said not to have misapprehended the Saṅgha. By saying, "Dhammarakkhita is seeking full ordination," one does not misrepresent the person.

"He omits the proclamation" means that he does not perform the proclamation at all within the formal act (*kammavācā*); in a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), he performs only the motion twice;
in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), he performs only the motion four times.

In this way, one omits the proclamation (*anussāvana*). Even in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*), if one sets forth the motion once but, while reciting the single formal statement (*kammavācā*), omits a syllable or mispronounces a word, this too constitutes omitting the proclamation.
However, in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*), after setting forth the motion once, [one recites] the formal statement either once or twice.

It should be understood that even one who performs the proclamation (*anussāvana*), yet omits a syllable or a word, or utters something wrongly, indeed fails the proclamation. Regarding the phrase "utters something wrongly" (*duruttaṃ karoti*), this is the analysis: for if one says something other than what ought to be said in a particular syllable, this is called "uttering something wrongly. Therefore, when a monk is performing the formal act (*kammavācā*), he— [The text continues: ...this [monk]... [should speak correctly]. If he speaks otherwise, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If he does not perform the proclamation at all, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation but omits a syllable or a word, or utters something wrongly, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation but forgets it, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation but is confused, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation but is distracted, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while sitting, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while lying down, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while walking, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing away, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing sideways, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing the opposite direction, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing the same direction as the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing the same direction as the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing the same direction as both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing a different direction from the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing a different direction from the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while facing a different direction from both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing behind the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing behind the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing behind both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing in front of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing in front of the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing in front of both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing to the side of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing to the side of the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while standing to the side of both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while seated behind the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while seated behind the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while seated behind both the Saṅgha and the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while seated in front of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he performs the proclamation while seated in front of the person being dealt with, it is an offense of wrong-doing. “Relaxed and tense, long and short, heavy and light, and the *niggahīta*;
connected, distinct, and released—thus is the tenfold classification according to the perception of phonemes.
This has been stated; it should be thoroughly observed. For herein, “relaxed” refers to the first and third consonants within each of the five groups.
“Dhanitaṃ” means the second and fourth [consonants] among those very [vowels]. “Dīghaṃ” refers to vowels such as *ā* that are to be pronounced over a long duration of time.

“Rassaṃ” refers to vowels such as *a* that are to be pronounced in half that time. “Garukaṃ” is simply what is long; or else, it is that which is spoken with a following consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), as in the case of the Venerable Elder Buddharakkhita, regarding whom it is said, “to whom it is not pleasing. “Lahukaṃ” is...
"Rassam eva" (only short): this is said by making it subordinate to "yaṃ vā āyasmato buddharakkhitatherassa yassa na khamati" (or whatever is not pleasing to the Venerable Thera Buddharakkhita).
"Niggahitam" (the *niggahīta*): that which is to be uttered nasally with the mouth unopened, having restrained the vocal organs (*karaṇāni*) and not released [the breath].
"Sambandham" (connected): that which is connected with the following word, as in "tuṇhissā."

Or it is called “*tuṇhassā*. Regarding “*vavatthitaṃ*”: that which is uttered by making a separation from the following word, dividing it as either “*tuṇhī assā*” or “*tuṇha assā*. Regarding “*vimuttaṃ*”:
that which is uttered without restraining the vocal organs, releasing them, with the mouth open and without nasalization.
In that context, where one should say "suṇātu me" (may he hear me), by changing the *ta*-sound to the *tha*-sound, the expression "suṇāthu me" occurs;

this is called the hardening of a soft sound. Likewise, where one should say "pattakallaṃ, esā ñattī" (it is the right time, this is the motion), there is the expression "patthakallaṃ, esā ñatthī," and so forth.
And where one should say "bhante saṅgho" (Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha), by changing the *bha*-sound and the *gha*-sound to the *ba*-sound and the *ga*-sound [respectively],...
Having uttered the words "Venerable sir, there is attachment," to make a harsh sound soft is called *dhanitassa sithilakaraṇaṃ*.
However, when one should speak with an open mouth as "May it be heard by me" (*suṇātu me*), saying instead "May they hear me" (*suṇantu me*);

or when one should say "This is the motion" (*esā ñattī*), saying instead "This is their motion" (*esaṃ ñattī*) with a nasalized sound and a closed mouth—such speech is called *vimuttassa niggahitavacanaṃ*. [Regarding] "It is opportune" (*pattakallaṃ*):

When one should speak with the nose [producing a nasal sound] by keeping the mouth closed, saying "pattakallā," yet instead speaks with the mouth open and without producing a nasal sound, that is called the *vimutta-vacana* (released utterance) of the *niggahīta*.
Thus, what should be soft is made harsh; what should be harsh is made soft; and what should be released is made *niggahīta*.
When *niggahita* ought to be used, [the use of] these four consonants—*vimutta*, etc.—vitiates the formal act (*kamma*) within the *kammavācā*.
For one who speaks thus is said to "speak otherwise than what should be spoken" and "to utter incorrectly.
However, regarding the other six consonants, such as the long and short vowels: in the place of a long vowel, only a long vowel [is correct], and in the place of a short vowel...
"Short indeed" means that the *kammavācā* (formal ritual procedure) should be performed by one who speaks each syllable exactly as it stands in its place, without breaking the traditional sequence.
However, if one does not do so, but instead pronounces a long vowel when a short one should be spoken, or a short vowel when a long one should be spoken;
likewise, if one pronounces a heavy syllable when a light one should be spoken, or a light syllable when a heavy one should be spoken; [the procedure is invalid].
He speaks of a connection when a distinction should be stated, or he speaks of a distinction when a connection should be stated;
even when spoken thus, the *kammavācā* is not invalidated. For these six phonemes do not invalidate the ritual act (*kamma*).
Furthermore, as the Suttantika Theras say: "The sound *da* becomes *ta*, the sound *ta* becomes *da*, and the sound *ca*..."
Some say: "The letter *ja* becomes *ca*; the letter *ca* becomes *ja*; the letter *ya* becomes *ka*; and the letter *ka* becomes *ya*.

Therefore, when it is necessary to use the letter *da* and so forth, the mention of the letter *ta* and so forth is not contradictory. However, this is not permissible when it comes to the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*).
Therefore, the holder of the Vinaya must not change the letter *da* to *ta*, nor... [and so on] ...nor change the letter *ka* [to anything else].

The syllable *ya*. Having purified the terminology according to the Pāli text, the formal act (*kammavācā*) must be performed by one who avoids the faults stated regarding the tenfold terminology of phonemes (*byañjananirutti*).
Otherwise, it is said that one "omits the proclamation" (*sāvana*).

Or, "one proclaims at the wrong time": this means that at an improper time or place for the proclamation, one fails to establish the motion (*ñatti*) and performs the first non-proclamation act (*anussāvanakamma*) before establishing the motion later on. Thus, through these five ways, formal acts fail because of the non-proclamation.
486. Regarding failure with respect to the boundary, a "boundary that is too small" is one that does not accommodate twenty-one monks.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "Where twenty-one monks are unable to sit.
Therefore, such a boundary—even if formally authorized—is as if unauthorized; it is just like the field of a village. Any formal act (*kamma*) performed therein—

It is disturbed. This same method applies to the remaining boundaries as well. In this context, however, what is called "excessively large" is that which is established having extended even by the measure of a hair’s tip beyond three *yojanas*.
What is called a "broken mark" (*khaṇḍanimitta*) refers to a mark that has not been joined together.
Having designated the mark in the eastern direction, one should then designate them in sequence in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Furthermore, it is proper to establish [the sign] only after re-describing the previously described sign in the eastern direction;

in this way, it becomes an unbroken sign (*akhaṇḍanimitta*). However, if one brings it in succession and, having described the sign in the northern direction, establishes it right there, it becomes a broken sign (*khaṇḍanimitta*).
There is yet another kind of broken sign, namely that which belongs to one who has not attained the sign (*animittupaga*).
It is valid when one makes a single sign out of a *tacasāra* tree, a stump, or any one of a heap of dust or a heap of sand, and then performs the formal act.
"By means of a shadow-sign" means it is valid when one makes any shadow—such as the shadow of a mountain—and uses that as the sign for the formal act.
"Without a sign" means it is valid when the formal act is performed without specifying any signs whatsoever.
"Standing outside the boundary, he establishes the boundary" means that having proclaimed the boundary markers, he establishes it while standing outside those markers.

Regarding "he establishes a boundary in a river, in the ocean, or in a lake": whatever boundary is established in these rivers and so forth, even though it has been established in such a way, [it is said]:
"Monks, every river is without a boundary; every ocean is without a boundary; every lake is without a boundary."
By virtue of the words [of the formal act], it remains indeed unconsecrated. "She merges her boundary with another boundary" means she merges the boundary of others with her own boundary.
"She overflows [upon] another boundary" means she overflows the boundary of others with her own boundary.
In this regard, how both the merging and the overflowing occur has been explained entirely in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka. Thus, these...
The eleven types of boundaries (*sīmā*) are likewise non-boundaries (*asīmā*), being exactly like village or field boundaries; any formal act (*kamma*) performed while sitting within them is invalid.
Therefore it is said: "By these eleven modes, formal acts fail on account of the boundary.
(487–488) Regarding failure of the formal act due to the assembly (*parisa*), however, there is nothing that has not already been explained. As for what is there...

The characteristic of being subject to a formal act (*kammappatta*) through desire for that act should be stated; that too has already been explained later in the manner beginning with, "Four bhikkhus who are regular members (*pakatatta*) are subject to a formal act.

In that context, "four bhikkhus who are regular members and subject to a formal act" means four bhikkhus who are regular members—those not suspended and not expelled, whose virtue is pure—who are subject to a formal act when a formal act is to be carried out by a quorum of four.

They are worthy of the formal act and appropriate for the presiding official. Without them, that formal act is not performed; neither their consent (*chanda*) nor their purity (*pārisuddhi*) is obtained.
However, as for the remaining members—even if they number a thousand—if they belong to the same community (*samānasaṃvāsaka*), all of them are indeed entitled to give consent.
Whether they come after having given their consent and purity or not, the formal act nevertheless...

He remains [in that state]. However, one for whom the Saṅgha performs an act such as probation (*parivāsa*) has neither attained the status of a formal act (*kammappatta*), nor is he eligible to give his consent (*chandāraha*).
Nevertheless, because the Saṅgha performs the act by taking that person as its subject (*vatthu*), he is called "one who is subject to the act" (*kammāraha*).
This same principle applies to the other formal acts as well.
489. The method beginning with "Again, there are four kinds of kamma" is stated for the purpose of showing that eunuchs and others do not constitute a formal assembly (*avatthu*).
The rest here is self-evident. 495–496.

In this context, regarding the statement: “The act of seeking permission (apalokanakamma) applies to five cases:

However, in actual practice, banishment comes first, and reinstatement follows later. In that regard, [the case] of the novice Kaṇṭaka...

The *daṇḍakamma-nāsanā* (expulsion by means of penal action) should be understood as "banishment. Therefore, even now, if a novice monk speaks in dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; if he proclaims what is improper as proper;
if he holds wrong view and is possessed of an extremist view—he must be restrained up to three times and made to relinquish that adherence.
If he does not relinquish it, the Saṅgha should be convened and he should be told, "Relinquish it.
If he still does not relinquish it, a competent monk, having performed an act of formal announcement (*apalokanakamma*), should expel him. And this is how the formal act is to be performed:
"Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: 'This novice named so-and-so [has spoken disparagingly] of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha...'"

“This novice [name] speaks dispraise and holds wrong view; he does not desire that which other novices receive—namely, sleeping together with the monks for two or three nights—and he desires his expulsion from the Saṅgha. For a second time...
for a third time, venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: “This novice [name] [speaks dispraise of the Buddha... does the Saṅgha approve?”
“Go away, perish!
On a later occasion, he should be reinstated by a formal act of notification (*apalokana-kamma*) after he has asked for forgiveness up to three times, saying:
“Venerable sirs, out of foolishness, ignorance, and lack of merit I did this; therefore, I ask the Saṅgha for forgiveness.”
However, he should be reinstated in this way: in the midst of the Saṅgha, a competent monk, with the permission of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: this novice named so-and-so is a disparager of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and holds wrong view;
whereas other novices receive [the privilege of staying] two or three nights together with the monks..."

"He was suspended for not relinquishing his shared lodging; yet now he is gentle, humble in conduct, has entered into a sense of shame, is established in moral dread, has undergone the penalty, and confesses his transgression.
Does it please the Saṅgha to grant this novice the restoration of physical communion as before?"
Thus it should be stated three times. In this way, the formal act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) applies to reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), as well as to expulsion (*nissāraṇa*).
The shaving ceremony (*bhaṇḍukamma*) has already been explained in the commentary on the Mahākhandhaka. The "brahma-punishment" (*brahmadaṇḍa*) is indeed mentioned in the Pañcasatika-khandhaka.
Furthermore, this was not prescribed solely for Channa; it applies to any other monk who is talkative and frivolous.
If a monk dwells harassing, reviling, and mocking other monks with harsh words, a [penalty] should also be given to him.
And it should be given in this way: in the midst of the Saṅgha, a competent monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"Venerable sirs, the monk named so-and-so is talkative; he dwells harassing other monks with harsh words."
Thus, that bhikkhu may say whatever he wishes. The bhikkhus should neither speak to, nor exhort, nor instruct that bhikkhu named so-and-so. "Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha:
does the Saṅgha approve the imposition of the *brahmadaṇḍa* upon the bhikkhu named so-and-so? A second time I ask, and a third time I ask.
—“Venerable sirs, does the Saṅgha approve the granting of the brahma-penalty to the monk named so-and-so?

At a later time, when he has conducted himself properly and is asking for forgiveness, the brahma-penalty should be lifted. And it should be lifted in this way: a competent monk should announce it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha of monks imposed the brahma-penalty on the monk so-and-so; that monk has become gentle and humble in his conduct...”
"Having entered into a state of shame, established in moral dread, and standing in future restraint through reflection, I ask the Saṅgha, venerable sirs:
does the Saṅgha approve the lifting of the brahmadaṇḍa for that bhikkhu?
Having spoken thus up to three times, the brahmadaṇḍa is to be lifted by means of a formal act of notification (apalokanakamma) alone.
The fifth [offense] is characterized by action (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*). Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*:
“Now at that time, the group-of-six monks sprinkled the bhikkhunīs with muddy water, thinking, ‘Perhaps they will feel passion for us.
They exposed their bodies and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; they exposed their thighs and showed them to the bhikkhunīs...”
They show themselves by uncovering their private parts and showing them to the bhikkhunīs; they flash upon the bhikkhunīs;
they engage in intimate contact with the bhikkhunīs, thinking, "Perhaps they might become infatuated with us.
Having prescribed an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for those bhikkhus regarding these matters, [the Buddha said], "I allow you, monks, to carry out a disciplinary act against that bhikkhu. Then...
It occurred to those bhikkhunīs, "What disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma) should be performed? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should be made subject to the act of non-acknowledgment (avandiya-kamma) by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. Thus the act of non-acknowledgment was authorized;
that very fifth type of formal act (kamma), characterized by its specific procedure, is the basis for this present act of seeking permission (apalokana-kamma).
For in this case, the characteristic is the formal act (*kamma*) itself, not the restoration (*osāraṇā*) and so forth; therefore it is called "characterized by the formal act.
Its performance is explained in that very same place. Furthermore, in order to show it here in detail along with its pacification (*paṭippassaddhi*), we shall speak of it here as well:
with the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs assembled at the bhikkhunī quarters, by one who is competent...
The nun must announce:

“Venerable ladies, the venerable one named so-and-so behaves in a way that is displeasing to the nuns; I ask the Saṅgha of nuns for its consent to perform the act of non-prostration against this venerable one. Having announced this three times—“A second time...
a third time I ask the Saṅgha of nuns”—the act of non-prostration is to be carried out by means of a formal motion (*apalokana-kamma*).
From that time forth, that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the bhikkhunīs.
If, while not being saluted, he maintains a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing and conducts himself properly, he must ask the bhikkhunīs for forgiveness.

When asking for forgiveness, he should not go to the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling place, but rather, remaining in the monastery itself, he should approach the Saṅgha, a group, or a single bhikkhu, sit down on his heels, and [speak].
Having raised his joined palms, he should ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable sirs, reflecting upon this, I stand firm in restraint for the future;
I will not again appear unpleasing. May the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs forgive me.
Then, having sent a single bhikkhu from that Saṅgha or Gaṇa, or having gone himself, that one bhikkhu should speak to the bhikkhunīs as follows: "This..."
“Reflecting thus, the bhikkhu stands firm in restraint for the future; having confessed this transgression, he has asked the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha for forgiveness.
Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha grant him the status of one to be saluted. He is to be granted the status of one to be saluted. And it should be done in this way:
with the consent of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha assembled in the nunnery, an experienced bhikkhunī should announce:
“Venerable ladies, this venerable one named so-and-so was declared ‘not to be saluted’ by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs because he displayed what is unpleasing to them.
Having fallen into a state of shame, reflecting upon it, and established in restraint for the future, he confessed his transgression and asked forgiveness from the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
I ask the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs: does it please you that this venerable one be made to be saluted?”

It should be recited three times; thus, by means of this very *apalokana-kamma* (act of seeking permission), the one to be honored (*vandīya*) is to be appointed. This, however, is a determination of the characteristics of the formal act (*kamma-lakkhaṇa-vinicchaya*) even apart from the canonical text (*pāḷi*). For this characteristic of the formal act is indeed prescribed with reference to the community of bhikkhunīs, yet it is applicable to the community of bhikkhus as well. For that which [is done] by the community of bhikkhus at the places for voting-slips (*salākāgga*), the places for the distribution of food (*yāgagga*), the places for meals (*bhattagga*), and the places for the *uposatha* ceremony (*uposathagga*)— [The text continues:

...is also valid for the bhikkhunī-saṅgha. Furthermore, this formal act is not restricted solely to the bhikkhunīs; rather, it is established as a general rule for both saṅghas. Thus, even though the specific procedure was laid down for the bhikkhunīs, it is understood through the principle of extension (*atideśa*) that it applies equally to the bhikkhus. Therefore, when a bhikkhu is to be appointed as a *vandīya*, the formal act must be performed exactly as described, ensuring the validity of the *kamma*. This concludes the exposition on the characteristics of the formal act regarding the appointment of those to be honored.
One performs a *apalokanakamma* (act of seeking permission); this too is indeed a characteristic of formal legal acts (*kamma*).

For it is permissible to give robe-cloth after having assembled the Saṅgha and performed an *apalokanakamma*—announcing it up to three times—by a competent monk on behalf of those whose robes have been stolen, worn out, or lost.
However, regarding the distribution of small items for one making robes, [the procedure] is explained in the commentary to the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
The items such as needles and so forth, of the types already mentioned, may be given even without obtaining permission; in their giving, he alone is the master.
When giving anything beyond that, one must give after obtaining permission; for regarding the giving of what exceeds that, the Saṅgha is the owner.
Medicines for the sick of the kinds mentioned therein may also be given by oneself; if someone desires an excess, it should be given after obtaining permission.
Furthermore, for one who is weak, unable to maintain the postures, whose path for alms-gathering has been cut off, or who is severely ill, one should—
after performing an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*)— give him from the provisions available there in the great monasteries, either daily a *nāḷi* or half a *nāḷi*,
or even on a single day five or ten *nāḷis* of rice, provided he is a well-behaved monk.
From that specific source of income (tatruppāda), it is permissible to provide even a debt-obligation for a learned bhikkhu who carries out the burdens of the Saṅgha;

it is also permissible to provide unassigned lodgings for him, as well as food and wages for the kitchen assistants and others performing the Saṅgha’s business, by means of a formal act of authorization (apalokana-kamma).
It is also permissible to have a residence belonging to the Saṅgha maintained from that specific source of income given for the four requisites. "This bhikkhu..."

However, in order to prevent such talk as "he manages [the monastery] out of a sense of lordship," he should be made to look after the residence only after consulting the Saṅgha at the voting stick-counting or during an intermediate assembly.
He should also be made to look after the residence after obtaining the formal consent (*āpuccha*) regarding specific offerings given for the sake of robes and alms-food;
yet it is also permissible even without obtaining such consent. "This bhikkhu is indeed brave regarding robes and alms-food..."

Regarding the statement, “He has it look after the dwelling because it was given to him,” one should have the dwelling looked after by performing only a formal act of notification (*apalokana-kamma*) in order to cut off such idle talk.
When it comes to a cetiya, whether one is constructing a parasol, a railing, a Bodhi-house, or a seat-house that has not yet been built,
or repairing what is dilapidated, or performing plaster work, it is permissible to do so after having exhorted people to do it.
If there is no donor, it should be caused to be made from an offering deposited at a cetiya.

If there is no such deposit, it should be caused to be made from funds arising for that purpose after performing an act of consultation (*apalokanakamma*), even using property belonging to the Sangha. For it is permissible to perform work for a cetiya after consulting regarding property belonging to the Sangha;
however, it is not permissible to perform work for the Sangha after consulting regarding property belonging to a cetiya.
However, having taken it on a temporary basis, it is permissible to restore it to its original state.

Furthermore, for those performing plastering work and other such tasks at a cetiya who do not obtain enough for their livelihood from alms-round or from the Saṅgha, it is permissible to perform the duties while taking and consuming what is sufficient for their livelihood from the property of the cetiya. [The duties]...

"One should not prepare a meal for the Saṅgha with fish, meat, and so forth. Regarding fruit trees planted in the monastery that have been formally accepted by the Saṅgha and receive the duty of cultivation—the fruits of which they distribute and consume after striking a bell—no formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) need be performed for them.

A formal act of seeking permission (apalokanakamma) should be performed. That may indeed be done at the head of the voting sticks, at the head of the procession, at the head of the meal, or at an intermediate gathering;

however, it is certainly appropriate at the Uposatha hall. For there, the consent and purity of mind of even those who have not arrived are brought forward, and thus that [act] becomes thoroughly purified.
And it should be done in this way: an experienced monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha of monks, should announce:

"Venerable sirs, whatever belongs to the Saṅgha in this monastery within the boundary—roots, bark, leaves, sprouts, flowers, fruits, fresh food, and so forth—it is pleasing to the Saṅgha that all of this may be used at will by whichever monks arrive."
"I ask you," he should say, and this must be asked three times.

What is performed by four or five bhikkhus is indeed well-performed. In a monastery where two or three people reside, even what is done by them sitting together is just like what is done by the Saṅgha. However, in a monastery where there is only one bhikkhu, by him—

When a bhikkhu has performed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks on the Uposatha day and sits down, even the observance of the agreed-upon practice (*katikavatta*) becomes exactly as if it were performed by the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, while performing it, he may do so according to a rotation of results, or by delimiting it for four months, six months, or one year.
It is permissible to do so even without making a formal delimitation. Once a delimitation has been made, one may use the area as delimited, and it must then be re-dedicated.
If no delimitation was made, it remains permissible for as long as the trees stand.
Even if other trees are planted from the seeds of those original trees, the same agreement applies to them as well.
If, however, they were planted in another monastery, the Saṅgha is the owner of them in that very monastery where they were planted.
Even those which were brought from elsewhere and planted later in the original monastery, a separate agreement (katikā) must be made regarding them.
Once the agreement has been made, they remain in the status of private property; it is permissible to enjoy their fruits and so forth as one pleases.
If, however, they enclose various areas there and construct monastic cells (*pariveṇa*) and maintain them, those [trees] stand in the private domain of those monks.
Others do not receive permission to use them; rather, they may be used by giving a tenth part to the Saṅgha.
The same rule applies even to one who protects a tree in the middle of the monastery by surrounding it with branches.
When a venerable monk who is worthy of respect has gone to an ancient monastery, people bring various fruits, thinking, "The Elder has arrived.

If a learned monk who masters the entire scriptural tradition (pariyatti) has resided there from the very beginning, one should consume [the fruits] without scruple, thinking, "Surely a long-standing agreement must have been made here. This applies even to alms-collecting monks regarding the fruits in the monastery.

It is permissible; it does not violate the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). When novices give many fruits to their own teachers and preceptors, other monks who do not receive any may become critical; this is merely a matter of criticism.
However, if there is a famine, even sixty people might live depending on a single jackfruit tree; in such a case...
At the proper time, for the sake of gathering everyone together, it should be divided and eaten; this is the proper course.
However, as long as the formal agreement (*katikavatta*) has not been rescinded, what they have eaten is indeed well-eaten. When, then, is the formal agreement rescinded?
When the harmonious Saṅgha, having assembled, proclaims: "From now on, let them eat after dividing [the food]. In the case of a monastery with only one monk...
However, even if one person recites [the formula] in the monastery, the previous agreement is indeed suspended. If, once the agreement has been suspended,
the novices neither cause [fruits] to fall from the trees nor take them from the ground and give them to the monks,
but instead wander about striking fallen fruits with their feet, then the compensation for them shall be calculated starting from one-tenth up to half of the portion of fruit.
It must be done. Surely, out of greed for a test of their service, they will bring [the fruit] and give it.

Later, when a time of plenty has arisen and the *kappiyakāraka*s (those who prepare what is allowable) have arrived, having performed the trimming of branches and so forth while guarding the trees, no test of service should be given to the novices;
rather, [the fruit] should be distributed and consumed.
“There is fruit and fruit in the monastery. People from the surrounding villages come for the sake of the sick or for pregnant women and request, “Give us a coconut;
give us a mango; give us a breadfruit. Should it be given or should it not be given? It should be given.
For if it is not given, they become dejected; however, by the one who gives it, the Saṅgha should be assembled.

After having announced it up to three times and performed a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*), it should be given; or else, having established a formal agreement (*katikavatta*), it should be set aside.
And this is how it should be done: a competent monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"People from the neighboring villages come and request various fruits for the sake of the sick and others; [we shall give] two coconut fruits."
"Taking two palm fruits, two jackfruit, five mangoes, and five plantains is not forbidden;
taking fruit from such-and-such trees and such-and-such trees is not forbidden—this is pleasing to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
This should be stated three times.
From that time on, when asking for things such as medicine for the sick by mentioning their names, one should not say, "Take [this]," but rather the proper conduct (*vatta*) should be explained thus:

"For those who take coconuts and so forth within this specific limit, and for those who take fruit from such-and-such a tree and such-and-such a tree, no prohibition has been made. However, after having investigated, [if one sees] "This..."

Nor should one say, "The mangoes are sweet; take them from here. However, when those who have come at the time of distributing the fruit arrive, half the portion should be given by one who has been authorized;
by one who is not authorized, it should be given after seeking permission.

Or, if someone whose provisions are exhausted, or a caravan leader traveling on the road, or any other superior person arrives and requests [the fruit], one must likewise give it only after seeking permission.
It should be given. One who has seized it by force and is eating it should not be stopped; for being angry, he might even cut down trees or cause other harm.
When he comes to a private dwelling (pariveṇa) and begs from the village for the sake of the sick person, he should be told:
"This was planted by us for the sake of shade and such; if there is any, you know that yourselves. However, if they are already laden with fruit...
There are trees; having tied thorns [around them], they eat the fruit by turns. One should give without expecting anything in return.
One who takes [the fruit] by force should not be stopped; the reason for this is exactly what was stated previously.
If there is a fruit grove belonging to the Saṅgha that receives no maintenance, and if someone maintains it under the pretext of performing their duties...

It belongs to the Saṅgha alone. Furthermore, if the Saṅgha entrusts the responsibility to a capable bhikkhu, saying, "Good man, look after this [robe] and give it back," and he looks after it under the pretext of observing the proper conduct (*vatta*), then in this case too it belongs to the Saṅgha alone.
However, for one who expects a reward (*phātikamma*), a reward should be given either by a third part or by a half. "It is burdensome..."

Having said, "It is [the result of] kamma," if he is still unwilling with that much alone, one should say: "Make it all your own property and take care of it after giving me a tenth part as the root-fee.
However, because it is a valuable article (*garubhaṇḍa*), it must not be given away by way of cutting off the root.
He, having paid the root-fee and while consuming [the fruit], whether he has made his dwelling or not, or having maintained the dwelling, [should do so].

He hands over the monastery to those who are dependent on it; they too must give the share belonging to the root. But when the monks are themselves capable of maintaining it, then they should not be given the duty of maintenance, nor should they be prevented while they are maintaining it;
rather, they should be prevented at the very time [before] they begin the maintenance. "You have consumed much; do not maintain it now. Only the Saṅgha of monks..."
One should say, "He will look after it.

However, if there is no one looking after it by way of duty, nor by way of personal effort, and the Saṅgha is not able to look after it, then one person may, without asking permission, look after it himself;
having increased his personal effort, he expects [the Saṅgha] to perform the act of formal authorization (apalokanakamma) for that personal effort.
Having increased [the number], it should be given. Thus, all of this constitutes the characteristic of a formal act (*kamma*).
The act of information (*apalokanakamma*) proceeds through these five bases.

However, regarding the classification of the bases for the act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), [it begins]: "Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs: such-and-such a person [of] such-and-such a venerable one..."
"One who desires full ordination has been instructed by me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let it be said:
'Let such-and-such a person come'; he should be told, 'Come. This is the formal admission (*osāraṇā*) of one desiring full ordination;
this is what is called "admission. "Venerable sirs, let my words be heard: this monk named So-and-so is a preacher of the Dhamma, yet neither the Sutta nor..."
There is no Suttavibhaṅga; failing to discern the meaning, he obstructs the meaning by means of the shadow of the phrasing.

"Venerable sirs, if it seems appropriate to you, let us have the monk named so-and-so expelled and we shall settle this legal issue"—this is what is called the "expulsion" of a monk who is a Dhamma-preacher in a formal decision by a committee (*ubbāhikāvinicchaya*).

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha. A motion (*ñatti*) established in this manner by way of the Uposatha procedure is called the Uposatha.

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth day. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā. A motion established in this manner by way of the Pavāraṇā procedure is called the Pavāraṇā.
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. So-and-so desires ordination from the venerable so-and-so. If...
“It is appropriate for the Saṅgha that I should instruct so-and-so. “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, let so-and-so instruct so-and-so.
“If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, I would question so-and-so regarding the obstructive states. “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, let so-and-so [question] so-and-so...”
“[The proposer] should ask about obstructive matters. “If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I would ask such-and-such a person about the Vinaya.
“If it is timely for the Saṅgha, such-and-such a person may ask such-and-such a person about the Vinaya.
“If it is timely for the Saṅgha, being asked by such-and-such a person about the Vinaya, I would answer. “If...”

"It is appropriate for the Saṅgha that such-and-such a person, when questioned on the Vinaya by such-and-such a person, should answer"—this motion (*ñatti*) established to authorize oneself or another is called an authorization (*sammuti*).
"Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: this robe-cloth, which is to be forfeited by the monk so-and-so, belongs to the Saṅgha."
“Relinquished. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so.
“If it seems appropriate to the Venerable Ones, may the Venerable Ones give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so.
In this way, the giving of robes, bowls, and so forth that have been relinquished is called “giving.”
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so remembers an offense; he discloses it, makes it plain, and confesses it.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I shall receive the confession of the offense of the monk named so-and-so.
Venerable sirs, if it seems appropriate to you, I shall [receive] the offense of the monk named so-and-so...”
“...should accept it. He should be addressed with: “Do you see it? “Yes, I see it. “You should exercise restraint in the future”—this is what is called the acceptance of an offense.
“Let the venerable residents listen to me. If it is the right time for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha.”
“Let us recite the Pātimokkha now, and let us perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony when the dark fortnight arrives.

If those monks who are quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, fond of strife, and creators of legal issues in the Saṅgha should remain there until that dark fortnight, a competent and capable resident monk should inform the resident monks: “Listen to me, friends...”
"Venerable residents of this monastery, if it is convenient for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha;
we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the following full moon. This is how the postponement of the Pavāraṇā is carried out; such is called "postponement.
Everyone must assemble together in one place, and having assembled, the Saṅgha [should be addressed] by a learned and competent monk.
He should inform [the Saṅgha]: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
While we have been living in a state of quarreling, disputing, and contending, we have habitually practiced much that is unbecoming of a recluse, speaking and uttering such things.
If we were to deal with one another for these offenses, this legal issue might lead to harshness, violence, and schism."

"If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha settle this legal issue by means of the 'covering over as with grass,' setting aside grave offenses and setting aside matters connected with householders"— this motion,
made by means of the settlement through "covering over as with grass," is called the "all-inclusive motion" which constitutes the formal characteristic of the legal act (*kamma*).

Likewise, following that, by taking one from each of the subsequent groups, there are two motions (*ñatti*). Thus, the ninth [type of] formal act (*kamma*)—which has the characteristics of a formal act—is the reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and the expulsion (*nissāraṇa*) according to the aforementioned classifications, and it pertains to these nine points.

Regarding the classification of formal acts consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), the expulsion mentioned in the *Khandhaka* on account of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi’s overturning of his bowl should be understood; likewise, the reinstatement mentioned on account of his righting of that same bowl should be understood.

Also, the authorization of the boundary (*sīmāsammuti*), the authorization for not being separated from the three robes (*ticīvarena avippavāsasammuti*), and the authorization for the rug (*santhatasammuti*).

"Formal authorization" (sammuti) should be understood by way of these formal authorizations: the appointment of the distributor of meals, the assigner of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the apportioner of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, the distributor of hard foods, the dispenser of minor requisites, the assigner of bathing cloths, the assigner of almsbowls, the appointer of monastery attendants, and the appointer of novices.
"Giving" (dāna) should be understood by way of the giving of the *kaṭhina* robe-material and the giving of robe-material as a legacy.

"Lifting" (uddhāra) should be understood by way of the lifting of the *kaṭhina*. "Instruction" (desanā) should be understood by way of the instruction regarding the site for a hut and the site for a monastery.

It should be understood as follows: regarding the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass) method of settling a dispute, after setting aside three motions—namely, the all-inclusive motion and one motion for each of the two sides—two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*) accompanied by a motion (*ñattidutiya*) are then uttered, one for each side.
By means of these, the characteristic of the legal act (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*) is to be understood. Thus.
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) pertains to these seven grounds.

Regarding the classification of formal acts consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), however, "expulsion" (*nissāraṇā*) should be understood in terms of the seven formal acts beginning with the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*), and "reinstatement" (*osāraṇā*) should be understood in terms of the suspension of those very same formal acts. [The category of] "authorization as an instructor of bhikkhunīs" (*bhikkhunovādakasammuti*)...
The formal agreement (*sammuti*) is to be understood [in this context]. The granting [of penance] is to be understood by way of the granting of the *parivāsa* (probation) and the *mānatta* (penance).

The disciplinary action is to be understood by way of the act of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya-paṭikassana-kamma*). The formal admonition is to be understood by way of these eleven types of admonitions: the eight cases of one who follows a suspended monk, and the three cases of "up to the third time" involving Ariṭṭha and Caṇḍakāḷī; these are the "up to the third time" cases.
Furthermore, the characteristic of a formal act (*kamma*) should be understood by way of the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) and the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*).

Thus, a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) proceeds through these seven points. 497. Thus, [the treatise has dealt with] the formal acts, the failure of formal acts, and the determination of the grounds for those formal acts that are free from failure.

Having thus shown [the nature of the acts], he now states "in an act performed by a quorum of four" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the specific definition of the Saṅgha who performs those acts.
Its meaning should be understood in the same manner as was explained in the commentary on the failure of the act (*kamma-vipatti*) regarding the assembly.
The commentary on the Chapter on Acts (*Kammavagga*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on the Eight Benefits (Atthavasavagga), etc., 498.

Now, in order to show the advantage in the promulgation of those training rules which serve as the basis for those [offenses], the passage beginning with “relying on two benefits” is commenced. Therein, regarding those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*):
"For the restraint of enmities" means for the purpose of restraining—that is, closing off—the five kinds of enmities pertaining to the present life, such as the taking of life and so forth.

"For the warding off of enmities pertaining to future lives" means for the purpose of warding off—that is, for the purpose of cutting off and ensuring the non-arising of—enmities pertaining to future lives, which consist of the suffering of karmic results. [And] for the faults pertaining to the present life...
"For the sake of restraint" means for the purpose of restraining those very five kinds of enmity. "Faults pertaining to future lives" refers to the suffering of their ripening (vipāka).
For it is precisely these sufferings of ripening that are called "faults" (*vajja*) here, in the sense that they are to be avoided.
"Terrors pertaining to the present life" refers to censure, defamation, acts such as condemnation (*tajjanīyakamma*), and [exclusion from] the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies.

"Setting aside" refers to the formal act (kamma) that reveals one's lack of integrity; these are called "fears pertaining to the present life," and [the restraint] is for the purpose of guarding against them.
As for the "fears pertaining to future lives," they are simply the suffering of karmic results, and [the restraint] is for the purpose of warding them off.
"Of unwholesome states pertaining to the present life" means for the purpose of guarding against unwholesome states, which are divided into the five crimes and the ten courses of unwholesome action.

Furthermore, unwholesome states pertaining to future lives are called "suffering in its ripening" in the sense that they are not to be endured; [the rule was laid down] for the purpose of warding them off.
"Out of compassion for householders" means for the sake of showing compassion by way of protecting the faith of those living as laypeople.

"For the purpose of cutting off the faction of those with evil desires" means for the purpose of breaking up the communal bonds of individuals who have evil desires; thus was the training rule on group meals established.
It has been laid down. The rest is clear everywhere. Whatever might need to be said here has all already been stated in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) by way of their purpose is finished.
499. Regarding the *Pātimokkha* and so forth, the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* is fivefold for monks and fourfold for nuns.

Regarding "the act of reinstatement (osāraṇīya) is prescribed for the granting of probation (parivāsa), etc.": this means that for one who is observing either the eighteen or the forty-three duties, the act of reinstatement is prescribed.
The meaning is that the formal act (kamma) by which one is reinstated is what is prescribed. Regarding "the act of banishment (nissāraṇīya) is prescribed":
this means that the formal act by which those who cause quarrels and so forth are banished is what is prescribed.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Unproclaimed" (*apaññatte*): "Proclaimed" (*paññatta*) refers to that which was proclaimed by someone in the interval between the time when the seven classes of offenses had not yet been proclaimed—excluding the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—and the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha [Gotama].
The narrative concerning the training rule regarding the monkey and so forth is called "subsequently proclaimed" (*anupaññatta*) once a training rule has already been proclaimed.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Chapter on Benefits (Ānisaṃsavagga) is finished. 501.
Now, in order to show the ninefold classification of all the training rules (sikkhāpada) according to each individual aspect, he said: “Nine classifications,” and so forth.

In this context, "inclusion by way of subject matter" (*vatthusaṅgaha*) means inclusion by means of the subject matter. The meaning of the term should be understood in the same way for the remaining cases as well. Here, however, is the construction of the meaning:
since there is not even a single training rule (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed without a subject matter, all [rules] are included by way of their subject matter;
thus, first of all, "inclusion by way of subject matter" is to be understood.
Since two classes of offenses are included under failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), five classes of offenses under failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*),
and six training rules under failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*), all of them are thus included within failure;
in this way, the inclusion by way of failure should be understood.

Since there is not even a single training rule that is free from the seven types of offenses, all [rules] are thus comprised within offenses; this is how the compendium of offenses is to be understood.
Since all [rules] were laid down in the seven cities, they are thus comprised within the introductory narratives (nidāna); this is how the compendium of narratives is to be understood.

Since there is not even a single training rule laid down in the absence of an individual who has transgressed, all [rules] are thus comprised within the individual (puggala); this is how the compendium of individuals is to be understood.
Furthermore, all [offenses] are comprised within the five and seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*);

all arise without exception through the six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), and thus they are comprised by way of their origin. All are comprised within the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) as the issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
And all reach their settlement through the seven methods of settling disputes (*samatha*); thus, they are comprised by way of their settlement.

They are included. In this way, the inclusion of the aggregates (*khandha*), origination (*samuṭṭhāna*), legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), and methods of settling disputes (*samatha*) should also be understood here.
The remainder is exactly as explained previously.
[End of] the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Nine Who Are Not Included is finished.
And the word-by-word commentary on the difficult points of the Parivāra is finished.
Concluding Remarks.
And to this extent— the Lord,
training those to be trained, has taught the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is analyzed into the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra.
The commentary named *Saṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Samantapāsādikā*, is completed with a text of approximately twenty-seven thousand [verses]. Herein,
regarding the all-encompassing clarity (*samantapāsādikatta*) of this *Samantapāsādikā*:
From the lineage of teachers, from the illumination of the origins, the bases, and the classifications;
from the avoidance of other systems, and from the purification of one's own system.
From the clarification of the phrasing, from the meaning of the words, and from the sequence of the connection of the texts;
Because it provides a definitive determination of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), because it demonstrates the various methods of analysis (*vibhaṅga*),
and because nothing unpleasing is seen here by those who perceive clearly,
this work is therefore called the *Samantapāsādikā* ("Completely Pleasing") to the wise.
The commentary on the Vinaya, which was spoken by the Lord of the World out of compassion for the world, has been set forth by one skilled in training those to be trained.
Both the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Mahā-paccarī*...
And the *Kuruṇḍi*: these are the three Sinhalese commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Having heard them in the presence of the elder named Buddhamitta, who was renowned, illustrious, wise, and an expert in the Vinaya.
In the Mahāmegha forest grove, situated upon a level stretch of ground,
stands the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra) of the Teacher, adorned by the Great Bodhi tree.
To its southern side is the supreme House of Exertion (Padhānaghara).
It is frequented by the Saṅgha of monks who possess virtuous conduct.
Born of a noble family, he is always a supporter of the Saṅgha;
with unshakable faith, he is devoted to the Triple Gem.
There, the one known as Mahānigamasāmī had constructed a delightful palace, adorned with beautiful ramparts,
endowed with trees providing cool shade, and possessing abundant reservoirs of water.
While residing there in the palace of the lord of the great city,
[the commentary] was undertaken and successfully completed by one who had dedicated it to the Elder named Buddhasiri, who was pure in virtue and conduct.
While King Sirinivāsa, whose fame was glorious protection, was safeguarding the entire island of Laṅkā for twenty years without blemish,
in this peaceful year of victory, the twentieth—
In the twenty-first year, when it had arrived,
the calamities in the family and the world were brought to an end.
Since this [kingdom] was free from calamity, it reached its conclusion within just a single year.
Thus, for the whole world, may all undertakings connected with the Dhamma proceed swiftly and without any obstacle. By me,
in composing this for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma—
By the power of all the merit that has been accumulated through great reverence for the true Dhamma,
may all living beings become partakers of the flavor of the true Dhamma under the Dhamma-King.
"May the True Dhamma endure for long! May the rains fall in season, and may the people live long!
May the deity satisfy them with justice, and may the king protect the earth!
[Thus it was written] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, gentleness, and humility.

[He was] a great poet, the foremost of debaters who spoke with logic and eloquence; one endowed with the analytical power of wisdom capable of penetrating and fathoming both his own tradition and the traditions of others;
possessed of unimpeded radiance of knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation—the Three Pitakas with their commentaries—as divided into the various branches of study;

adorned with the excellence of the fourfold analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) and the various qualities such as the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā), which were embellished by the perfection of his speech—sweet, noble, and flowing forth from the bliss produced by the mastery of his craft.

This *Samantapāsādikā*, a commentary on the Vinaya, was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— so called by his teachers— a jewel of the lineage of the Elders who dwell at the Mahāvihāra, who were lamps of the Elder tradition and possessed minds firmly established in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), and who was endowed with vast and purified intelligence, serving as an ornament to that lineage.
May he remain as long as possible in the world for those seeking to cross over the world,
showing the way to noble sons regarding the purification of virtue—
so long as even the name "Buddha" exists for that Pure-minded One, the Tathāgata.
"In this world, the Great Seer acts for the World-Supreme One.
Thus ends the Commentary on the Vinaya named Samantapāsādikā.
